articles.title: Jordan attacks militants in Syria in retaliation for last week’s church attack
articles.summary:
Jordanian air force says it carried out strikes against ‘terrorist groups’ tied to killing of nine in Karak

Jordan has carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation for…

blocks.text: Jordan has carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation for Friday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Jordanian city of Karak that killed nine people, the Jordanian air force has said in a statement.

It said the operation “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”. It did not specify who the groups were or the precise location of the strikes.

Syrian state media reported that civilians had been killed in the strikes. The director of health in the southern province of Daraa, where the strikes took place, told the Syrian national news agency, Sana, that at least five civilians had been killed, including women and children and a 65-year-old man.

Jordan’s armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus, but Syria’s government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the ⁠Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas.

Earlier Monday, Jordanian authorities arrested three men for last week’s attack, which also wounded more than two dozen people. The arrests followed a dawn shootout, and all three men were wounded, officials said.
The attack struck the Greek Orthodox church during a funeral in Karak, about 55 miles (90km) south of the capital, Amman, on Friday. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.
The attack shocked the nation, and Jordan declared three days of mourning for the victims. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack; the attackers’ motive remained unknown.

Later on Monday, Jordan’t Public Security Directorate identified the three arrested men as brothers Hazzah Zaidan Mohammad and Mishal Zaidan Mohammad, and their brother-in-law Ahmad Sami Hussein. All three are Jordanian; they were taken into custody in Karak, south of Amman.
The agency’s chief described the gunmen as “takfiri,” a term used for Sunni militants, but said they were not tied to any organised group.

“They only represent themselves,” Maj Gen Obaidallah Abd Rabbo Al-Maayta told a news conference. He also said a large cache of munitions was found in the abandoned house where Jordanian forces apprehended the men.
Jordan’s interior minister, Mazen al-Faraya, said the attack by the three men was the result of “a terroristic, extremist way of thinking”.
“If this way of thinking is not resolved, we will see incidents like this again,” he told reporters.
Jordan’s King Abdullah II had ordered authorities to respond with “an iron fist” against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.
“We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he said in a statement on Monday.
Relatives of the victims said the arrests brought them some relief.

“Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief, and the grief of the Jordanian people – not just for us, the families of the martyrs,” Khaled al-Borqan, himself a survivor of the attack and a relative of three of the people killed, told Al-Mamlaka.
“Despite the sadness and pain, the news brought us joy,” Fares Halaseh, an uncle of one of the victims and a survivor of the attack, told the TV station.
But the pain remains, he added. “We will not forget this agony for years to come.”

articles.title: The U.S. put surveillance drones in the Great Lakes, and this border town mayor isn't happy
articles.summary: When Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley first spotted an unusual, unmanned vessel in the St. Clair River, he says he thought it looked "like something from Mars." Then he found out it was one of…

image.caption: Sarnia Mayor Mike Bradley says he was not informed about plans for the U.S. Coast Guard to put drones on the Great Lakes. (CBC News)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New

When Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley first spotted an unusual, unmanned vessel in the St. Clair River, he says he thought it looked "like something from Mars." Then he found out it was one of several surveillance sail drones deployed to the Great Lakes this summer by the U.S. Coast Guard.
'We have thousands of boaters,' says Sarnia, Ont., mayor. 'They're going to be photographed and watched'
When Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley first spotted an unusual, unmanned vessel in the St. Clair River, he says he thought it looked "like something from Mars."

Then he found out it was one of several surveillance sail drones deployed to the Great Lakes this summer by the U.S. Coast Guard to "gather critical weather data for emergency response planning, track illicit activity and keep maritime borders safe."
The U.S. Coast Guard, which operates under the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, told CBC in June the vessels aren't there to surveil Canadians. But Bradley isn't convinced.
"We have thousands of boaters on the river St. Clair, Lake Huron, Lake Erie, and now they're going to be photographed and watched," he told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.

"Even though they're saying right now it's benign, I don't have the trust down the road, especially with the rapidly deteriorating relationship with the U.S., that they won't use it for other purposes."
CBC has reached out to the U.S. and Canadian Coast Guards for comment. Both said they could not respond by deadline.
LISTEN | Interview with Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley :
As It Happens7:00Sarnia, Ont., mayor speaks out against U.S. surveillance drones in the Great Lakes
The vessels are called Voyager unmanned surface vehicles, and each one is affixed with 360-degree high-resolution cameras, advanced radar, and automatic identification systems.
They are owned and operated by Saildrone, a private U.S. company whose $15.5-million US contract with the Coast Guard is funded by U.S. President Donald Trump's "One Big, Beautiful Bill."

“This Voyager fleet will help the Coast Guard maintain persistent, scalable maritime domain awareness across these expansive waters, identifying threats in real time and enabling focused, high-impact interdiction," Saildrone president John Mustin said in a press release.
The U.S. Coast Guard now has two sail drones on Lake Erie as a part of a new program that launched in May. (U.S. Coast Guard)
York University researcher Petra Molnar says Canadians should be concerned that this data is being collected by a private company and sold to the U.S. government.

“This is a very troubling arrangement from a privacy and accountability standpoint," Molnar, the author of The Walls Have Eyes: Surviving Migration in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, told the Guardian newspaper.

"We have very little public information about data retention, who can access what data is collected, or how people using the region recreationally [can] be swept up in a data system built for border enforcement.”
Saildrone did not respond to requests for comment from CBC.

items: On America's northern border, the threats are not unidirectional
U.S. claims about higher drug trafficking from Canada don't match the data: fentanyl czar

blocks.text: The U.S. Coast Guard has said drones are nothing for Canadians to worry about.

"They're just out there for awareness," Lt. Junior Grade Samuel Rodriguez Garcia told CBC Windsor in June, when the vessels were deployed in Lake Erie. "Think of them as mobile cameras that kind of help us gain a better insight into what's going on live on scene."
He said the vessels' cameras are monitored 24/7 by U.S. Coast Guard staff, who can also manually move the drones when necessary. But the footage isn't recorded, officials say.
U.S. and Canadian agencies, including law enforcement, could have access to the drone technology after going through the proper channels, he said.
The Canadian Coast Guard told CBC Windsor it works closely with its U.S. counterpart, but has no involvement with the drone sail program.
Mayor says he was left in the dark
The U.S. Coast Guard first announced the Voyager project in May in a press release issued by the U.S. Department of War.
But Bradley says this is the first he's heard of it.
In fact, he says he only learned what the vessel in the St. Clair River was when he was contracted by the Detroit News, which has been reporting on the drones.
As mayor of the largest city on Lake Huron, he says being kept in the dark is unacceptable.
"If the Canadian government knew and agreed to it, that, to me, is a big issue," he said. "They should have let Canadian cities, Canadian mayors, know that this was happening."
CBC reached out to Public Safety Canada for information about the drones, and was redirected to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA).
The CBSA did not respond to questions about Bradley's concerns, saying the RCMP is responsible for "enforcing Canadian legislation between ports of entry, including on the water."
The U.S. Coast Guard sail drones will be deployed in Lake Erie and be pulled from the water once ice forms. (U.S. Coast Guard)
Bradley says it's no coincidence the project comes during a period of heightened tension between Canada and the U.S.
With both countries locked in an impasse in the trade war, Trump and other Republicans have repeatedly framed the Canadian border as a dangerous security threat.
However, the numbers tell a different story. A U.S. Border Patrol officials told Congress in June that drug seizures and arrests of undocumented immigrants are both down along the U.S-Canada border.

items: Detroit tourism bureau halts advertising in Canada amid trade war, hopes Canadians won't 'hold grudge'
Searches of cellphones, laptops by U.S. customs up more than 32% so far this year

blocks.text: Bradley called the drones "an answer to a problem that doesn't really exist." He called on the Canadian government to "show some backbone" and push back.
"The Elbows Up movement seems to have died away, and I was a big supporter of that because I know the American psyche so well from 40 years of dealing with them," he said.
"If you don't stand up or push back they will just walk all over you."
Interview with Mike Bradley produced by Chris Trowbridge

articles.title: Brazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passports
articles.summary:
Far-right senator banned from leaving country as supreme court judge’s ruling makes reference to money-laundering case

The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil…

blocks.text: The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil and ordered to surrender his passports just hours after his dramatic loss in the presidential election to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The ruling was issued by supreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same justice who oversaw the trial of the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for attempting a coup.
Bolsonaro posted a video saying the decision was based on an interview his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, gave last Friday urging his brother to leave Brazil if he lost the election.

The brief ruling, however, only refers to a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over his possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme. The ruling orders him not to have any contact with his friend Willer Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were being used to launder about £680m.
It also cancelled all of Bolsonaro’s passports, including the diplomatic one he holds as a congressman, and ordered him to hand them over within 24 hours.
Bolsonaro was the first to speak publicly about the matter, before Brazilian media were even aware of the judge’s decision.

In a video posted on social media, he said he had just left a visit to his father, who is under house arrest in Brasília, when “Lula’s federal police were at his door and in the middle of the street, and I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also prohibited from leaving the country”.
He added that, although his brother – who is in self-imposed exile in the US – told a US podcast on Friday that he favoured the senator leaving Brazil if he lost the election, “I never said that”.
When his Senate term ends early next year, Bolsonaro will be out of public office for the first time in 24 years, and therefore without the special jurisdiction afforded to officeholders.

He is under investigation in another criminal case, too, over what happened to the £20m he was captured on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father.
Like Jair Bolsonaro four years ago, the senator has still not conceded defeat to Lula.

The Folha de S.Paulo newspaper also reported that Flávio Bolsonaro had been persuaded to drop his plan to seek to annul the election, which he had announced after the result was declared on Sunday night.

Bolsonaro had claimed that the two-hour extension of voting – intended to allow voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport to cast their ballots – had harmed the election, despite the fact that his own campaign had also argued for an extension.
According to the newspaper, allies and lawyers told him his argument was legally weak.

Bolsonaro had still not publicly reversed his demand for an annulment, and in the same video he said he would file another case to have Lula’s ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of economic power, a similar case to others his legal team brought during the campaign.

articles.title: British politicians among international delegates barred from entering West Bank
articles.summary:
Group was on visit to meet Palestinian children, farmers and civil leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forces

An international delegation including British politicians has been…

blocks.text: An international delegation including British politicians has been barred from entering the West Bank on a trip to meet Palestinian children, farmers and society leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forces during olive harvest season.

The delegation of 23 people, including four elected representatives, was drawn from countries including France, Spain, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Greece, Holland, Ireland and the US. It included Clive Lewis, MP for Norwich South, Lara Bird, MP for the Scottish National party, Kate Nevens, MSP for the Scottish Green party and Sam Tarry, a former Labour MP.

Lewis told the Guardian: “We were detained, taken aside and then interrogated. I use the word interrogated because people were shouted at. We were asked why we were going in, what was happening, why our stories were one way or the other. The bottom line was it was a deeply unpleasant experience.”

The delegates were set to participate in Progressive International’s Second Ramallah Congress, a gathering to oppose Israeli occupation in Palestine. The congress was organised by Progressive International in partnership with Birzeit University and includes a programme of meetings with Palestinian academics, students and civil society organisations.

Tarry told the Guardian that he thought the delegation had a “genuine chance of going across” into the West Bank but they were detained at the Allenby/King Hussein Bridge by Israeli forces in Jordan for nine hours. “They made a political decision very clearly based on the fact they didn’t want people to witness what’s been going on in the West Bank, especially ahead of the elections,” he added.

The exclusions occurred amid attacks by Israeli forces on Palestinian olive farmers and foreign press and activists in the region. International travel to parts of the West Bank is permitted but subject to military checkpoints. Earlier this month, Israeli media reported that the defence minister, Israel Katz, had instructed officials to pursue exclusion orders against activists accompanying Palestinian olive harvesters.

In the first two weeks of October, the UN aid coordination office recorded at least 160 Israeli settler attacks linked to the olive harvest, often under the protection or with the participation of Israeli forces.

Israeli forces attacked European diplomats and a French mayor accompanying Palestinian farmers, and about 80 olive-harvest volunteers, including US congressional candidate Brad Lander, were also recently detained.
Bird said in a statement: “I came to stand alongside Palestinians being attacked for harvesting olives on their own land. Instead, we were turned away at the border with no reason given.

“It is more important now than ever that we bear witness and show our solidarity. But we were prevented from doing so. If Israel has nothing to hide, why is it so determined to stop us seeing what is happening in the Occupied West Bank?”

Laila Hazaineh, a political coordinator for Progressive International, said in a statement: “Despite escalating violence, our delegation remained determined to cross to Palestine to participate in the olive harvest, and actively engage with Palestinian communities and institutions. Every refusal of entry will only strengthen this determination.”
The embassy of Israel has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Ex-South Carolina governors endorse Democrat Annie Andrews in Senate race
articles.summary:
Republican and Democrat come together for a rare joint endorsement of candidate in unexpected competitive race

Two South Carolina former governors, David Beasley and Jim Hodges, a Republican…

blocks.text: Two South Carolina former governors, David Beasley and Jim Hodges, a Republican and Democrat respectively, have come together for a rare joint endorsement for Democrat Annie Andrews’s Senate bid.

Andrews, a pediatrician, is looking to flip the seat, currently held by Darline Graham, the Trump-endorsed sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham, in what has become an unexpectedly competitive race for the usually reliably red state.

“This country is too divided, and the political rhetoric has gotten way, way out of hand,” says Beasley in the former governors’ joint endorsement video. “That’s why we’re coming together to support Annie Andrews,” says Hodges.
The two former governors, who once faced off against each other, acknowledged that while they don’t agree on everything, they agree on Andrews as the best candidate to put South Carolina first.
“Annie understands that leadership isn’t about making people angrier. Well, it’s about making things better,” says Beasley. “She’s willing to put people ahead of politics,” adds Hodges.
Beasley adds: “We may have served as your governor from different political parties. But we agree South Carolina deserves better than more of the same political fighting.”

Last week, Beasley, a Democrat-turned-Republican who served as governor of the Palmetto State from 1995 to 1999 before losing re-election to Hodges, wrote an opinion piece for the Charleston-based Post and Courier paper, lamenting the state of the party under Donald Trump.

“What has happened in the Republican Party today is just heartbreaking,” he wrote. “Too many in the party have gone along with winning by tearing others down and pitting people and communities against one another … I have yet to see President Donald Trump, as leader of the Republican Party, show compassion or even respect to someone or some group that he disagrees with.
“The vitriol is toxic, and it is undeniably feeding into the hearts, minds and souls of Americans.”
It is “not the party that I knew, and it is not the party that I consider myself a member of”, he added.

Recent polling has indicated that Graham still holds a lead over Andrews, though the nonpartisan Cook Political Report has moved the state in the Democrats’ direction, from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican”.

And it isn’t the only time in this year’s midterms that prominent Republicans have crossed party lines and backed Democrats. In usually deep-red Kansas, two former Republican governors, Bill Graves and Mike Hayden, endorsed the Democratic candidate, Adam Hamilton, in his bid to unseat the Republican incumbent, senator Roger Marshall.

In Texas, another unexpected Senate battleground, the Democratic nominee, James Talarico, has received public endorsements from more than 20 Republican leaders, as well as members of the Bush family, over Republican Ken Paxton. There have also been cross-party endorsements from Republicans for Democrats in Georgia, Montana, Florida, Virginia, Illinois and South Dakota.

articles.title: Britain's minimum wage to rise nearly 4%, Times reports
articles.summary: British finance minister John Healey will announce on Wednesday plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4%, the Times reported on Monday.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 5:06am
LONDON, United Kingdom - British finance minister John Healey will announce on Wednesday plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4%, the Times reported on Monday.

Britain's National Living Wage, which applies to those aged 21 and older, is expected to rise to about £13.20 ($17.63) an hour from £12.71 — an increase of 3.9%, the newspaper reported, without naming sources.
The report added that the National Minimum Wage, which applies to those aged 18, 19 and 20, will rise broadly in line with the rate for older workers — to around £11.27 an hour from £10.85.
The finance ministry declined to comment on the report.

If confirmed in Wednesday's budget announcement, those increases would take effect in 2027 and end a trend seen in recent years in which the minimum rate for younger workers has increased by more than that for older workers.
Britain's minimum wage is one of the highest among advanced economies as a share of median earnings, following efforts by successive governments to lift it to two-thirds of median hourly pay.
Some analysts and employers have previously pointed to the rate payable to younger workers as a cause of increasing youth unemployment.

In April, the Low Pay Commission, which advises the government on minimum wage rises, said the National Living Wage would probably need to increase by around 3.7% in 2027 to £13.18 an hour to keep up with how it expected average pay to rise.

In March, the government tweaked the commission's remit to give it more scope to take labor market conditions into account when setting the minimum wage for 18- to 20-year-olds. ($1 = 0.7487 pounds) — Reuters

articles.summary: The UN has sounded the alarm on Israeli action in the West Bank city of Hebron after hundreds of families were displaced at the weekend. Israel has ordered the military to demolish homes after…

image.caption: The Israeli military demolished homes in Hebron after a deadly attack there killed two Israeli soldiers [FILE: October 23, 2026]Image: Ammar Awad/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Israeli military operation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron was met with sharp criticism from the head of the UN as well as the UN's human rights commissioner in comments made on Monday.

The criticism comes after an Israeli military operation was launched in the occupied West Bank in response to a shootout on Friday that left two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian gunmen dead. Three more Israeli soldiers were also injured.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the military to demolish buildings in the West Bank city of Hebron and to close off the West Bank. It came just days before Israel's general election on Tuesday.
What did the UN say about Israeli operation in the West Bank?
The United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres said on Monday that "settlements are expanding, evictions are unrelenting with Palestinians driven from their lands," in a post on X.
"We are seeing an increasingly coercive environment, with the spectre of ethnic cleaning looming ever larger," he wrote.

The UN Human Rights High Commissioner Volker Türk also issued a statement condemning Israeli actions, saying the "aggressive operation" has resulted in the forcible displacement of thousands of Palestinians, "demolished homes and commercial property, and deprived residents of the ability to move freely."
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law. Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing," he said.
Israeli army demolishes Palestinian buildings in Hebron
A UN report, also released on Monday, that accuses Israel of committing war crimes in the West Bank, was rejected by the Israeli Foreign Ministry as "propaganda."

The ministry said that the findings were "not a human rights report but a propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel's right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens."
What is the Israeli operation in the West Bank?
Israeli troops entered the Deir Baha neighborhood, where the assailants lived, and ordered residents to pack up and leave.
The Hebron municipality said that more than 3,000 people, including 200 babies, were ordered to leave.

The Israeli military said at the weekend that its troops were carrying out precise, targeted and thorough searches to "locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure and locate weapons, alongside questioning suspects" in Hebron.
The military said the operation was expected to continue "for several days" and would focus on Deir Baha.
The largescale response to the firefight in the West Bank comes in the run-up to elections in Israel on Tuesday that could bring an end to Netanyahu's premiership.
Netanyahu has frequently painted himself as the only person who can keep Israel safe but his opponents have accused him of lacking a plan.

articles.title: Man found dead in Queensland floods named as former councillor and One Nation candidate
articles.summary:
Fraser coast mayor described James Hansen as ‘always ready to help others, contribute to the community and advocate strongly’

  • Get our

blocks.text: James Hansen, a former Queensland councillor, has been identified as the man who died in flooding on the state’s Fraser Coast.
Hansen, 57, was a dairy farmer and fourth-generation resident of the area. He served as a councillor for the Fraser Coast regional council between 2012 and 2024.
George Seymour, the mayor of Fraser Coast, paid tribute to Hansen, saying he was someone “who was always ready to help others, contribute to the community and advocate strongly”.

“His passing is a great loss to our community and my thoughts are with his family and friends as they come to terms with this sudden tragedy,” Seymour wrote on Facebook. “He was one of a kind and will be missed.”
Hansen, 57, also served as a councillor for the Woocoo Shire council from 2004 to 2008. He ran for One Nation in 2017, challenging a sitting MP, but finished second.
Paul Truscott, the division 3 councillor for the Fraser Coast regional council, said he was shocked and saddened by Hansen’s death.

“James and I worked together on Council for eight years,” Truscott wrote in a statement. “He was pretty old fashioned at times, a man who always spoke his mind, someone who you knew where you stood with, and a bloke who would give you a hand if you needed it.

“Through plenty of challenging times on Council, it was always good to be able to share a laugh with James along the way and I’ll always remember him as someone who stood up for what he believed in, and stood up for the farmers and the ‘little guy’”.

Emergency services were called to a creek at Boompa on Queensland’s Fraser Coast shortly after 11am on Monday after reports a man had been found unresponsive. The man was declared dead after being found in Smothering Creek on Boompa Road, Queensland police said.
An investigation into his death has begun, with police to prepare a report for the coroner.
Further south, six campers were rescued after becoming stranded by flood waters at a public campground in Leyburn in Queensland’s Southern Downs.

Queensland Fire and Rescue Swiftwater crews responded to the call for help at 7.45am on Monday. They rescued three men aged 71, 47 and 26 and two women aged 68 and 26 without incident at about 11.15am.
Torrential downpours across Queensland between Thursday and Monday left many rivers and roads flooded across the state’s south and east.
Flash flooding hit Laidley Creek and Glenore Grove in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane, closing some roads, Queensland police said on Monday.
after newsletter promotion
The highest recorded four-day totals were spread across the state, with Blackdown Tableland, near Rockhampton, recording 439.4mm to early Monday.
Lower Springbrook, near the Gold Coast, recorded 325.2mm, while Nambour, near the Sunshine Coast, copped 314.2mm.
Brooweena, inland of K’gari, received 299.6mm.
Meteorologist Angus Hines said the system behind the downpours was unusual.

“The widespread rain bands with heaps of cloud cover, much cooler temperatures, and then the storms in that situation are really driven by what’s going on in the higher parts of the atmosphere,” he said.
The Bureau of Meteorology said Queensland’s weather was set to return to more typical spring conditions as the week continued.
Hot and humid days are expected to give way to more subdued afternoon showers and storms.

articles.title: Protest leaders urge French pupils to keep barricading their schools
articles.summary:
Activists say struggle must go on until their ‘maximum’ demands are met over teacher shortages and building repairs

French children should continue to

blocks.text: French children should continue to barricade their schools and take part in street protests, a student union said on Monday after the government announced a package of education measures to try to stem the crisis.

“Today we’re at the negotiating table, we’re able to negotiate with the government,” Pierre Sourzat of Les Lycéens told France Info television. “We’re in a power struggle and we still need to call for continued mobilisation to meet a maximum of our demands.”
The government told high school student representatives it would cap some class sizes and review the university application system. But Sourzat said: “We want measures, not half measures.”

More than five weeks after the start of high school blockades in September, the government made the proposals to address the demands of what has become the biggest youth protest movement in years. It has been joined by trade unions and cost-of-living protesters in regular mass street demonstrations on Saturdays.

High school pupils had demanded an end to teacher and staff shortages and for repairs to decrepit school buildings that had collapsing ceilings, mould, broken toilets, a lack of chairs and windows that did not shut.
The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said some schools were so dilapidated they were “not fit” for teaching. He announced a government loan of €4bn to regional authorities to begin repairs.

blocks.caption: Emmanuel Macron, kneeling centre, meets police officers in Marseille. He told them the authorities had ‘to hold the line’. Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/EPA

blocks.text: Responding to complaints of overcrowded classes, Geffray said class sizes for 15-year-olds in the first year of high school would be capped at 28 in the 50% of schools in the lowest-income areas, increasing to all high schools next year. He said more teaching posts would be created and there would be a review of the French baccaulaureate system.

The university application platform, Parcoursup, which has been described as opaque and unfair, will be changed in 2027 and replaced by a new system in 2028, according to the government. Parliament will hold a debate on the issue on Wednesday.
The higher education minister, Philippe Baptiste, said 15,000 extra student places would be created in higher education, focusing on vocational courses.

Louis Letoublon, who attended a meeting with the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on behalf of Les Lycéens, said: “Bravo to the high school students who have demonstrated. We’ve got something: the government is afraid and knows it must do something and listen to us. “Not all our demands were ⁠met. We’ll go on for as long as it takes.”
Baptiste said the government’s door was “open” for more discussions.
Several children have been maimed or seriously injured in the protests, allegedly by police explosive weapons. Hundreds of children have been arrested and held in police custody.

The authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrations after France saw its worst day of violence in years on 17 October, with looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings. Curfews have been put in place in certain cities, alongside protest bans. Protest routes were pushed to the outskirts of cities on Saturday when demonstrations passed off largely peacefully.
after newsletter promotion

The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez-Belda, said there had been a new phenomenon in cities such as Nice and Montpellier at the weekend with ultra-right groups arriving in “organised formations” and targeting protesters. Eleven suspects are to face charges.
In a visit to Marseille on Monday, Emmanuel Macron said nationwide street protests were likely continue, and that the next day of street demonstrations on 31 October would also be a “day of risk”.

The French president said the looting and vandalism seen on 17 October should never happen again. Speaking to members of the police, he said it was “not normal” for the country to be in “such a state of turmoil” six months before a presidential election.
Macron steps down next spring and the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading the polls.

Macron said: “We will continue to hold the line. If we all do our jobs well, this movement will subside – because we will address legitimate expectations, and because order will be maintained. But nothing is a foregone conclusion.”
Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes on 17 October.

articles.title: How this Brooklyn bar owner had Conan O’Brien in stitches on SubwayTakes
articles.summary: Debbie Shields took a seat on a New York City subway and ended up joking with comedian Conan O'Brien about their fictional family. Their exchange on internet talk show SubwayTakes went viral. The…

image.caption: New Yorker Debbie Shields, left, strikes up a conversation with comedian Conan O'Brien, right, while he films a segment for for Subway Takes with Kareem Rahma, centre. (SubwayTakes with Kareem Rahma/YouTube)

blocks.text: LISTEN | Interview with Debbie Shields:
As It Happens5:53Meet the Brooklyn bar owner who stole the show on Conan O'Brien's episode of SubwayTakes
It's not everyday you go from running a comedy night at a bar to doing improv with an Emmy-winning comedian on the New York City subway.
Debbie Shields wasn't expecting to strike up a conversation with comedian Conan O'Brien when she set out to run errands, but her quick-witted humour meant she was prepared.
"I mean, if you give it to me, I give it right back to you," she told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.
Shields has become an internet sensation after her exchange with O'Brien aired on the most recent episode of SubwayTakes.

O'Brien was a guest on the popular internet talk show hosted by comedian Kareem Rahma, where regular New Yorkers and celebrities humorously discuss their controversial opinions while riding the subway.

items: How SubwayTakes became an Emmy contender

blocks.text: Toward the end of his episode, O'Brien apologized to Shields as she moved into an empty seat next to Rahma. She and O'Brien shook hands and jumped into a spontaneous scene together, with O'Brien joking that the two used to be married.
Shields quickly responded that they had two kids. "One's in medical school, the other one's in jail," she said, causing the former late night host to crack up.
Some viewers said they loved her wit and ability to keep up with O'Brien. He was impressed, too.
O'Brien told New York Magazine he's open to working with Shields again. "I'll do a sitcom with her," he said. "Or we can just hit the road, do a two-person show."
Shields told Köksal she'd love to collaborate with him again. Here is part of their conversation.
Debbie, what is your relationship status with Conan O'Brien now? Is remarriage in the cards? He walked out on you again?
He just did his interview and walked off the train. "Bye Debbie."
Typical. How are the kids feeling?
They're fine. They're used to him not being around.
In all seriousness though, how are you doing with all of this attention?
It's crazy right now. SXM radio, I was in the New York Times, 1010 radio.
Internationally, are they interested, too?
Yeah, somebody called me from Japan, 1:30 in the morning, Australia, England. Oh boy, it's been busy.
On that day on the train, did you have any idea what you were walking into?
Not at all. I was going to see my accountant for my business.
O'Brien appeared delighted with the random encounter. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images/SiriusXM)
Did you just see that shock of orange hair and the pasty skin? He would say that about himself, so I feel like can say that.

No, I saw a camera crew. And when I saw the camera crew, my friend said, "Oh, that's Conan O'Brien." I was like, "Oh, OK." But I was looking for a seat because I'm always looking for a seat on the train. So I got me a seat and I told him "You hold the seat and I'm just going to go over and say hi." And that's all it took.
And you did not miss a beat, a millisecond even. Have you always had that kind of comedic timing?
Yeah, I mean if you give it to me, I give it right back to you. That's how it goes.
That's the New Yorker in you, I would imagine. But you are at another level, though.
Thank you.
You didn't seem nervous, but were you at all nervous inside?
No, I was having a ball.
He was, too.
Yeah, we had a good time doing that.
You were a fan of Conan before. What about him do you like?
Yes, I like his style of comedy. He's witty, he's fast, he's risky, he is risque. I just like him.
Did you have any idea about the show SubwayTakes?
No, I didn't know anything about that show, nothing.

It's really cool when you meet a celebrity whose work you admire and the exchange goes really well. Sometimes, it could be not as pleasant. You go about your day, you went to your accountant. And then when did you start getting a sense that this was more than this great memory for you?

Tuesday evening. Somebody told me, "Oh, you're on Conan, we saw it." I was in my bar and people started showing me. Then Wednesday morning, it went crazy. People were calling me at eight in the morning. "Oh, you were all over the internet. You've got five million hits." Then somebody called me at like about 10 in the morning, "You're on television, on channel five. You're on channel four." And I'm like, "Oh my God." It was surreal.

That's what I do with people, even in my bar. The name of my bar is Confessions Bar, I have comedy on Friday nights. I introduce the host of the comics and I really go off on the people. I make them laugh, I talk about their outfits, whatever it is, and they all love me. I like to see people happy. And if I lay my head to rest today, I want people to remember that I made people laugh.
Oh, they're sure going to remember, Debbie. Conan's at the top of that list. Do you think he's going to drop by?
He's been in touch with me. Kareem's team has been in touch with me to do another show with him.
Oh my goodness. What would be your dream show?
Saturday Night Live.
I think at least Conan could arrange that for you. Conan said he'd do a sitcom with you.
Yes he would, and I would love to do one with him.
What does this tell you about life?

Life is funny, you never know where your blessings are coming from. That's why you have to live your life in a certain way. So when the aura of God, or whatever you want to see or call it, sees that you're doing your best and you're trying really hard and you genuine, he always throws you a ball.
You've got the comedy night at Confessions, are you incorporating this new part of your life and your ex-husband into the bar?
Yes, we invented a drink called Baby Daddy O'Brien. We've got whiskey, Triple Sec, lemon, lime, and blood orange.
Can we expect you to bring your show to Toronto sometime?
That would be fun. I love Toronto. I love Canada. I've been to Canada so many times.
I'm sure people would love to see you riding the subway here, too, Debbie. Thank you for this.
My pleasure. You just always laugh your ass off.
That's the key to life.

articles.title: Russell Brand had ‘insane sexual appetite’ and his bad behaviour was normalised, trial told
articles.summary:
Brand, charged with rape and sexual assault, was ‘sleeping with people day and night’, former assistant alleges

Russell Brand had an “insane sexual appetite” and his bad behaviour was…

blocks.text: Russell Brand had an “insane sexual appetite” and his bad behaviour was “normalised and dismissed” by those around him, his former personal assistant has told a court.
Helen Berger alleged she had seen Brand treat women badly and that she once had to stop his mother and girlfriend walking in on him having sex with someone in his dressing room.
She also told the court she had overheard the comedian receiving oral sex in a toilet cubicle and once found a celebrity leaving his bedroom in the morning.
Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.
Wearing a grey suit and white shirt, Brand sat still in the dock as statements from prosecution witnesses were read to Southwark crown court on Monday.

Berger worked for Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, when he was at the height of his fame. She said the job was one of the hardest she had had because Brand had “non-stop energy”, and she left because she was “sick of him” and burnt out.

“Though I’d worked with celebrities before and seen a lot of people normalising bad behaviour, this was on another level. I think everyone else normalising and dismissing Russell’s behaviour made me think, I guess, this is just the way it is,” Berger said in a May 2024 witness statement to police.

Describing his behaviour, she added: “He was always in his underwear, he loved walking around in his underwear with no shirt on. I remember Sadie Frost came over to interview him. He did the whole interview in his underwear and no shirt and an open robe.”
At the time, Brand had filming commitments for Channel 4’s Big Brother as well as MTV and the BBC, a radio show, a national comedy tour, a weekly Guardian column, and was writing a book.

“In addition to his busy work, he had an insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night. He was very open about what his needs were,” Berger said in the statement, which was read out by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC.

“He never seemed happy after sex, more so depressed,” Berger alleged. “There were times when I was at his house and he would be on a deadline … and he would get antsy and joke with me: ‘May I go and have sex now?’”

She recalled Brand turning to the website Myspace to find random women to sleep with and how women, including an unnamed celebrity, would often be at his flat in Camden, north London, for sexual liaisons. “He was like a peacock, women always approached him,” she said.
When Brand was recording an MTV show, Berger alleged, he told her to ask women for their phone numbers, which she said made her feel uncomfortable.

She alleged that on other occasions she had to keep Brand’s mother and girlfriend away from his dressing room because he was having sex, and she overheard him receiving oral sex in a women’s toilet. Berger described overhearing Brand talking and recognising his trademark cowboy boots in the cubicle next door.

Berger recalled that when Brand was headlining the Edinburgh festival, he ended his show by asking that anyone with “a vagina and heartbeat” meet him at a pub afterwards. Many women showed up, Berger said, and she later found him having sex in the shower at the apartment he was renting.
“I never witnessed Russell doing anything against the law,” she said, before adding: “I did see Russell treat women poorly.”

She recalled how he was once “hitting on” a woman who revealed she had a boyfriend, before Brand “turned in a way” that startled his then PA. “He literally just switched off his charm and moved on to the next woman,” Berger said.

The court also heard a witness statement from the manager of a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Brand when she worked at Channel 4 in 2009. The manager said she recalled the alleged victim telling her that Brand’s associates Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy had “told her she had to give Mr Brand a massage” or he would not continue with the day’s recording.
The manager recalled being told that Bayles and Roy “were both there the whole time and watched and laughed while Mr Brand sexually assaulted her right in front of them”.
The sister of a woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted and then orally raped by Brand at a Soho bar in 2004 told the court she was “upset and almost in shock” the next morning.
In 2023, the woman called her sister in tears and told the “full story” of what had happened, the court heard.
“It sounded like she was struggling to catch her breath,” the witness recalled. “She said his [Brand’s] eyes had gone completely black and he was possessed or had been a completely different person.”
The trial continues.

articles.title: A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses
articles.summary: The recent announcement that Syrian tertiary institutes will not allow women into some courses has triggered debate. Critics worry it may be a sign that the new Syrian government is restricting…

image.caption: When Syria's dictator was ousted in late 2024, Syrian women celebrated — but many wondered how the new government, with conservative religious roots, would see women's rightsImage: Aaref Watad/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Recent changes to university admissions rules in Syria have put a dent in Lin Najab's plans. The 23-year-old from Damascus is one of the few women at her college studying mechatronics engineering.

"My original plan was to pursue a master's degree," Najab told DW. But earlier in October, new rules were announced by Syria's education ministry regarding two newly created colleges, the National University of Defense Sciences and the Syrian University for Security Sciences. The former now restricts certain courses exclusively to male students, and the latter almost all of them.
These new policies could derail Najab's plans. "Now I have to start thinking about other options," she explained. "For example, I might have to move to another province to study."
It is still possible for Syrian women to study the subjects offered by the two new security institutes, but only at other more generalist universities or colleges.

Moving to another province, away from family, brings other difficulties, Najab continued. Student accommodation in dormitories is uncomfortable, but a woman living alone is still frowned upon by conservative Syrians.

"Even if a girl decides she won't give up and wants to go study outside her province, her parents will be opposed to the idea, either for security reasons or because we simply don't want our daughters to go study somewhere else," said Najab.

blocks.caption: Females only make up just over 10% of Syria's members of parliament — 22 out of 210 politicians — despite the country's target of 20%Image: LOUAI BESHARA/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Controversial ban
The decision to ban women from courses at the new defense and security-related colleges has caused controversy both inside and outside the country.

"Gender doesn't define ability. It should be about high academic standards, the ones I'm trying to meet," Najab argued. "In Syria, we need better education and good graduates, so let's see where the best people are, regardless of gender."

Fatoun Kharbatli, an activist from Aleppo, is also opposed to the idea of limiting certain subjects to one gender. "A person should choose the field in which they see their abilities as lying," she told DW. "We were oppressed for 60 years, so now let's be a nation that keeps pace with global civilization, but without straying from respect and from the basics of our religion.
Qamar al-Yaser, a mother of three in rural Damascus, believes the ban is justified.

The sectors from which women have been excluded "require a strong physique, they need big efforts, travel, organization out in the field and may require staying overnight at remote work sites," said al-Yaser. "These conditions suit young men more than women."

A closer look at some of new admission rules indicate they may be less about restricting Syrian women from certain studies and more about keeping them out of the army. For example, attending the National University of Defense Sciences requires that students serve in the Syrian military. Graduates of the University for Security Sciences must also commit to serving up to 20 years with the internal security forces.

blocks.caption: Syria's military leadership has already rejected the integration of Syrian Kurdish female fighters into the Syrian national militaryImage: Sebastian Backhaus/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Bad omen?
Does this mean Syria's new government is heading in an increasingly restrictive direction when it comes to women's rights?

Human Rights Watch believes so. A few days after the admissions announcement, the organization released a statement criticizing it. "The discriminatory rules clearly violate Syria's international legal obligations and are part of a concerning pattern of actions by the transitional authorities that restrict women's role in state institutions and reinforce gender stereotypes," the organization said.

Besides the military college bans, there were also other, possibly even more disturbing aspects to the new admissions rules. Restrictions on female students were also applied at a railways institute in Aleppo, oil and gas training organizations in Rmeilan, Homs, Deir el-Zour and Baniyas, and a radio and television course in Idlib. Elsewhere men were barred from kindergarten and nursing school training and midwifery courses. These were to be women-only.

blocks.caption: The National Defense Sciences University in Damascus was only founded in mid-2026Image: Rami Alsayed/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: All these come on top of a number of other concerning restrictions and worrying comments by officials. The most recent incident in the education sector involved the government's alteration of school textbooks for the 2026-2027 academic year.

The education ministry had already announced it would be removing images and symbols associated with the previous authoritarian regime headed by dictator Bashar Assad. But this week journalists also noticed other changes: Pictures of females in the textbooks who had uncovered hair had been removed, or altered so they were now wearing headscarves. A bare-chested statue pictured in one textbook was now wearing a vest. A picture of men dancing was also gone.
Common attitudes towards female soldiers

Officials have said that some of the gender-exclusionary rules implemented at the new security institutes were actually carried over from the Assad-era colleges that were fused together to create them earlier this year.

Opposition to female soldiers and military leaders isn't an uncommon attitude in the Middle East's more conservative circles either. Although many Arab countries allow women to attend military colleges and serve, females are often restricted to non-combat or symbolic roles, a 2024 study by the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Institute, or MEI, reported.

In Syria, while women have historically participated in the security services, it was "in a limited and largely symbolic capacity," the Syrian Center for Defense and Security Studies confirmed in a policy paper this year.
But just because an idea is widespread obviously doesn't make it right, human rights advocates have said.

blocks.caption: Even in Germany, women were not allowed to serve in the military until a 2001 landmark court case forced a change Image: Juliane Sonntag/photothek.de/picture alliance

blocks.text: Gender stereotypes

"Gender diversity in the security sector allows all citizens of a country to be perceived as equal in all aspects of their duties and obligations to the nation state, including defending it," Dina Arakji, author of the MEI study, argued. "Allowing women to join the military … can advance a society's perspective on females in nontraditional gender-based roles."

The admissions ban gives young Syrian women a message about what they can and cannot do, Syrian activist Rana al-Ash argued in a commentary about the ban for Paris-based organization, the Syrian Women's Political Movement.

"When these messages are reflected in admission requirements, confronting familial and societal expectations becomes even more difficult because the educational institution endorses them," al-Ash argued.
For Nadra Bunni, a Syrian analyst at the Middle East Institute Switzerland, it's still unclear as to whether "gender-based restrictions will become a feature of the new Syria."

But the anger over the admissions ban also raises another important question, she noted. "Will Syria's new authorities institutionalize an expectation that government decisions can be questioned and potentially reversed," she asked in a commentary for the online publication, Syria In Transition. "Or [will they] teach citizens that their voices carry little consequence?"
Women push for political power and equality in new Syria

articles.title: 'It's time to abolish the Indian Act,' Manitoba premier tells PM during historic meeting with chiefs

image.caption: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew speaks with journalists during the meeting in Ottawa on Monday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba·Updated
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says he's calling on the federal government to abolish the Indian Act.
Wab Kinew says it's 'long overdue' that Canada's relationship with Indigenous Peoples 'reflects who we are'
Kinew shared that request during a scrum in Ottawa on Monday, as First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers meet to discuss Indigenous rights for the first time in two decades.

"I don't know how many folks in Canada have seen one of these before, but this is a status card, and it says your friend Wab Kinew is an Indian, within the meaning of the Indian Act," he said, holding up his own card in front of reporters during a midday break in the historic meeting.
"I'm not sure if that lines up with your vision of Canada, that we still have a race-based form of identification in this country. But this is a reality."

Kinew said he raised the issue with Prime Minister Mark Carney earlier Monday, calling it "long overdue that we have a relationship with Indigenous Peoples in Canada that reflects who we are as Canadians today.
"I think it's time to abolish the Indian Act," Kinew said. "And it needs to be done with First Nations people and First Nations governments."
The controversial legislation has governed the lives of First Nations people for the last 150 years.
Abolishing Indian Act 'long overdue,' says Wab Kinew
Coming into effect in 1876, the act came to control almost every aspect of First Nations people's lives, dictating things like how communities were governed and who could be considered an "Indian."
While the act has had many amendments, it remains the overarching legal document for First Nations in Canada.
'Nothing to lose but your chains'

Carney and most of the premiers sat down with chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations in Ottawa for a discussion. Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, the assembly's national chief, said the meeting is intended to help build prosperity for coming generations.

Monday's closed-door meeting is the first such gathering since the Kelowna Accord talks of 2005, which brought premiers and then-prime minister Paul Martin together with Indigenous leaders to discuss ways to close the socioeconomic gaps in Indigenous communities.

items: First Nations want tangible results as 'historic' first ministers' meeting opens

blocks.text: The Kelowna agreement was not implemented after the Conservative government under former prime minister Stephen Harper took office only a few months later.
Monday's meeting comes as Carney's government works to speed up major project approvals and development — efforts some First Nations chiefs have said threaten their rights.

Tensions between Ottawa and First Nations spiked soon after Carney was elected in 2025, when his government passed legislation to create a new office tasked with streamlining major project developments and approving projects within one year.

Kinew said he supports Carney's work at the international level, "saying that we are going to be a leader when it comes to human rights and democracy, and a leader among middle powers." But he called the Indian Act's continued existence inconsistent with that message.

items: Carney government is stalling on Indian Act reform bill, advocates, lawmakers charge
After 150 years, Canada still has an Indian Act. Why is it so hard to get rid of?

blocks.text: The premier said though doing away with the Indian Act would bring changes, things like treaties and constitutional rights would still be able to exist for First Nations people.
"You can have self-determination, and you can have strong Indigenous nationhood, while at the same time not having the paternalism and the barriers that come with the Indian Act," Kinew said.
"You have nothing to lose but your chains."
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: UN commission says Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza since truce
articles.summary: A United Nations commission says Israel ​continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October's U.S.-brokered ceasefire in the enclave, in a report published Monday that Israel dismissed as part…

image.caption: Palestinians walk through a displacement camp in Gaza City on Oct. 18. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A United Nations commission says Israel ​continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October's U.S.-brokered ceasefire in the enclave, in a report published Monday that Israel dismissed as part of a "misinformation campaign."
Israel dismisses report as 'misinformation'

The report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian ‌Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel examined violations against Palestinian children since the start of the war between Israel and Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, up to September this year.
It said Israeli authorities had kept committing "genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, ​in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza."

The commission also accused Israeli soldiers and prison guards of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence and persecution against civilians.
The commission said that it had recently documented six cases in which Israeli guards were sexually violent toward male detainees from Gaza in the Sde Teiman military prison.

Another report by the commission in September last year found that Israel had committed genocide in ​Gaza and that top Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu incited these acts — ⁠accusations that Israel called ⁠scandalous.
The Israeli mission in Geneva said the ‌latest report was part of a misinformation campaign to demonize Israel.

“The attempt to destroy the Jewish state ... continues today through efforts by actors such as the UN Commission of Inquiry to undermine Israel’s legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend ⁠itself," Ambassador Daniel Meron said in a statement.
Life is brutal inside Gaza, one year into the ceasefire
Munitions, sniper fire
The commission found that Israeli forces continued using heavy munitions, drones, quadcopters, artillery and sniper fire in densely populated areas during the ceasefire ‌in Gaza.

It said the "Yellow Line" which was presented as a temporary ceasefire demarcation, was encroaching increasingly into Gaza, and becoming a de facto border, which the report said reflected Israel’s expanding territorial control of Gaza.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel's ​assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

items: Netanyahu 'fighting for his political life' in 1st election since Oct. 7
Israelis are leaving the country in record numbers. Could a looming election accelerate the trend?

blocks.text: In its report to the ⁠UN Security Council, the commission said the situation in the West Bank had also deteriorated sharply, with the ⁠number of Palestinians killed in airstrikes increasing from six between 2008 and Oct. 6, 2023, to ⁠254 between ⁠Oct. 7, 2023, and Sept. 30, ​2026.

Commission Chair Srinivasan Muralidhar said the intentional killing of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West ​Bank formed part of a ⁠broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians.

Military operations since January 2025 have led to the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank since 1967, with 34,176 Palestinians remaining displaced as of August 2026, the report said.
The commission also faulted the Palestinian Authority, saying it had targeted Palestinians who voice dissenting views and that journalists and ⁠human rights defenders had been ‌killed and injured.
