articles.title: NHS consultants to go on two-day strike in England in November
articles.summary:
Industrial action by senior doctors to begin on 25 November with only emergency cover provided, BMA says

England’s most senior hospital doctors will strike next month in a dispute over their…

blocks.text: England’s most senior hospital doctors will strike next month in a dispute over their pay and hours, prompting NHS bosses to warn that patients will suffer “pain, discomfort and inconvenience”.

Consultant doctors, who earn an average of £152,000 a year inclusive of overtime and merit awards, will stage a two-day walkout on 25 and 26 November, as hospitals gear up for the extra pressures winter brings.
On those days, hospitals will operate with consultants providing only emergency cover, in the way they do on Christmas Day, because most will withdraw their labour.

Consultants decided to strike after 18 months of talks with the government did not lead to agreement on key issues, including their call for action to address a 25% fall in the real-terms value of their salaries since 2009-10, the British Medical Association (BMA) said. The senior doctors also want a 10% cut in their working hours.

The BMA accused ministers of ignoring consultants’ concerns about burnout related to their workloads and said last week’s well-below-inflation pay offer of a 2.4% increase for next year was the last straw.

Consultants voted in July to take industrial action. The BMA said that since then, informal talks with the Department of Health and Social Care had produced no meaningful progress, only another cut to the value of their pay.

blocks.caption: Consultant doctors last went on strike in 2023, when they walked out for nine days. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: Ciarán Devane, the head of the NHS Alliance, which represents NHS leaders, said he was “astonished and dismayed” by the BMA’s move at a time when the health service was working to tackle a backlog of more than 6 million patients awaiting more than 7m treatments.

“NHS leaders will be both astonished and dismayed by the BMA’s decision to proceed with walkouts by consultants at a time when plans to restore waiting time targets hang by a thread and as teams make wider preparations for winter after a gruelling summer,” Devane said. “Any decision to down tools risks throwing these plans further off course and will once again disrupt patient care while severely hitting NHS finances.

“A consultant walkout will result in non-urgent outpatient appointments, elective surgeries and follow-ups being postponed or rescheduled. While [postponement] is needed in the interests of patient safety, it will potentially leave patients in unnecessary pain, discomfort, and inconvenience.”
The BMA’s decision presents the prime minister, Andy Burnham, with a considerable challenge as he grapples with tight public finances and Labour’s aim of improving access to NHS care.

In June, resident doctors – formerly known as junior doctors – accepted a deal to end a campaign of strikes that had lasted more than three years. Consultants last staged stoppages in 2023, when they walked out for nine days during four strikes.

“Since we entered into dispute over 18 months ago we have engaged in good faith with the government, proposing practical solutions,” said Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta, the co-chairs of the BMA’s consultants committee. “But time and time again ministers have kicked the can down the road. Unfortunately, that road has now run out, and we have been forced to announce strikes.
“Consultants take their responsibilities incredibly seriously, and striking does not come naturally, but we are hearing loud and clear from the profession that they have had enough.
after newsletter promotion

“Not only is our pay still a quarter down in real terms on what it was 17 years ago, having fallen more steeply than the rest of the economy, but we are also not being given time to dedicate our all to the NHS and patients, with quality and improvement being traded for the treadmill of target-chasing, driving colleagues to burnout through excessive workloads.”
Ben Morrin, the chief executive of NHS Employers, which represents England’s 205 health trusts, urged the BMA to be realistic about what size of pay rise was affordable.

“We need to be honest and transparent about what the NHS can afford at this time. If that limit is reached and industrial action takes place, we owe it to patients to focus on delivering the safest care we can,” he said.
He added that the strike would “weaken the clinical teams in every NHS hospital, which are essential to delivering high-quality patient care this winter”.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, urged consultants to “not take irresponsible action that would place our health service under even greater pressure” during what would be a tough winter for the NHS.

A Department of Health and Social Care source said: “The BMA’s consultants committee is threatening strikes because they want a five-hour cut to the working week and to reduce the proportion of their week spent treating patients, changes that would cost taxpayers over £2bn. This is despite average earnings of £152,000 a year and a £25,000 increase to average earnings over the last four years.”

articles.title: No 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movement
articles.summary:
Clarification comes after PM fuelled speculation about EU-UK relationship in series of interviews at weekend

Downing Street has been forced to clarify Andy Burnham’s stance on whether the UK…

blocks.text: Downing Street has been forced to clarify Andy Burnham’s stance on whether the UK would return to having freedom of movement with the EU after the prime minister said an “honest discussion” was needed on the issue.
Burnham fuelled speculation about a return to freedom of movement in an interview at the weekend, prompting questions about how close the UK could become to Brussels.
Confusion deepened after further interviews were interpreted as leaving the door open to an eventual return to freedom of movement and another referendum on the issue.
It forced a Downing Street spokesperson to say the prime minister was not proposing a return to freedom of movement, or any particular option.

“He is saying that it’s time for us to discuss what kind of long-term relationship with Europe is best for Britain and he is referring to the types of areas that that agreement and long-term future could cover,” she said.

“He is crucially not leaning either way, and that will be for the British public to decide. And his focus for now is on next month’s summit and the practical arrangements that we hope to make there, which will add billions to the economy.”
She said the government was not yet at the stage of confirming whether the public would decide on proposals for the UK to move closer to the EU.

Asked whether Burnham accepted that returning to freedom of movement would mean Britain lost control over legal migration, the spokesperson said: “He’s not setting out a concrete position either way. What he’s saying is that he wants to have a conversation with the British public about what our long-term future with the European Union looks like.”
In an interview with the Sunday Times, Burnham indicated that staying out of free movement would no longer be a red line in discussions about how the UK can move closer to the EU.

On Monday, Burnham ruled out the possibility of rejoining the EU within this parliament and indicated he could fight the next general election on a promise to take the UK back into the EU. He said: “I’m not going to move away from the red lines that were in the Labour manifesto.”
Hours later, Burnham told journalists “no” when asked if he would allow the UK to join the EU freedom of movement scheme without a referendum.

When asked whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, he said: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.”

Challenged on how his constituents in Makerfield would feel about his discussions about the EU, given 65% of them voted to leave, Burnham added: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’m doing.
“The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation to Brexit.”

Burnham even ruled out an early general election on a manifesto change on this issue. He told GMB: “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.” However, he left the door open to a future fight on a promise to fully rejoin the EU.

Burnham will be in Brussels for the UK-EU summit on 20 November, as he seeks to strike a better deal with the bloc. He believes the Brexit deal has “weakened our economy [and] weakened our control of immigration” and is not good enough for the country.

articles.title: Fifteen-year-old arrested in shooting near Florida university that injured 12
articles.summary:
All but one of the victims sustained gunshot wounds as boy faces 11 charges of attempted second-degree murder

A 15-year-old boy was remanded into secure detention in Florida on Monday…

blocks.text: A 15-year-old boy was remanded into secure detention in Florida on Monday charged with 11 counts of attempted murder following a mass shooting at a college homecoming party on Saturday.
Six adults and six minors were injured, all but one with gunshot wounds, in the gunfire near the Florida Agricultural + Mechanical University (Famu) campus in Tallahassee.

It was among five mass shootings over the weekend – cases in which at least four victims were wounded or killed, according to the Gun Violence Archive. The archive, a nonpartisan resource, has recorded 386 such cases in the US for the year so far.

On Monday, the Tallahassee police department posted on Facebook that detectives had arrested a suspect in the Famu shooting two days earlier. The agency identified the suspect as Anthony Rivers III, 15.

Police do not typically identify criminal suspects who are minors, though the severity of the charges facing Rivers made him an exception. He faces 11 charges of attempted second-degree murder and one of possession of a firearm by a delinquent after being arrested on Sunday, police said.

Rivers appeared in juvenile court on Monday dressed in a white T-shirt and gray shorts. He was not handcuffed and did not speak during the brief hearing, during which Leon county circuit court judge Anthony Sheeran ordered him to remain in secure detention pending an arraignment.
Tallahassee police chief Lawrence Revell said in a statement that the investigation into Saturday’s shooting was ongoing, and further arrests were possible.
“What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families,” Revell said.

“While this arrest marks a significant step forward, our work is far from over. We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family [affected] by this tragedy.”

The department earlier said three of the victims were seriously wounded, with one in critical condition in the hospital. Nine others had gunshot wounds, the agency said – and another person injured an ankle as they attempted to escape the gunfire.

The shooting took place just before 8pm on Saturday at an intersection near the university’s Bragg stadium, where a homecoming football game had just ended. Officers were on the scene quickly and carried some of those injured to safety through a mass of people, Revell said.
According to police, Rivers opened fire after an altercation between two groups of people who were known to each other. None of those struck was believed to have been an intended target, Revell said.
Revell on Sunday thanked members of the community who had come forward with cellphone video of the shooting and its aftermath, which he said was “vital to investigative efforts”.
Famu president Marva Johnson posted a video message on X on Sunday condemning the “senseless and despicable” violence of the night before.

“As a neighbor and community partner, we are providing our full assistance to the Tallahassee police department,” she said. “Our pride, our identity, and our future will not be defined by the challenges we face, but how we respond to them together.”

articles.title: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil
articles.summary:
A viral WhatsApp channel and student-led protests played a key role in the veteran Brazilian leftist’s election victory

After the first round of the Brazilian presidential election three…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Brasília and Tom Phillips in São Paulo

blocks.text: After the first round of the Brazilian presidential election three weeks ago, the leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva reportedly told allies he could not understand how he finished second after a government he considered the best of his three terms.

A mood of dismay swept Brazil’s left, and because 9 million voters for the other candidates, all of them on the right, were expected to mostly transfer to senator Flávio Bolsonaro, analysts widely saw the far-right senator’s victory as certain.

Then, on the night after the election, students from the Fluminense Federal University took to the streets of Niterói, a city of 480,000 across Guanabara Bay from Rio de Janeiro, to protest against the return to power of a member of the Bolsonaro family, whose patriarch, former president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father, is under house arrest for attempting a coup.

Two days later, another student protest took over downtown Rio and, in the days that followed, similar ones spread across the country in organic demonstrations that analysts and Lula himself agree gave new life to his campaign and played a decisive role in his historic comeback in the runoff.
“I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” Lula said in his victory speech on Sunday night after defeating Bolsonaro.

Political scientist Fábio Vasconcellos said Lula’s victory, in which for the first time in Brazil’s democratic history a second-placed candidate overturned a first-round defeat in the runoff, could be explained by a combination of the streets, social media and the machinery of government – in recent weeks, Lula approved a “package of benefits” at the limits of what electoral law allows, including increasing and bringing forward payments from the main cash-transfer programme for poor families.
“The streets and social media almost overlap,” said Vasconcellos, a researcher with the Representation and Democratic Legitimacy group at the Federal University of Paraná.

Two days after the first round, congressman André Janones, a Lula ally, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army”, where Janones sent audio messages, videos – often beginning with shouts of “Guys, urgent!” – and dozens of daily instructions on how to make pro-Lula content perform well on social media.
The channel had 60,000 followers by the end of its first day and, by election Sunday, more than 10 million, and Lula’s digital reach overtook Bolsonaro’s.

In his victory speech, Lula called Janones “our general”, who had the role of “raising the morale of our troops every day”. The congressman’s relentless efforts, which included a 24-hour YouTube live stream on the eve of the vote, led to him being admitted to hospital last week – the only day the WhatsApp channel went silent.

Lula’s campaign also overhauled his online communications, and the incumbent, who turns 81 on Tuesday, began recording selfie videos despite not owning a mobile phone. On Sunday night, he said he had been given a phone and that “from now on I’m going to talk a lot to the Brazilian people, many times a day, directly”.
With the streets and social media, “the mood of defeat was gradually replaced by hopes of a comeback over those three weeks,” said Vasconcellos.
Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, said Lula’s comeback also represented “a broad rejection of the Bolsonarista project for Brazil”.

She has been interviewing undecided voters since May and said “the fear voters had, workers had, of losing rights and also of a possible concentration of power in Bolsonaro’s hands was very clear”, which meant that even people who did not like Lula voted for him this time.

Bolsonaro had won 56.1m votes in the first round and received 3.7 million more in the runoff. Lula, by contrast, went from 53.9m to 64.2m. The more than 10m-vote increase came both from persuading voters to turn out after historically high abstention in the first round and from convincing voters from other candidates, including Bolsonaro.

“Some undecided voters we interviewed said Bolsonaro was a playboy who sided with big business, while at the same time spontaneously saying that, if he won, there would be a dictatorship in which people would lose rights,” said Rocha.

Bolsonaro was also embroiled in several controversies recently, including saying he would use the new, even more conservative congress to change the constitution and “re-democratise” Brazil, as well as the two federal police inquiries in which he is under investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering.
Many analysts have also pointed to the weight of Lula himself. “If it were another candidate, Bolsonaro would already have won in the first round,” said political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles.

Marco Aurélio de Carvalho, Lula’s campaign manager, answered without hesitation when asked what explained the historic election fightback: “President Lula. We have a great statesman on our team. We have a star player. That’s what absolutely made the difference. I haven’t the slightest doubt about it.”
The question already occupying the minds of Brazil’s left is what happens next, given that Lula has said this was his last election.
“That is a very big challenge because, in the polling on this, Lula’s dominance is still very strong. There is no one in his party with the same leadership,” said Rocha.
Vasconcellos believes Lula’s re-election campaign, “from what we saw on the streets, offered the Brazilian left an opportunity for renewal”.
“Lula’s party can learn from what happened and find better ways to connect with young people and urban voters who feel their concerns are not being heard,” he added.

items: The Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips will be answering your questions about the election and the future of Brazil from 1500 GMT on Tuesday 27 October as part of our Conversations series. Email questions to conversations@theguardian.com.

articles.title: Tagle visits hometown, leads celebration of a new parish in Imus, Cavite
articles.summary: Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle made his first trip home after being selected as the Dean of the College of Cardinals and he led the Thanksgiving Mass of a new parish in Imus, Cavite, according to the…

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 1:55am

Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle made his first trip home after being selected as the Dean of the College of Cardinals and he led the Thanksgiving Mass of a new parish in Imus, Cavite, according to the report of GMA News' Mariz Umali on "24 Oras."
The Parish of San Roque in Imus, Cavite celebrated its elevation as a parish with Cardinal Tagle leading the thanksgiving activities.
It can be recalled that Tagle was the Bishop of the Diocese of Imus in Cavite for 10 years, before becoming the 32nd Archbishop of Manila. In 2012, Pope Benedict XVI appointed him cardinal.
In 2019, Pope Francis named him prefect of the Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples, a key Vatican department responsible for missionary work.

In March 2022, Tagle became pro-prefect of the section for First Evangelization and New Particular Churches. The role involved overseeing matters concerning missionary territories and newly established local churches.
In November 2022, Pope Francis replaced Tagle and the leadership of Caritas Internationalis following a Vatican-ordered review that identified deficiencies in management and procedures.
Pope Leo XIV approved the election of Filipino Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle as dean of the College of Cardinals on October 8, 2026.

Tagle, 69, pro-prefect of the Dicastery for Evangelization’s Section for First Evangelization and New Particular Churches, succeeds Cardinal Giovanni Battista Re, 92, who has held the post since January 2020.
Dean of the College of Cardinals
The Imus native is the first Filipino and Asian cleric selected to lead the elite group that one day will choose Leo's successor.

The College of Cardinals is composed of senior Church leaders who advise the Pope and, when the papacy becomes vacant, elect his successor in a conclave. Only cardinals who meet the requirements under Church law may vote in the papal election.
The Dean serves as the head of the College of Cardinals in a coordinating and representative capacity. The position is often described as primus inter pares, meaning “first among equals.”
Although the Dean does not govern the Church in place of the Pope, the role becomes particularly important when a Pope dies or resigns, and the Church prepares for a new pontificate.
Homily
His homily centered on the celebration of the church's elevation as a parish.
"Biro niyo, ngayon, parokya na ang ating sambayanan... at natutuwa po ako dahil dito sa atin, gumagawa ng bagong parokya," he said.
(Now our community is now a parish... and I'm happy because here among us, a new parish is being built.)
"Sa ibang bahagi ng mundo, nagsasara ang parokya. Alam niyo kung bakit sinasara ang ibang parokya? Wala na kasing pinagpasahan ng pananampalataya," he added.
(In other parts of the world, parishes are closing. Do you know why some parishes are closing? There is no longer any one to pass the faith to.)
The prelate named three actions that San Roque also implemented.

"Una, sa salita ng Diyos. Salita ng Diyos na pinahahayag, pinakikinggan, tinatanggap, sinasapuso, sinasabuhay. ang ikalawa po, ang mga sakramento lalo na ang eukaristiya, ang misa. Patuloy na pinadadaloy ng Panginoon ang kanyang biyaya sa bawat yugto ng ating buhay," Tagle said.

(First, in the word of God. The word of God that is proclaimed, listened to, accepted, taken to heart, and lived. Second, the sacraments, especially the Eucharist and the Mass. The Lord continues to pour out his grace in every stage of our lives.)
The third one he said, "Paglilingkod ng may pag-ibig (Serving with love)."
Cardinal Tagle is staying until Sunday before going to his next mission in Macau. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Jury selected for trial of four accused of sexually assaulting man’s drugged ex-wife
articles.summary:
Mr Justice Saini tells the eight men and six women at Winchester crown court the case is likely to be upsetting

Jurors being selected for the trial of four men accused of sexually assaulting…

blocks.text: Jurors being selected for the trial of four men accused of sexually assaulting the ex-wife of a former Conservative councillor, who has admitted repeatedly drugging and raping her, have been warned the case is likely to be upsetting.
Philip Young, 50, has pleaded guilty to multiple charges of abuse against his former wife, Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity.
A jury at Winchester crown court will this week begin hearing the trial of four other men charged with sexually assaulting Joanne Young.

The alleged offences carried out by the four – Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, Richard Wilkins, 62, Norman Macksoni, 48, and Mohammed Hassan, 38 – are said to have taken place between the summer of 2016 and the winter of 2023.
Philip Young is named in each of the counts as having committed the alleged offence with the other men.

blocks.caption: A court artist’s sketch of Philip Young, right, who has pleaded guilty to charges of abuse against his former wife. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA

blocks.text: A jury panel-in-waiting of 14 – eight men and six women – was randomly selected on Monday to hear the case. After they were brought into court, they were asked to look at the defendants in the dock to check if they recognised them.
Mr Justice Saini told the jury they would have realised from a questionnaire they had been asked to fill in that the case they were to hear might upset them.

He told them it would involve evidence and videos involving “graphic and sexually explicit imagery” that some people could find upsetting. “It’s not going to be an easy case to be a juror in,” the judge said.
Saini asked the panel to reflect overnight if they had any concerns and to let him know on Tuesday morning.
The judge also warned the potential jurors not to do any research about the case or discuss it with anyone else. As the panel left the court, one juror could be seen comforting another.
Young, formerly of Swindon, has previously admitted offences including voyeurism, rape and administering a substance with intent. He had pleaded guilty to offences over a 13-year period.
Young is to be sentenced at the conclusion of the trial, which is expected to last about four weeks.
Born in Enfield in June 1976, Young graduated from the University of Westminster in 1998. He was a Conservative councillor on Swindon borough council from 2007 to 2010.
He resigned as the cabinet member for culture, regeneration and economic development in May 2010 to devote more time to his family and run his own business, the Swindon Advertiser reported.
On the first day of the trial of the four men, a number of women stood outside the court holding up banners in support of the rights of female victims of sexual crimes.
Sarah Jones KC is scheduled to open the case on Tuesday.
The trial continues.

articles.title: Southern California prepares for flooding amid forecast of ‘record-breaking tides’
articles.summary:
Residents of coastal towns told to avoid beaches during high tides and keep further away from the ocean than usual

Southern California coastal communities are preparing for days of flooding…

blocks.text: Southern California coastal communities are preparing for days of flooding amid potentially “record-breaking tides” this week.

The National Weather Service warned that significant coastal flooding was expected in San Diego and Orange counties through Thursday that could close roads and inundate homes, businesses and critical infrastructure. To the north, a wide swath of the coast from San Luis Obispo county to Los Angeles county could see “minor to moderate” coastal flooding with tides as high as 8ft.

“Avoid the beaches during high tides, keep farther back from the ocean than usual (waves will run much farther up the beach that expected), stay off rock walls/jetties, and make sure flood-prone property is protected this week,” the NWS office in San Diego said in a statement.

More than a week before the exceptionally high tides were forecast to arrive, the Orange county city of Newport Beach declared a local emergency to prepare for flooding. Staff were deploying across the area to inspect infrastructure, reinforce beach berms and install sandbags and other equipment, the city said. Newport Beach is providing free sandbags and advised residents to inspect vulnerable areas around their properties.
Due to El Niño and the Kelvin wave, ocean water levels in the region have already been about 15 to 22in higher than expected, the Newport Beach city manager, Seimone Jurjis, said in a statement.

“A foot and a half may not sound like much, but in a coastal community like ours, it can mean the difference between water staying below a seawall and water spilling into streets, garages and homes, especially during some of the highest tides of the year,” Jurjis said.

This month has already brought extreme weather in the region, including flooding that overtook city streets and large waves that struck beachside homes. The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel left a trail of destruction in California, significantly damaging homes, destroying a boardwalk and forcing residents to evacuate.
With a historic El Niño unfolding in the Pacific, California is expected to face severe storms this winter.

articles.title: Walter Koenig, Ensign Chekov on Star Trek: The Original Series, dead at 90
articles.summary: Actor Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, the youthful Russian navigator on the Star Trek television series and several movies, has died. He was 90.

image.caption: Walter Koenig, seen here as he was honoured with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on Sept. 10, 2012, died Monday at the age of 90, his talent agent said. (David Livingston/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Actor Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, the youthful Russian navigator on the Star Trek television series and several movies, has died. He was 90.
U.S. actor 'was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man and a loyal friend,' wrote co-star George Takei
Koenig died Monday at his home in the North Hollywood neighbourhood of Los Angeles, talent agent Zachery McGinnis said in a statement.

In Star Trek, Chekov was the sole Communist-bloc member of the starship Enterprise's bridge staff. His friendly, supportive presence showed how the rival nations (in the far-off future in which the show was set) were capable of working together.
Speaking heavily Russian-accented English, Chekov embodied stereotypical Russian personality traits, including fierce pride, love of poetry and blind loyalty.
Star Trek ran on NBC from 1966 to 1969 and has had an almost unprecedented afterlife as fans, or Trekkies, kept interest in the show alive.
"My heart is heavy," Koenig's castmate George Takei said in a post on social media. "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend."
George Takei as Sulu, left, and Walter Koenig as Chekov are shown in an archival photo from the set of Star Trek: The Original Series. (Getty Images)

"Walter's legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it," McGinnis said. "Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before."
McGinnis said Koenig died surrounded by his daughter and niece.
Koenig played Chekov in seven Star Trek movies starting in 1979, as well as innumerable other spinoffs, including writing a Star Trek book, Chekov's Enterprise, in 1980.
The TV show has also inspired multiple spinoff TV series, with new casts, and conventions that draw thousands of fans.
Koenig returned to the science-fiction genre with occasional appearances in the syndicated 1990s TV series Babylon 5.

articles.title: Shabana Mahmood launches review into murder of student Henry Nowak
articles.summary:
Move comes after claims there were warning signs killer had history of threatening behaviour and obsession with weapons

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has launched a review to examine…

blocks.text: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has launched a review to examine whether opportunities were missed to prevent the murder of the student Henry Nowak.
It follows claims that there were several warning signs that the perpetrator, Vickrum Digwa, had a history of threatening behaviour and an obsession with weapons.

Nowak, 18, died in December after being fatally stabbed as he walked home from a night out in Southampton. He was handcuffed by police officers while bleeding to death after Digwa falsely accused Nowak of racial abuse.
In police body-worn camera footage which prompted a public outcry, Nowak was heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replied: “Don’t think you have, mate.”

Nowak’s death sparked widespread protests, allegations of “two-tier policing” and a spike in racist attacks against the UK’s Sikh community. Digwa, a Sikh, was carrying two knives, including a kirpan, on the night of the killing. Carrying the blade is permitted in the UK for religious purposes.
Digwa, 23, has subsequently been accused by young local Sikhs of using threatening behaviour in a Southampton gurdwara, or temple, in the months leading up to the fatal attack on Nowak.

The Sun reported that Digwa was seen brandishing an airgun in his back garden in October 2022. A neighbour who recorded him firing shots said she reported this to the police, but Hampshire constabulary was unable to find a record of the incident.
Speaking in the Commons, Mahmood said the review would be led by the former Conservative lord chancellor Alex Chalk KC and would report its initial findings within five months.

“Last December, Henry Nowak’s life was cut short in a horrific and senseless act of violence. My thoughts today are with Henry’s family and his friends, who have shown extraordinary courage and dignity,” she said.
“It [the review] will investigate what was known about the perpetrator, including any missed opportunities to intervene.
“It will look at the Nowak family’s experience of the criminal justice system and whether they were supported in the manner they should have been.
“Once the Independent Office for Police Conduct [IOPC] has concluded its investigation into the police response, this review will also consider the actions of the IOPC and, if necessary, the police.”
Two officers, who were the first to arrive on the scene, are being investigated by the IOPC for potential gross misconduct.
The investigation is looking at why they did not recognise that Nowak needed urgent medical attention and at the decision to arrest him rather than provide first aid.
after newsletter promotion
Nowak’s family welcomed the review as a “significant moment” in their fight for justice.

“Since Henry was murdered, we’ve fought tirelessly for answers to questions no family should ever have to ask. The emotional toll of that fight, on top of the unimaginable grief of losing Henry, has been immense,” the family said.
“We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for.
“Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have.”
Digwa was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years. He has been given permission to challenge the length of that sentence at the court of appeal on 5 November.

Kiran Kaur, Digwa’s mother, was also jailed for three years for assisting an offender after she removed the knife used by her son. The knife was found by police at their family home along with more than 20 other weapons.

articles.title: Judge rules Trump administration illegally fired prosecutor Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director
articles.summary: The Trump administration last year illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, from her job as a federal prosecutor in New York, a federal judge ruled Monday.

image.caption: Maurene Comey, then an assistant U.S. attorney, arrives to a New York City court on May 19, 2025, when she was part of the prosecution team trying Sean (Diddy) Combs. She was fired by the Trump administration weeks later. (Ted Shaffrey/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
The Trump administration last year illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, from her job as a federal prosecutor in New York, a federal judge ruled Monday.
Comey's lawsuit is among a number of wrongful dismissal claims from former Justice Dept., FBI officials

Maurene Comey, who was an assistant U.S. attorney for a decade, was illegally fired in July 2025 despite her work on some of the country's highest-profile cases and consistently receiving "the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike," Judge Jesse M. Furman found.

After her firing, Comey sued the U.S. Justice Department and others, saying her termination violated the constitutional separation of powers, the First Amendment and the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment.

She asserted she was fired because she was the daughter of James Comey, whom U.S. President Donald Trump has long viewed as an enemy, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, the judge noted.

The judge granted Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through Dec. 20 to "make her whole" and ensure that she doesn't suffer adverse employment consequences for the "unlawful termination."

In her lawsuit, Comey asked for the retroactive pay so that she could get back pay and qualify for retirement benefits. In February, she was hired as a partner at New York law firm Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler.
Firing violated constitution, statutes: judge
Furman rejected the government's claim that Comey could be fired because federal prosecutors exercise the president's "conclusive and preclusive" powers.
He said the government's claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors "flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent."
Furman added: "Indeed, to accept defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation's constitutional system."
The firing violated the separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights, the judge ruled.
Former FBI director James Comey indicted again over social media post | Hanomansing Tonight

Furman reserved judgment on Comey's First Amendment claim pending further arguments to be submitted by each side, though he said he was inclined to dismiss the claim because it was largely moot since she is now in private practice and no longer seeks actual reinstatement.
Comey's lawyers, Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan, lauded the ruling.
"This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the president is not above the law," they said.

The Justice Department, during the Trump administration, has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of President Donald Trump or who were perceived as opposed to the administration's agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits.

items: Ex-FBI director Comey's lawyer says government tracked his phone, interviewed mob killer
Gavin Newsom says Trump directed U.S. Justice Department to investigate him

blocks.text: The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father's longtime adversarial relationship with Trump.

The president fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican's successful 2016 campaign for the White House. In the years since, Trump has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his Justice Department has worked with mixed success to make that happen.

An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of "86 47," a case he has sought to dismiss and that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.

When James Comey was originally indicted, his son-in-law, Troy Edwards Jr., resigned from his position as assistant U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia. He is married to another daughter of Comey's.

The Justice Department and the FBI are facing a number of court challenges related to the ouster of dozens of attorneys and agents who were dismissed after participating in earlier investigations of Trump, or because they were perceived as insufficiently loyal to the Republican president's agenda.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Walter Koenig, actor best known as Chekov on Star Trek, dies aged 90
articles.summary:
The actor appeared in the cult 1960s show as well as many of the films but also worked as a writer

Walter Koenig, the actor known for playing Pavel Chekov throughout the Star Trek franchise,…

blocks.text: Walter Koenig, the actor known for playing Pavel Chekov throughout the Star Trek franchise, has died, his representative confirmed to the Hollywood Reporter. He was 90.

Koenig died at his home in north Hollywood surrounded by his daughter and niece, according to a Facebook post by Zachery McGinnis, the founder of Galactic Productions, an appearance agency that counted the actor as one of its clients. His death was attributed to “old age”, with no other details provided.

“Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world,” McGinnis wrote. “Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it.”
The post concluded: “Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.”

“My heart is heavy,” wrote Koenig’s Star Trek costar George Takei on Facebook on Monday. Takei first met Koening in the 1960s, “on the bridge of the Enterprise” and remained friends for six decades; Koenig served as Takei’s best man at his wedding in 2008.

“Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend,” Takei wrote. “To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too. Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.”

Jesse Thorn, the host of the NPR show Bullseye, also confirmed the news on Bluesky, citing his friend Danielle Koenig, the late actor’s daughter. “Something I was struck by knowing Danielle, her husband and her late brother Andrew (and talking with George Takei) was the very sincere love those Star Trek cast members had for each other,” he wrote. “That whole thing was thrust upon them and their obvious deep friendship was so clear. What a gift.”

Born in Chicago but raised in Manhattan as the child of Lithuanian immigrants, Koenig began his acting career in 1962, with an uncredited role as a sentry in Combat!. He joined Star Trek for the start of the second season and appeared in 36 of the 50 episodes that aired between 1967 and 1969.

He continued his role as the Russian Chekov in the first seven Paramount movies derived from the show, released between 1979 and 1991, as well as in a two-part crowdsourced Renegades series that debuted online in 2017. He most recently reprised the voice of Chekov in a 2023 episode of the animated series Star Trek: Picard.

Koenig also worked as a writer, penning episodes for such series as The Powers of Matthew Star, Family, Land of the Lost and The Incredible Hulk. He wrote, produced and starred in the 2010 sci-film InAlienable, starring Richard Hatch.

Koenig was married to actor Judy Levitt, with whom he appeared in three Star Trek movies as well as another acclaimed sci-fi series, Babylon 5, which ran from 1994 until 1998. The couple were together from 1965 until her death in December 2022 at age 83. Their son Andrew, who played Richard “Boner” Stabone in the ABC sitcom Growing Pains, died in 2010 at age 41.
Koenig is survived by his daughter, the actor and screenwriter Danielle Koenig.

articles.title: Serbia’s Student List preparing for talks on forming government despite no clear leader
articles.summary:
Non-hierarchical movement is seeking to ‘rebuild society’ in Balkan country after years of authoritarian rule

Serbia’s triumphant but untested Student List movement is preparing to start…
articles.byline: Jon Henley and Ana Milosavljevic in Belgrade

blocks.text: Serbia’s triumphant but untested Student List movement is preparing to start talks on forming a government capable of reversing 14 years of increasingly authoritarian nationalist rule, after a seismic weekend election win.

Supporters of the movement, which has no experience of government, took to the streets in the west Balkan country on Monday after the strongman former president, Aleksandar Vučić, was defeated in a historic landslide.

Vučić conceded defeat late on Sunday, bringing his domination of Serbian politics to an abrupt end and capping two years of anti-government protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy at the Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.

With 100% of ballot samples counted, projected results from the Centre for Free Elections and Democracy in Belgrade showed the Student List on 53% of the vote, giving it 141 MPs in the 250-seat parliament, while Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS) won 39%, giving it 103. The remaining seats went to national minority party lists.

As yet, there are few clues as to how the winning movement, built around collective decision-making, will actually govern. Its candidates included academics, actors and farmers as well as students, but it is deliberately leaderless with no hierarchy, so it is unclear who it will appoint as the prime minister and cabinet.

Prominent Student List figures include: ​Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist who headed the candidate list; Dejan Šoškić, a former central bank governor; and Radomir Saičić, a chemistry professor at Belgrade ​University who spoke on behalf ‌of the List after its ​victory.

Much like Péter Magyar’s Tisza party, which ended Viktor Orbán’s 16 years of illiberal government in Hungary this spring, the List faces public institutions staffed with civil servants loyal to the outgoing regime, complicating the task of institutional overhaul.

“Everyone in the student movement, and every candidate on the list, has a complete and very clear understanding of the weight of the responsibility before us,” said Ana Mirković, a university educationist, psychologist and Student List candidate.
“We do not see the election result as gaining power and privileges, but as taking on a historic debt to our own people and to our own children.”
Mirković told the Guardian the movement’s first priority was “the social and psychological detoxification” of the country.

Vučić’s 14-year rule has been described as a “textbook regime” of autocracy, with his party extending control over the media, judiciary and other state institutions and elections marred by registration irregularities, media bias and voter bribes.

The students’ platform centres on a pledge to fight corruption and restore the rule of law, including creating an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors, not the interior ministry, and a purge of police officers linked to organised crime.

blocks.caption: Student List supporters in Belgrade react to the rightwing Serbian Progressive party conceding defeat on Sunday. Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/AP

blocks.text: It also aims to ban appointments of party loyalists to state-owned companies and to promote financial accountability and public scrutiny – by new independent bodies – of all major state infrastructure contracts ⁠to curb the misuse of public funds.

Mirković said the new government would dismantle a “system of intimidation” that encouraged “fear and polarisation”, by “urgently opening up” the media, putting an end to pressure on public-sector workers and “stopping institutional violence”.

She added that the aim was to “rebuild society from the ground up: full disclosure of all contracts and financial flows; depoliticising and strengthening the judiciary; renewing the education and healthcare systems”, and that state capture should “never again” be possible.

The Student List deliberately kept divisive foreign policy issues, including relations with the EU and Russia, in the background. The Kremlin said on Monday it hoped the new leaders “understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interests”.
after newsletter promotion

Dušan Vučićević, an analyst, said that, from the outset, the movement “insisted as much as possible that Serbia must first and foremost address domestic political issues – the literal dismantling of every institution, from the national to the local level”.

The students’ win marks a profound political shift in Serbia and could potentially offer inspiration to other student movements that have cropped up across Europe in recent weeks demanding better education standards and prospects.

However, Vučićević said it was distinct from other protests. “This experiment in grassroots democracy ultimately secured more than 50% of the vote,” he told Agence France-Presse, but it was “unclear whether a similar model could work in other countries”.

Nikola Burazer, programme director at the Belgrade-based Centre for Contemporary Politics, said on Monday that the movement’s decision-making process also needed to “be sped up”, as its process for choosing candidates “actually took a long time – months”.

He added: “After people are done celebrating and thinking about what happened yesterday, we will focus a bit more on what’s coming up, and how the government will look. Twenty-four hours ago that all seemed like a fantasy.”

On Sunday, Vučić, who maintained close ties with Russia throughout his tenure, blamed his party’s defeat on “the direct support of various European countries and the US deep state, the one that is also against President Trump”.

International leaders, meanwhile, joined a chorus of welcome to the students on Monday. “This is clearly a new chapter in the history of the country and its people,” said the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

“We wish ⁠Serbia success, real development, and warm ⁠relations with the European community. ​We in Ukraine thank Serbia for respecting our people, our state, and our independence. And we always celebrate our shared achievements.”

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said Berlin would “actively support Serbia’s European path” after the victory, saying the students “with their demand for the rule of law, fighting corruption and fundamental freedoms, have reached the people”.
Serbia’s constitution requires the new parliament to convene within 30 days of the official election result, and sets a 90-day deadline after that for formation of the new government.
The country must also hold new presidential elections before 27 December, since Vučić stepped down to run for prime minister.

articles.title: German police probe cruise ship captain after Bremerhaven collision
articles.summary: A three-ship collision has led to the cancellation of a cruise and expensive damages. Shipyard repairs are needed, and further cruises could be affected.

image.caption: Police are investigating whether the captain breached his duty of care during the ship's departureImage: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German police are investigating the captain of the Mein Schiff 3 cruise liner after it collided with two container ships in Bremerhaven.
The collision caused damage estimated to be in the millions of euros and forced the cancellation of a 20-day Canary Islands cruise, with further voyages potentially affected.
Why are police investigating the captain?

A police spokesperson said proceedings over a possible administrative offense had been opened to establish whether the captain breached his duty of care. Police have not specified the suspected lapse.
Broadcaster RTL reported that investigators spoke to the captains of all three vessels overnight into Monday.
How did the collision happen?
Tugboats were helping the nearly fully booked cruise ship leave the northern German port on Sunday evening when a gust of wind pushed it toward two moored container ships, police said.
The liner was carrying 2,428 passengers and 922 crew members. Nobody was injured, and none of the vessels took on water.
The larger container ship suffered substantial damage, with several meters of its port side torn open and container guides deformed. The smaller vessel sustained minor damage.
The cruise ship was also significantly damaged. Photographs showed damage to its lifeboats and bridge.

blocks.caption: The collision forced the cancellation of a 20-day Canary Islands cruise, with police investigating the captainImage: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: All damage was several meters above the waterline. The liner returned to the cruise terminal after the collision.
Could more cruises be canceled?
Technical experts boarded the ship shortly after the accident and determined that shipyard repairs were necessary, operator TUI Cruises said.

The company called canceling the Canary Islands voyage "the only responsible decision," saying passenger and crew safety had "highest priority." Passengers were initially allowed to remain aboard while the company arranged assistance.
It remained unclear whether other voyages planned for this year could go ahead.
The collision initially caused no disruption to other harbor traffic.

articles.title: Drug, roadworthiness tests at bus terminals as PH readies for Undas 2026
articles.summary: Authorities carried out drug and alcohol tests on provincial bus drivers and tested buses for roadworthiness at several terminals in Metro Manila ahead of Undas 2026.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 12:56am

Authorities carried out drug and alcohol tests on provincial bus drivers and tested buses for roadworthiness at several terminals in Metro Manila ahead of the expected deluge of passengers leaving town for Undas 2026.
With a few days to go before the Undas properly begins at the weekend, many people are already at the bus terminals, having decided to leave to beat the bulk of the holiday rush.
In Mark Salazar's report on Saksi on Monday, Samantha Pilapil was among the passengers waiting to board the bus to Masbate at a terminal in Cubao, Quezon City.
"Kaya ako bumiyahe nang maaga kasi ayoko pong makisiksik sa maraming tao," she said, cradling one-year-old child on her lap.
(I'm traveling early because I don't want to squeeze in with the crowds.)
Some buses were also stopped from traveling due to deficiencies, with passengers having to disembark to move to another bus.

According to the Land Transportation Office (LTO), 51 out of 52 passenger buses passed the roadworthiness inspection conducted at the terminals in Manila, Parañaque and Caloocan City. The lone failure didn't pass due to a broken reverse light and plate light, and an expired fire extinguisher. The driver was instructed to have the defects repaired and the expired fire extinguisher replaced before traveling again.
NAIA preps

Meanwhile, the country's gateway NAIA is preparing for an estimated 1.25 million passengers during the Undas travel period from Oct. 27 to Nov. 4, with airport authorities projecting Oct. 30 to be the busiest day.

In a news release, New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC), the airport operator, said it expects passenger traffic during the nine-day period to increase by 1% from the 1.24 million recorded during the same period last year. About 149,000 travelers are expected to pass through the airport on Oct. 30 alone.

To manage the holiday rush, NNIC said it would deploy additional personnel, strengthen security and passenger assistance services, and maintain round-the-clock monitoring of airport operations. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: More than 60 Christians killed in Ethiopia 'massacre', church official says
articles.summary: One resident, whose 75-year-old father was killed, described it as an ambush, saying they were surrounded.

blocks.text: More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks on Christians in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the country's Orthodox Church.

One resident, whose 75-year-old father was killed, described it as an ambush. "We were completely unprepared and had no prior knowledge. They surrounded us from all four directions," he told BBC Amharic.
The regional government said that it would take action against those responsible.

A local official blamed the attacks on a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has not commented but has denied carrying out previous such attacks.
A statement from the Holy Synod of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church said that 20 houses were burnt to the ground in the attacks. It did not say who was responsible.
Eyewitness told BBC Amharic that five of those killed were children.
A church official described the attacks on three areas in the Shirka district as a "massacre", saying security forces arrived at the scene but were unable to stop the assault.
Many residents have now fled the area.

Condemning the violence, the Orthodox Church said attacks against Christians had been increasing recently, and that "such actions undermine the country's values of mutual respect and peaceful coexistence".

In a statement posted on Facebook, the Orthodox Church said it had repeatedly raised concerns about insecurity with authorities at different levels of government, but that "so far there has been no solution".
The Ethiopian Human Rights Council, a non-governmental organisation, said in a report released in July 2026 that 458 people had been killed in attacks in that area over the previous four years.
But this is one of the most deadly attacks in that period.
The report said armed groups had repeatedly targeted local communities, particularly followers of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, in what it described as religiously motivated attacks.

The government has previously blamed the OLA for the attacks, with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed saying violence targeting civilians and religious institutions was part of a plan to destabilise the country.
The group, which says it is fighting for greater rights for the Oromo people, denies these allegations.
Previous reports have also documented attacks against Muslims in the area. Residents who spoke to the BBC on various occasions have described the violence as both ethnic and religious in nature.
About two-thirds of Ethiopians are Christians, mostly Orthodox, while one third are Muslim.

articles.title: Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global
articles.summary: The next fortnight sees two elections on different continents. The outcomes will shape geopolitics and the global economy, writes James Landale

blocks.text: Image source, Getty
By
Diplomatic correspondentReporting fromJerusalem

blocks.caption: James Landale

blocks.text: In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.
By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.
Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.
A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.
For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.
The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.
And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.
Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has highlighted his alliance with US President Donald Trump - including in this Likud party election billboard in Tel Aviv

blocks.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has highlighted his alliance with US President Donald Trump - including in this Likud party election billboard in Tel Aviv

Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC.

But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and much of the world's energy supply.
The Iran question
The sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran.
He has made new claims – without providing evidence – about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown.
His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel.
US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran.

Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war.

blocks.caption: Image caption, President Trump has been campaigning on behalf of Republican congressional candidates, including in Michigan on Sunday, where there's a tight Senate race

blocks.text: Image source, REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst
President Trump has been campaigning on behalf of Republican congressional candidates, including in Michigan on Sunday, where there's a tight Senate race

So might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election.

He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity – involving him – rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption.

So real is this speculation that Netanyahu's rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has already ruled out joining any unity government. Like all mainstream Israeli politicians, Eisenkot sees Iran as an existential threat to Israel and supports military action against the Islamic regime. But he has explicitly warned against escalating the war for political purposes.
'Legacy mode'

Certainly, Trump may be more willing to attack Iran after the midterms if he is unconstrained electorally and hoping to extract himself from the war with one more push. Some analysts believe Iran is so economically weak from the war and economic sanctions that a fresh round of military strikes might encourage Iranians to overthrow the regime. Others see this as yet more wishful thinking. It is a strategy that has repeatedly failed, but still has currency in Washington.
"After the midterms, he will be in legacy mode," one well-placed Western diplomat told me. "He will want to show agency on anything that is not the quagmire at home."

In Israel there is a broad consensus across most parties about the threat from and the need to constrain Iran. But if voters elect a new government, they might have a prime minister with less political and personal investment in fresh attacks.

In those circumstances, Trump has suggested his thinking may change, too. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi [a nickname for Netanyahu], America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote on social media.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Netanyahu has used this year's election campaign to talk up the possibility of a fresh attack on Iran

blocks.text: Netanyahu has used this year's election campaign to talk up the possibility of a fresh attack on Iran

Little wonder policymakers in Tehran have been following US opinion polls as closely as any analyst inside the Washington beltway. The risk, of course, is that any post-electoral strikes would plunge the Middle East into fresh chaos if Iran were to retaliate hard.
Publicly and privately, Iranian officials have threatened to hit airports, pipelines, undersea cables, energy facilities, desalination plants as well as US bases and warships.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, wrote in the Financial Times that new attacks would put "civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk".
It's the economy

The two elections again intertwine around the global economy. Affordability and cost of living have dominated campaigning for the midterms, issues made worse by Trump's war that raised prices as Iran choked the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz.

The economy is also an election issue in Israel, where voters face high costs and low wages. But here, too, the war plays its part with soaring defence spending putting even more pressure on the public finances.

Trump has sought to appease voters ahead of the midterms. He has lifted sanctions on Russia, hoping in vain that by importing diesel from Moscow, prices might fall significantly. He has been taking a tough line with Ukraine, calling on its leadership to make concessions in the hope – also so far in vain – of claiming a foreign policy victory.

But Republican ire at his controversial strategy is growing. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a frequent critic of Trump, told CBS News: "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid [favour] for Vladimir Putin."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Early voting has already started in many US states for next month's midterms

blocks.text: Image source, Chris Torres / EPA/Shutterstock
Early voting has already started in many US states for next month's midterms

One consequence of the Iran war – along with Israel's military operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank – is that traditional bipartisan support in the US has fractured. Abdul El-Sayed, the left-wing Democratic candidate for the Senate in Michigan, campaigns on cutting military aid to Israel. "An ally that takes your money, to push you into wars you shouldn't be fighting, is not an ally," he told ABC News.

The US and Israel initially attacked Iran to destroy its ballistic missiles, degrade its nuclear capability, weaken its support for proxy militias and even oust the entire regime. Since then its war aims have changed to reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Brad Lander, a Democratic congressional candidate in New York who also sits on the left of his party, chose even to travel to the West Bank only days before polling. He helped Palestinians harvest olives and was briefly detained by Israeli forces, all grist to his social media electoral mill. In the history of US politics, this is not normal. Even Netanyahu is warning that Israel may in future have to survive without a US security blanket.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The leader of Israel's Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, has ruled out joining a unity government after the elections

blocks.text: Image source, Abir Sultan Credit / EPA/Shutterstock
The leader of Israel's Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, has ruled out joining a unity government after the elections

Of course, if Israel's prime minister were to lose, his departure would end a scratchy bromance that has seen Trump blow hot and cold. Last week the president called his Israeli counterpart a "great warrior prime minister". During the summer, he said Netanyahu was "effing crazy". A new Israeli leader would have to forge a new relationship with an outgoing US president, a very different dynamic.

If the Democrats were to win greater control in Congress, that might place some check on blanket US support for Israel. Congress has traditional powers that it can use to restrain military spending. It could also cut military aid to Israel. But as president, Trump would retain significant executive power – and a veto – to continue prosecuting the conflict as he saw fit.

The decision by Israel and the US to go to war with Iran earlier this year transformed the global economy and international geopolitics. The choices voters in both nations make in coming days may shape where the world goes next.
Top image credit: Getty.

articles.title: Horse-drawn carriages are still a tradition in some Canadian cities
articles.summary: The horse-drawn carriage industry is again getting a lot of neigh-sayers, after New York City council passed a bill last week that would ban the rides by June 2028.

image.caption: Caleche driver Nathalie Matte gives a carrot to horse Marilyn during a demonstration in front of Montreal City Hall on May 24, 2016, four years before horse-drawn carriage tours were banned in the city. (Paul Chiasson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada
The horse-drawn carriage industry is again getting a lot of neigh-sayers, after New York City council passed a bill last week that would ban the rides by June 2028.
You can take a horse-drawn carriage tour in places like Victoria, Vancouver, Quebec City and Charlottetown
The vote came after a teenage tourist died last spring when he was thrown from the carriage as a horse bolted away from its driver.

The legislation requires Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office to develop a plan by next April to help the more than 150 remaining drivers and the rest of the industry find other jobs, and it's revived an ongoing debate in North America over the practice of using horses to pull tourists on city streets.

items: New York City council votes to advance bill that would ban horse-drawn carriages

blocks.text: In Canada, several large cities still permit horse-drawn carriage rides — or calèches, as they're known in Quebec — though this hasn't been without controversy.

Toronto banned the carriages in its downtown core in 1998, but Montreal didn't look into doing so until 20 years later. In 2018, a horse collapsed and died in the middle of a guided tour, prompting then-mayor Valérie Plante to propose a ban on the calèches that took effect in 2020.
The city worked with the provincial labour department to help calèches drivers find other work and offered to pay owners $1,000 per horse to retire the animals.
The move drew outcry, with horse carriage owner Denis Murray telling CBC at the time it was "stupid." Murray said he and his horse Sissi shared a close bond and that she enjoyed the work.
She was later adopted by a veterinarian couple in Quebec's Eastern Townships, where Murray said he was happy to see she appeared to be doing well.
Denis Murray with his horse Sissi. (Submitted by Denis Murray)
Canadian cities should 'take note': animal rights group
The tours have persisted elsewhere in the country, including Victoria, Vancouver, Quebec City and Charlottetown.

"It's time for other Canadian cities to take note," said Bianca Del Bois, a spokesperson for the Animal Alliance of Canada, who added that while the group is "delighted" to see Manhattan undertake a ban on the carriages, it also welcomes the measures for workers accompanying the legislation.
"I don't think the humans are lost in this," she added.
Sinikka Crosland of the Canadian Horse Defence Coalition agrees.
"This is an important consideration, making the end of the industry more fair and palatable," she told CBC.
'Hot-button issue' in Victoria

The opposition in Victoria has been spirited in the past decade, to say the least. In May 2018, a video showing two Victoria Carriage Tours horses slipping, tangling harnesses and collapsing near the Ogden Point cruise terminal after a minor bump with a bus went viral and caused outrage.
The B.C. SPCA called on Victoria City Council to ban horse-drawn carriages from busy downtown streets or restrict them strictly to park environments.

Activist groups like the Victoria Horse Alliance and the Animal Protection Party of Canada — which shares many members with the Animal Alliance — gathered tens of thousands of signatures and pushed for a complete phase-out or ban.

A horse-drawn carriage is seen in Victoria on March 24, 2016. Victoria councillors at the time considered tightening city regulations governing horse-drawn carriage tours as part of proposed wholesale changes to its animal control bylaw. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)

In May 2019, councillors weighed phase-out proposals and carriage operators threatened legal action against the city. Victoria's council ultimately struck down a motion to ban the horse-drawn carriage industry by a six-to-two vote in March 2020, allowing the operations to continue.
Protests continued, but Donna Friedlander, the owner and operator of Tally-Ho Carriage Tours, decried animal activists in The Times Colonist newspaper for harassing her employees.

She said protesters filmed her staff throughout their work day and surrounded them as they set out on tours, "hurtling unrelenting verbal assaults at my staff who are horse professionals, working tirelessly out of love to ensure the safety, health and happiness of the carriage horses," Friedlander wrote.
Colleen Mycroft, a spokesperson for the City of Victoria, recalled the issue being a "hot-button topic," with some of the protests taking place outside city hall.

"There were motions from councillors. There was pleading from those that were supporting the businesses. And then there were folks that thought it was cruelty to the horses … but nothing came of it," Mycroft said.
Changing practices ahead of city legislation
Two horse-drawn carriage tour companies continue to operate in Quebec City, where the 400-year-old buildings in the old quarters draw tourists from around the world.
One of them, Calèches Québec, notes in a voice message on its phone line that since 2025 it no longer offers last-minute or day-of tours, in the best interest of its horses.
The company did not immediately reply to CBC's request for more information.
A horse-drawn carriage carries people on the Plains of Abraham as part of Quebec City's winter carnival on Feb. 4, 2010. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)

In Vancouver, park board staff considered removing "animal-powered transportation" from Stanley Park, where it is permitted. But, according to a statement from the board to CBC, "a review of recent Park Board records did not identify any motions from recent years seeking to end horse-drawn carriage tours in Stanley Park."

Whether the New York ban will convince these Canadian cities to rein in the horse carriages remains to be seen. Until then, the push and pull of those for and against this storied tradition is bound — just like time and the tides — to carry on.
With files from The Associated Press and The Canadian Press
