articles.title: 10 percent of pupils in Grades 1-3 are struggling readers
articles.summary: Ten percent of Grades 1 to 3 learners are struggling readers, according to the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM2).

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Ten percent of Grades 1 to 3 learners are struggling readers, according to the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM2).
Based on the End-of-School-Year 2025-2026 assessment, EDCOM2 said 10 percent of the 5,127,670 learners covered were still struggling to read.

The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao recorded the highest proportion of struggling readers at 25.5 percent, followed by Soccsksargen at 17.7 percent and the Zamboanga Peninsula at 14.7 percent, according to the EDCOM2 Early Childhood Dashboard.
Bicol ranked fourth at 12 percent, followed by the Davao region at 11.7 percent and Mimaropa at 11.3 percent.

The Negros Island Region and Central Visayas both recorded 10.4 percent, while Caraga had 10 percent, Ilocos 9.4 percent, Northern Mindanao 9.3 percent, Cagayan Valley 8.6 percent, Western Visayas 8.2 percent, Central Luzon 7.9 percent, Eastern Visayas 7.2 percent and Calabarzon 6.7 percent.
The Cordillera Administrative Region and the National Capital Region recorded the lowest proportions of struggling readers at 5.3 percent each.
In Davao del Sur, struggling readers accounted for 9.5 percent of learners, while Davao City recorded 9.3 percent, EDCOM2 said.
Meanwhile, only 25 percent of senior high school students in Davao City were considered independent readers based on the Senior High School Learning Needs Assessment results for EOSY 2025-2026.
The EDCOM2 early childhood dashboard consolidates local data on child nutrition, early literacy and Child Development Center coverage to support targeted early childhood interventions.
Social media

In a separate development, Education Secretary Sonny Angara yesterday backed efforts to regulate social media use among minors, saying the government cannot control children’s exposure to online platforms at home.

Angara’s statement came after the Senate passed on third and final reading a bill requiring high-risk digital services to suspend, restrict, disable or remove accounts owned, operated or used by individuals under 18.

“The proposed bill is important. I know that there are debates on what is the right age, etc.,” Angara said after attending the Comprehensive Media Program for Children and Its Role in Policy Making summit in Quezon City.

The proposed Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act seeks to prohibit minors from accessing high-risk digital services, including Roblox and GoreBox, online platforms where vulnerable young people are reportedly groomed into committing violent acts.

“But for us, we can’t control everything. We prohibit the use of those apps in schools. But when it comes to their own homes, we can’t control it. That’s why we appreciate those kinds of social media regulations. And it’s proven that if children use apps for a long time, their depression and anxiety will increase,” Angara said.

The proposed ban does not cover email services, private messaging services, online gaming services not primarily used for social networking, educational platforms, news services and professional collaboration services.

articles.title: All senators should reject VP offer – Alan Peter
articles.summary: Just like impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero, fellow senators should reject any offer from Malacañang to take over the country’s second highest post in case Vice…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:00am
Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano on July 27, 2026.
Ryan Baldemor / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — Just like impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero, fellow senators should reject any offer from Malacañang to take over the country’s second highest post in case Vice President Sara Duterte is convicted in her impeachment trial, Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano said yesterday.

In a Facebook post, Cayetano lauded Escudero’s stand not to accept any offer to become vice president, as he called on the rest of the senator-judges to be neutral and focus on evaluating the pieces of evidence presented.

“This is correct. All of us senator-judges should make this declaration. It’s essential that in all impeachment proceedings (especially of presidents and vice presidents), senator-judges are politically neutral and will have no incentive to convict except for evidence that proves the article/s of impeachment,” Cayetano said.
According to the 1987 Constitution, the president may nominate a vice president in case of vacancy from among the members of the Senate or the House of Representatives.
Cayetano was reacting to Escudero’s remarks during a recent podcast, where the latter said it would be a conflict of interest if he were to benefit from Duterte’s removal from office.
“I will not accept for a simple reason, conflict of interest,” Escudero said.
Escudero said it was his personal stand not to accept the hypothetical offer and is not being imposed upon anyone. He stressed that there was nothing to reject because there was no proposal.

articles.title: ‘Government began preparing for super El Niño last year’
articles.summary: Contrary to public perception, the Marcos administration began preparing for the effects of the anticipated super El Niño as early as 2025, Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian said.

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:00am
DSWD Secretary Rex Gatchalian explains the agency’s science-backed pail with a filtration system.

MANILA, Philippines — Contrary to public perception, the Marcos administration began preparing for the effects of the anticipated super El Niño as early as 2025, Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian said.
“When we talk about El Niño, we have to understand that yes, it is a concern, but yes, we (also) saw this coming,” Gatchalian told The STAR’s “Truth on the Line” yesterday.

Gatchalian said the government is adopting a whole-of-government approach to address the effects of the weather phenomenon, citing preparations that include food stockpiling, solar-powered water pumps, water impounding projects and additional water treatment facilities.
He said the Department of Agriculture has 75 days’ worth of buffer stocks of rice, both locally produced and imported, as well as more than 100 days’ worth of supplies of pork and chicken.

“Our supplies are in those cold storages. So, this means this had been laid out already ahead of time. So, from helping our farmers to stockpiling food, we have more than enough, because that falls into food security,” he said.

The government has also been rolling out solar-powered water pumps to reduce reliance on electricity-driven systems, with President Marcos inaugurating completed facilities in Ifugao, Cagayan and Cananga in Ormoc, Leyte.

“Why solar? Because it is very important that you don’t want to be overly reliant on electricity-driven pumps. Now these pumps, as early as 2024, I went with him to Isabela, they’ve been rolling this out over the years,” he added.
Gatchalian said the government had also been building small water impounding facilities since 2023 to store water from springs, rivers and streams, including in remote communities.
Authorities have likewise been encouraging the use of deep wells to help communities secure water supplies during the dry season.
The government has activated more than 60 to 70 dormant deep wells and expects to bring more back into operation, he said.
Six new water treatment facilities, mostly in Luzon where many of the country’s dams are located, are also expected to become operational this month.

“We’re asking our citizens to collect rainwater. But how are they going to use it? So, we need some type of filtration system to make sure the water they will be drinking is potable. Now this system – it’s by a group called Waves for Water,” Gatchalian said.
Waves for Water operates in more than 40 countries and provides clean water facilities.
The filtration system, initially used for camping and outdoor activities, is among the government’s interventions to help communities access potable water.

Meanwhile, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System, Local Water Utilities Administration and Department of Agriculture are working to repair water distribution systems and reduce water losses, Gatchalian said.
The Department of Energy, for its part, is working to maintain stable power supply through measures that include battery storage systems and energy barges in island provinces.

articles.title: Expanded SOVFAs with like-minded countries eyed
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. yesterday raised the possibility of expanding the Philippines’ Status of Visiting Forces Agreements (SOVFAs) with like-minded countries to strengthen…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:00am
Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr..
STAR / Mong Pintolo

MANILA, Philippines — Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. yesterday raised the possibility of expanding the Philippines’ Status of Visiting Forces Agreements (SOVFAs) with like-minded countries to strengthen international peacekeeping cooperation and enhance military interoperability.

Speaking at the opening ceremony of the Association of Asia-Pacific Peace Operations Training Centers 13th Annual General Meeting and Workshop 2026, Teodoro said expanding the SOVFAs with other nations will advance collective security efforts under the auspices of the United Nations.

The Philippines has SOVFAs with France, Canada, Australia, Japan and New Zealand, anchored on shared principles of international law, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, interoperability, collective security and deterrence.

“It opens up my eyes, too, to the possibility of stronger relationships to include perhaps Status of Visiting Forces Agreements with countries where we do not have a misalignment of fundamental values,” Teodoro said.
He emphasized that such partnerships could facilitate more realistic joint training, strengthen force protection and improve the delivery of essential services to conflict-affected communities.

The defense chief also urged the Armed Forces of the Philippines to actively cooperate with regional peacekeeping partners and explore opportunities to enhance defense cooperation, citing peacekeeping as a powerful instrument of military diplomacy that builds knowledge sharing, professional relationships and partnerships among participating countries.

He stressed the necessity of having proper rules of engagement, effective command-and-control arrangements and adequate force protection measures to ensure that peacekeepers can perform their mandated tasks without being unnecessarily exposed to harm while maintaining the credibility and effectiveness of UN peacekeeping operations.
Regional defense
Teodoro will also lead discussions to advance regional defense dialogue and strengthen cooperation among ASEAN member-states and dialogue partners during the meetings in Lapu-Lapu City, Cebu.

The Philippines, through the Department of National Defense, will host the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting and the 13th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) on Oct. 28 and 29 as part of the Philippines’ 2026 ASEAN chairship under the theme “Navigating Our Future, Together.”
As chair of the ADMM and ADMM-Plus for 2026, Teodoro is scheduled to hold meetings with his counterparts to discuss bilateral defense cooperation and matters of mutual interest.

articles.title: Ombudsman to monitor budget, review SC ruling
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman plans to form a group that will review the Supreme Court ruling that struck down the national budgets in 2024 and 2025 along with portions of the 2026 outlay as…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:00am
An undated photo of the Ombudsman office.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman plans to form a group that will review the Supreme Court ruling that struck down the national budgets in 2024 and 2025 along with portions of the 2026 outlay as unconstitutional.
The ombudsman also vowed to look at alleged anomalies in the budget proposals.
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said his agency “always (evaluates) decisions of the (SC) when they pinpoint culpability.”

Remulla made the remark after journalists asked if the ombudsman would study the SC ruling that invalidated the 2024 and 2025 national budgets, as well as specific provisions in this year’s national budget, primarily due to unlawful increases in unprogrammed appropriations (UA).

“We have to act so we will study all of that and look at where the fault was, and how to make people explain their side or at least be made responsible for what they did,” he said at the SC yesterday.

The former congressman said after President Marcos finishes the proposed budget for the year, “the action goes on inside Congress, and it’s very hard to follow the action, especially for those who were scheming to add things and subtract things.”
One aspect of the budget that the ombudsman might look into is the “parked” allocations which, according to Remulla, was a “sign of bad faith, of playing with people’s money.”
Remulla attended the signing of the memorandum of understanding between the Justice Sector Coordinating Council and the ombudsman yesterday.
The ombudsman, outgoing Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo and representatives from the Department of Justice and the Department of the Interior and Local Government signed the agreement.

Meanwhile, Baguio City Mayor Benjamin Magalong is calling for an ombudsman probe and a Commission on Audit (COA) review of the SC ruling and demanded accountability among officials behind the questioned appropriations.
Magalong urged the COA to scrutinize the increases and called on the Office of the Ombudsman to investigate and hold accountable any official found responsible for any wrongdoing. — Artemio Dumlao

articles.title: DepEd: Complete suspension of classes if temperature hits 42 degrees Celsius
articles.summary: Education Secretary Sonny Angara has issued comprehensive guidelines for schools amid the threat of the super El Niño, ordering the suspension of all physical and home-based academic…
articles.byline: EJ Macababbad, Louella Desiderio, Bella Cariaso

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Education Secretary Sonny Angara has issued comprehensive guidelines for schools amid the threat of the super El Niño, ordering the suspension of all physical and home-based academic activities once ambient temperature hits 42 degrees Celsius, to ensure the safety of learners and teachers.
“We cannot afford to wait until extreme heat hits before we act. Our plan this year is proactive, deliberate and organized,” he said.

Angara signed Department of Education (DepEd) Memorandum 64, Series of 2026, which aims to keep school environments safe, protect the health of learners and personnel and ensure that learning continues throughout the anticipated dry spell.

“We are making sure our schools are fully prepared to manage heat stress, water shortages and health risks, protecting the safety and well-being of our learners and personnel without unnecessarily sacrificing precious classroom time,” he added.
Under the guidelines, physical classes will be suspended when temperatures reach 33 to 41 degrees Celsius, with learners shifting to lighter home-based tasks and health check-ins.
When temperatures range from 27 to 32 degrees Celsius, school heads may shorten in-person hours or shift to hybrid and flexible home-based schedules.
Regular face-to-face classes with scheduled hydration breaks may continue when temperatures remain below 27 degrees Celsius.

“Every community experiences weather conditions differently. Through our 4H framework and daily classroom-level monitoring, we are empowering our school heads with the flexibility to adjust hours or shift to modular learning only when local conditions genuinely require it,” Angara said.

The policy takes effect immediately and will remain in force until the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration officially announces the end of the 2026-2027 El Niño episode.

Beyond its impact on classroom activities, the anticipated El Niño could put further pressure on household budgets, as the Philippines is among the economies most exposed to rising prices from the weather phenomenon, according to research and analysis firm BMI.
BMI expects drought-driven food inflation to be the main economic risk from the El Niño episode.

“Local food inflation has historically been 1.8 to 2.5 pp (percentage points) higher within a year of an extreme drought and El Niño makes such droughts significantly more likely in exposed regions,” it said in its report.
While food stocks could cushion the impact, BMI said Southeast Asia has thin buffers, putting rice, palm oil and coffee supplies at risk.
“Rice stocks have fallen below 2023 levels in Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines, leaving the Philippines, which imports around a third of its rice, most exposed to higher prices,” BMI said.
However, well-stocked global rice markets limit the risk of a repeat of the price spike seen in 2023 to 2024.

BMI said El Niño could increase drought risks for cropland across Southeast Asia, Southern Africa, Central America and northern South America, threatening the production of rice, maize, sugar, palm oil and coffee.
Overall inflation accelerated to 7.2 percent in September, ending a four-month downtrend, driven mainly by faster increases in food prices.
Food inflation rose to 6.8 percent from 4.6 percent in August, largely due to higher vegetable prices.
From January to September, overall inflation averaged 5.4 percent, above the government’s two to four percent target.

articles.title: DFA: No deal with Taiwan on undersea cables
articles.summary: The Philippines has no special arrangement with Taiwan for the protection of undersea cables or for dealing with Beijing’s “gray zone” activities, the Department of Foreign Affairs…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines has no special arrangement with Taiwan for the protection of undersea cables or for dealing with Beijing’s “gray zone” activities, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) clarified yesterday, denying a declaration made by Manila’s deputy chief of mission in Washington.
“The department clarifies that there is no cooperative arrangement with Taiwan on subsea cables or other critical undersea infrastructure,” the DFA said in a statement.
“The department reiterates that the Philippines adheres to its longstanding and consistent One-China Policy, which was outlined recently in the statement dated 22 October 2026,” it said.

The DFA was reacting to reports quoting Manila’s deputy chief of mission in Washington Felipe Cariño III as saying during a seminar that the Philippines was exploring deeper cooperation with Taiwan on protecting undersea cables and addressing “gray-zone” activity.
Cariño said this “pragmatic and practical approach” with Taiwan is necessary to protect mutual interests in the Bashi Channel between Taiwan and the Philippines.

“These are very important features that should be protected, so much so that we are exploring deeper cooperation with our friends in Taiwan,” Carino said, adding that the Philippines was doing so “notwithstanding our one-China policy.”

On Sunday, a China Coast Guard ship and two rigid-hull inflatable boats tailed a Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) vessel while it was in an operation to drive away a Vietnamese fishing vessel near Pag-asa Island.
According to PCG spokesman for the West Philippine Sea Rear Adm. Jay Tarriela, the Vietnamese vessel was spotted in the morning about 2.7 nautical miles west of the island, near Sandy Cay.
Tarriela said the PCG deployed a high-speed response boat to drive the vessel from the vicinity.
But during the operation, a CCG ship with bow number 21581 and two rigid-hull inflatable boats followed the PCG vessel apparently to interfere in its operation.

“The China Coast Guard has no lawful authority to exercise any policing role within the territorial sea of Pag-asa Island, and its persistent presence in these waters is being closely monitored and documented,” Tarriela said.
The operation marked the PCG’s seventh repel mission in less than four weeks to drive away foreign vessels from the Kalayaan Island Group.
“Under international law, the Philippines exercises full sovereignty over its territorial sea, where no foreign vessel may fish without authorization,” the PCG official said.
Philippine ships shadow China carrier group

Last Thursday, the Philippine Navy’s guided missile frigate BRP Diego Silang and patrol ship BRP Emilio Jacinto conducted shadowing operations on the Chinese navy’s Liaoning carrier group when it passed through the Basilan Strait, the Western Mindanao Command said yesterday.

The PCG’s BRP Sarangani joined in the monitoring of the carrier group initially spotted northwest of Talulu Point, Siocon, Zamboanga del Norte, and later in the waters southwest of Maitum, towards the Celebes Sea.
A Black Hawk helicopter and an NC-212i aircraft of the Philippine Air Force also helped monitor the movement of the carrier group. The Chinese carrier group had its communication line shut down.
“The presence of the transiting carrier group was observed to be continuous and expeditious,” the Westmincom reported.
Reacting to the operation of the Chinese carrier strike group, former lawmaker Robert Ace Barbers said the Philippines will never be cowed by China’s show of military might.

“China must understand one fundamental truth: the Philippines is not a doormat, and our silence must never be mistaken for weakness. We will not be intimidated by aircraft carriers, escort warships or calculated displays of military power,” Barbers declared.
“If Beijing expects respect for its own interests, it must also respect the Philippines, our institutions and the men and women entrusted with protecting our maritime domain,” Barbers said.
He said what was also alarming was the carrier group’s switching off its automatic identification system or AIS.
“That is a direct challenge that crosses the line into disrespect. China must explain its actions instead of expecting the Filipino people to simply look the other way,” Barbers pointed out.
Villegas: Be firm, unyielding

In a pastoral letter, Lingayen-Dagupan Archbishop Socrates Villegas asked the government to defend the country’s maritime rights firmly, but peacefully, saying the dispute is not only about sovereignty and international law but also about the welfare of families who depend on the sea.
“In the name of God, I ask the government to be firm and unyielding about what is lawfully ours and rightfully our people’s without provoking hostilities,” Villegas said.
“The West Philippine Sea is God’s gift to His people. Defending it is taking the side of the people whom God has favored by the gift of the sea,” he added.

Meanwhile, the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) has criticized the Philippines’ participation in the US-Japan Keen Sword military exercises, saying the war games could only heighten regional tensions and threaten communities.
In a statement, Bayan raised concerns over the deployment of missiles and other military systems, calling the drills provocative amid tensions in the region.

The exercises involve 45,000 Japanese troops, 11,000 US service members and forces from allied countries. — Delon Porcalla, Bella Cariaso, Mark Ernest Villeza, Andrew Villanueva, Roel Pareño, Enrick Saez

articles.title: If Bato doesn’t surrender, what next?
articles.summary: Efforts to track down Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa would continue if he does not turn himself over to authorities within the one-week deadline set by the police, Malacañang said…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Efforts to track down Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa would continue if he does not turn himself over to authorities within the one-week deadline set by the police, Malacañang said yesterday.
The government has offered a P50-million bounty for the capture of Dela Rosa, who has a standing arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court for alleged crimes against humanity.
Dela Rosa, the former Philippine National Police chief who implemented the Duterte administration’s bloody drug war, was given one week to surrender.
Asked yesterday what would happen if Dela Rosa does not surrender within the week, Palace press officer Claire Castro said the police would continue its operation to locate him.
“As (Interior) Secretary (Jonvic) Remulla said, there would be no mercy so the law should be implemented. Arrest the one who should be arrested,” Castro told state-run Radyo Pilipinas.
Castro justified putting up a bounty for Dela Rosa’s arrest, saying it is part of the operations of the Department of the Interior and Local Government and the PNP.
“The confidential and intelligence funds given to the DILG and the PNP are allocated to this because it is a real operation,” Castro said.
“If this is the way they spend the intelligence fund, this is just appropriate as long as they can prove that they are conducting operations and if they are producing results,” she added.

Remulla said Dela Rosa is hiding in Mindanao and is being protected by a powerful group. He claimed that the fugitive senator’s protectors have armed personnel and that a confrontation could result in fatalities worse than the 2017 Marawi siege.
Malacañang has urged Dela Rosa to surrender to avoid bloodshed.
No negotiation

National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag said there is no negotiation between the NBI and Dela Rosa, saying the bureau is processing information that could lead to the senator’s immediate capture.
“We want to get him as soon as possible because we have a commitment to the international community and the people. We need answers, so hopefully we can arrest him soon,” Matibag told reporters.
NBI agents failed to apprehend Dela Rosa while the latter was under Senate custody prior to the senator’s escape on May 14.
PNP tracker teams
The PNP has formed tracker teams, including Special Action Force personnel, to locate and arrest Dela Rosa after authorities gave the senator until Thursday to surrender.

PNP spokesman Col. Allen Rae Co said yesterday the operation was intensified upon the order of President Marcos, with a task force led by deputy chief for administration Lt. Gen. Wilson Lopez coordinating the manhunt.?

“The full force of the PNP is in play to bring justice within the folds of the law,” Co said, adding that police prefer a peaceful resolution to avoid putting the lives of the senator, law enforcers and the public at risk.?
Co said authorities had received no feelers from Dela Rosa regarding a possible surrender.
He added that the latest information gathered by police indicated that the senator remained in the Philippines, although investigators were still verifying his last known whereabouts.
Ping: Bato safer in Philippines
Sen. Panfilo Lacson said Dela Rosa may be safer in the Philippines instead of fleeing the country and getting arrested abroad.
Speaking to dzMM yesterday, Lacson said Dela Rosa is more prone to arrest overseas using the warrant from a foreign tribunal like the ICC, especially in countries with extradition treaties.
“What’s difficult is that it’s an international warrant. So where does he go? He is more exposed overseas,” Lacson said.
“It’s safer here in the Philippines,” he added.
Speaking in an interview at the Senate, Sen. JV Ejercito said Dela Rosa deserves due process.
“I’m hoping it’s peaceful. No need to use force or anything like that, but a peaceful resolution,” Ejercito said. — Mark Ernest Villeza, Delon Porcalla, Marc Jayson Cayabyab

articles.title: DOTr’s Lopez, DPWH’s Dizon swap posts
articles.summary: President Marcos carried out yet another change in his Cabinet, with Transportation Secretary Giovanni Lopez and Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon swapping posts, in an arrangement supposedly meant…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos carried out yet another change in his Cabinet, with Transportation Secretary Giovanni Lopez and Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon swapping posts, in an arrangement supposedly meant to solve commuters’ woes and sustain reforms in a system that “protected” corruption.

Presidential Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano said Dizon, who is returning to the Department of Transportation (DOTr) after a year-long stint as public works chief, has been tasked to make daily commute easier, shorten lines at the Land Transportation Office, get rid of fixers and push for the completion of mass transport projects.

Lopez, who assumed the post of transportation chief in September last year, has been directed to boost and safeguard reforms in the Department of Public Works and Highways (DWPH), which has been dogged by corruption issues arising from the multibillion-peso flood control scam.

“Secretary Dizon disrupted a system that had protected waste and corruption for years, thousands of projects are now open to the public, long-unfinished projects are being completed and the new culture of transparency and accountability has begun to take root,” Cayetano said at a media briefing yesterday.

“Secretary Giovanni ‘Banoy’ Lopez will secure these gains and build a system to last. A lawyer and a certified public accountant, he has been tasked to strengthen safeguards and institutionalize the reforms, turning them into rules, processes and systems that will keep serving Filipinos even after this administration for decades to come,” he added.
Describing Dizon as a “disruptor” and “reformer” and Lopez as a “systems builder,” Cayetano said Marcos “puts the right people where they can deliver the most.”

“The President’s direction is clear: Secretary Dizon will accelerate and sustain reforms at transportation; Secretary Lopez will strengthen and sustain reforms at public works,” the Palace communications chief said.

“Secretary Vince and Secretary Banoy are two of the most high-performing Cabinet secretaries. They are distant from politics and are focused on their job. I don’t know if others were considered, but personally I think, you know, the two fit the kind of job the President wants to be done in those two departments.”

One of his final acts as DPWH chief was to direct regional directors to eliminate all highway obstructions and single-lane bottlenecks across national highways, specifically along the Maharlika Highway to ensure smooth traffic flow during All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day.

He issued the directive yesterday during the partial reopening of the Kilicao-Binitayan Bridge along the Maharlika Highway. “For 15 years, our people suffered because this bridge was left idle by corrupt practices. When I reported this to the President five months ago, he ordered us to finish it immediately,” he said.
Due to lower President Marcos ratings?
Cayetano clarified that the latest change in the Cabinet was not triggered by Marcos’ lower survey numbers, but is a “direct response to the needs of our countrymen.”
“Our President doesn’t look at daily numbers when it comes to approval rating. What is important to our President is what can be done for the benefit of our countrymen,” he said.

A Social Weather Stations nationwide poll conducted from Sept. 21 to 27 found that 35 percent of adult Filipinos were satisfied, 20 percent were undecided and 46 percent were dissatisfied with Marcos’ performance. This translated to a “poor” net satisfaction rating of -11, lower than the “neutral” -7 he obtained last June.
Asked why “high-performing” officials need a position swap, Cayetano said their two agencies are in varying levels of need.

“The DPWH is in a position where the reforms have been implemented. What we need now is a systems builder, somebody who can take these reforms, make sure from Luzon, Visayas to Mindanao will be implemented... In DOTr, the President needs a disruption, a quick intervention to alleviate the experiences of our countrymen commuting to work, to go to school. He said there should be less time on the road, more time with their families,” he said.
“We believe that it’s the right time for the two of them to take over the agencies based on their capability and experience.”

Dizon was appointed transportation secretary in February last year and as public works secretary six months later, replacing Manuel Bonoan, who stepped down at the height of the flood control controversy.
Lopez succeeded Dizon in the transportation department where he used to be undersecretary for administration, finance and procurement.
Cayetano said he was not aware of future changes in the Cabinet, but maintained that Marcos continues to check on how agencies are serving the public.
Mixed reactions
The reappointment of Dizon as DOTr chief drew mixed reactions from transportation groups.

“Why the sudden change? Marcos is positioning his allies in various government agencies to help him push the administration’s agenda,” Piston national president Mody Floranda said while also stressing that “there is nothing to celebrate” in Dizon’s return.

“He was surely appointed to that position to further push the World Bank’s rotten and trashy Jeepney Phaseout program, the privatization of MRT-3 and other government programs that reek of pro-business and pro-foreign interests,” he added.
On the other hand, Pasang Masda national president Obet Martin welcomed Dizon’s reappointment and wished that he would continue the modernization efforts in the transportation sector.
Manibela chairman Mar Valbuena expressed his support for the returning secretary and thanked the outgoing transportation chief.

“We are one with the good programs of DOTr, but we will remain strong critics of those that do not serve the interests of the people, especially when it comes to transportation,” Valbuena said. — Rainier Allan Ronda, Andrew Ronquillo

articles.title: House budget insertions reached P1 trillion – watchdog
articles.summary: The House-approved version of the P7.2-trillion 2027 national budget contains “red flag” levels of insertions worth over P1 trillion, including around 7,000 infrastructure projects…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The House-approved version of the P7.2-trillion 2027 national budget contains “red flag” levels of insertions worth over P1 trillion, including around 7,000 infrastructure projects totaling P190 billion, a budget watchdog said.

“The lawmakers padded numerous infrastructure projects without any details. In the House version, they augmented by P43 billion the multipurpose buildings in the budget of the DPWH (Department of Public Works and Highways), which also included access roads and bridges to basic infrastructure program,” People’s Budget Coalition (PBC)’s Kenneth Isaiah Abante told the Senate committee on finance yesterday.

Abante said allocations for the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS) and the Department of Health’s Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) both went up by P24 billion.
A separate allocation of P10 billion was also included for Presidential Assistance to Farmers and Fisherfolk (PAFF).
Abante said these questionable allocations sacrificed more noble programs for education, transportation, health and disaster risk reduction, among others.

“They made a substantial reduction in foreign-assisted projects, about P27 billion in the Laguna Lakeshore Road, nearly P20 billion in the Metro Manila Subway, a P15-billion cut in the budget for the North-South Commuter Rail project and P10-billion cut in pension and gratuity,” he noted.

“And this is the worst – P7.75 billion cut from the National Disaster Risk Reduction Management Council fund,” he said. “We don’t agree with the prioritization of the House for those multipurpose buildings, which we believe is not at all an urgent need of our citizens.”
Hard, soft, shadow pork

Breaking down the more than P1 trillion of flagged insertions, PBC co-convenor AJ Montesa said it is composed of P695 billion in “hard pork” for “politicized infrastructure,” P210-billion “soft pork” or “patronage-driven ayuda” and P112-billion “shadow pork” tucked in unprogrammed appropriations.

Montesa said the “soft pork barrel” increases by the House were for discretionary programs such as AICS, MAIFIP, PAFF, the Department of Labor and Employment’s Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers (TUPAD) and Commission on Higher Education’s Tulong Dunong program.

While the subsidy for state insurer Philippine Health insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) was cut from P129.8 billion in 2026 to P74.4 billion in the National Expenditure Program, the House did not increase its funding, opting instead to double the MAIFIP budget to P49.2 billion.
The group scored the MAIFIP as a program that encourages indigent patients to seek favors from politicians by asking for guarantee letters.

“The House wants us to get sick so we can beg them to pay for our hospital bills,” Montesa said. “Are we building a system that guarantees people their rights, or one that leaves them dependent on political favors?”
In the DPWH budget alone, the House inserted 6,200 projects – most of which are multipurpose buildings – worth P172 billion.

Other insertions included over 180 health facilities worth P2 billion in the DOH budget; over 350 farm-to-market roads worth P6 billion in the Department of Agriculture budget and over 200 irrigation projects worth P7 billion in the National Irrigation Administration budget.

House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos topped the list of DPWH projects “inserted” in the House General Appropriations Bill with 405 projects worth P4.37 billion going to the 1st district of Ilocos Norte.

The 6th district of Isabela, represented by Speaker Faustino Dy III, ranked fourth in the PBC’s list of DPWH project insertions, with the 147 DPWH projects worth P1.68 billion shared with Isabela 4th district Rep. Joseph Tan.

House appropriations committee chair and Nueva Ecija 1st district Rep. Mikaela Suansing ranked seventh in the list, but she also shared the P1.35 billion worth of 107 DPWH projects with the Nueva Ecija 2nd district.
Batangas 2nd district Rep. Gerville Luistro ranked eighth in the list with her fifth district counterpart with P1.31 billion worth of 77 projects.
The PBC clarified that their figures on budget insertions were based on budgets to DPWH district offices, not to the district representatives themselves, and thus are not “evidence of wrongdoing.”

As for the “shadow pork,” the PBC said unprogrammed appropriations – recently flagged by the Supreme Court as an unconstitutional way of bloating the 2024 national budget – became a “dumping ground” for foreign-assisted projects because these were not included in the programmed budget, causing further delays in implementation.
‘Mini-Zaldy Co budget’

Describing the 2027 spending plan as a “mini-Zaldy Co budget,” Caloocan 2nd district Rep. Edgar Erice lambasted in particular the P62-billion Local Government Support Fund (LGSF), which he said will not necessarily trickle down to local government units (LGUs) across the country.

“It (LGSF) did not result in the equitable distribution of funds for LGUs. And it is not consistent with the national fiscal program. The guidelines are all-encompassing with the government projects,” he told Bilyonaryo News Channel.

“This is also the reason why I call it (LGSF) the President’s pork barrel, precisely because it is by nature a discretionary fund of the President: he sets the identification of the project, sets the amount for the project and decides when to release the funds,” Erice explained. — Marc Jayson Cayabyab

articles.title: ‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election win
articles.summary: Leaders and governments worldwide congratulate Lula on dramatic comeback seen as an important signal to rest of Latin America
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in São Paulo and Tiago Rogero in Brasília

blocks.text: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has vowed that dictatorship and fascism will never return to Brazil after winning a historic fourth term in power by defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro.

“This is God’s work – and it’s thanks to all of you,” Lula told tens of thousands of supporters who had gathered in central São Paulo in the early hours of Monday to celebrate his dramatic election comeback.

A few hours earlier Lula pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history, bouncing back from a first-round defeat in early October to trounce Bolsonaro by more than 4m votes in the runoff.
“Today is a historic day,” Lula declared, before telling a sea of elated supporters: “Democracy always, dictatorship never again. Democracy always, fascism never again.”
Never, since the return of democracy after the 1964-85 military regime, had the first-round loser managed to win the second vote.

But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo and cities all across Brazil, where he won 64.2m votes to Bolsonaro’s 59.8m – a 51.79% to 48.21% victory. That was at least 10m more votes than Lula secured in the first round.

“This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defence of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme right candidate entailed,” Lula’s health minister, Alexandre Padilha, told the Guardian shortly after the result was confirmed at the hotel where the president’s team was following the count in São Paulo.
“It’s a massive victory – not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” Padilha added.

Following in the footsteps of his father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who refused to concede after losing the 2022 election to Lula and was later convicted of plotting a coup, Flávio Bolsonaro rejected the result. Bolsonaro called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word which roughly translates as “bullshit”.
But political leaders and governments from across the spectrum were quick to recognise Lula’s victory.
“Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won,” tweeted Mexico’s leftwing president, Claudia Sheinbaum.
“The global progressive resurgence has just begun,” wrote Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez.

Rightwing South American leaders also recognised Lula’s victory, with Chile’s president, José Antonio Kast, calling Lula to offer congratulations and Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, saluting “the Brazilian people for this democratic day”.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil.”
A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said: “China respects the choice of the Brazilian people.”

There was silence from Donald Trump, whose administration had been rooting for a Bolsonaro victory that would have seen the so-called pro-Trump “orange wave” continue its sweep across the region into Latin America’s largest democracy.
In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, the US had been accused of seeking to influence the result through a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure.

Erika Hilton, a transgender lawmaker who recently became the most voted woman in Brazil’s congress, said those efforts had failed. “We have defeated the interference of the US government, which thought it could turn our country into its backyard. Brazil and the Brazilians are too gigantic to be anybody’s backyard,” she said.
Lula’s victory will also have profound consequences for the environment and the Amazon rainforest in what is the world’s most biodiverse nation.

On the eve of the vote, the former environment minister Marina Silva had warned that, if elected, Bolsonaro would seek to finish the “perverse project” of rainforest destruction started by his father, whose 2019-2022 administration saw a surge in deforestation.
On Sunday night, Silva was in a buoyant mood, telling the Guardian: “My heart is happy and filled with gratitude to God and the Brazilian people.”

“The thing I most feared was that our Indigenous territories would be invaded again [under another Bolsonaro government]. Now, I am certain that they will be preserved and that there is no risk of illegal miners returning to destroy these populations,” Silva added.

For Flávio Bolsonaro, the future looks bleak. As the scale of Lula’s victory became clear on Sunday night, the mood at the Brasília mansion where Bolsonaro was watching the count soured, with what had initially seemed like a lively birthday party turning into something resembling to a wake. Like football supporters heading for the exits midway through the second half because their team is being thrashed, crestfallen guests began heading home.
One of them approached the dozens of journalists waiting for Bolsonaro’s speech to shout that it was the “north-east’s fault”, insulting the region where Lula has historically won most of his votes.

One photograph circulated by Lula supporters showed a dejected Bolsonaro in tears, although it was taken on the eve of the vote. Another image showed a red-faced Bolsonaro flanked by visibly mortified allies as they came to terms with their defeat. São Paulo’s pro-Bolsonaro governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, sits next to him covering his face with his hand.

On Paulista Avenue, where huge crowds had gathered to hear Lula speak, one reveller wore a costume of Flávio Bolsonaro behind bars. Some suspect the senator is likely to flee the country to the US once his term runs out in February and he loses parliamentary immunity. Bolsonaro is facing a series of federal police investigations over suspected misdeeds, including money laundering, although he maintains he is innocent.
Lula supporters delighted in the idea that the far-right politician may soon join his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his coup attempt, in jail.

“Oh, how awful! Poor little thing!” João Maluf, a 27-year-old psychologist, shouted sarcastically he held up his mobile phone to the crowd to show them a photograph of a visibly distraught Bolsonaro. “We want rid of these fucking Bolsonaros,” Maluf said.

articles.title: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting
articles.summary: Two bishops in images that show them praying with Trump have said they believed the meeting was private.

blocks.text: Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were released and prompted many to ask if they were making a political statement.
Photos and video of the 22 October meeting show a group of bishops standing around Trump at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.
Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, one of those pictured, said he had believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity".
Trump and Pope Leo XIV have a contentious relationship, and some US bishops have criticised the administration's immigration policies. But Trump has typically enjoyed the support of Catholic voters.

In a statement posted online, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, said the meeting was arranged by officials with the White House Faith Office to discuss issues including immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons".
"In no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," Joensen said.
"I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes," he added.
A video of the meeting was released by Margo Martin, a special assistant to the president and communications adviser who frequently shares behind-the-scenes images of Trump on social media.
Archbishop Grob said that after 90 minutes of meetings with officials, the religious leaders were ushered into the Oval Office to pray with Trump.
Grob said images of the meeting later caused concern among some of his congregants.
"I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he wrote.
"I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family have been harmed by the president's policies," he added.
Grob said none of the participants in the meeting gave permission for the public distribution or posting of video or photos of the event.
When contacted for comment by the BBC, the White House did not directly address questions regarding the meeting or subsequent comments by the two bishops.
"There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it," White House Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.

According to Pew Research Center, which analyses religion in the US, opinions of Trump's performance have slipped among all major religious groups. In a survey this month, 30% of all US Catholics said they approved of his job performance, compared to 47% when he returned to the White House in 2025.

That could have an effect on the 3 November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress. More Catholics in the survey, 42%, said they preferred the Democrats running in their local House of Representatives races, where slightly less, 39% favoured Republicans.
During his second term, Trump has had a tense relationship with the head of the Catholic church, Pope Leo, as he has moved aggressively to remove people believed to be in the US illegally.

Nine days before the Oval Office meeting with the bishops took place, Bishop Brendon Cahill and Walter Kim, the president of the National Association of Evangelicals, issued a statement urging "Christian compassion and wisdom in the immigration debate".
They said the immigration clampdown has led to the "sowing of fear, the fracturing of families, the deprivation of due process, and the vilification of our neighbors."
The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also recently condemned the Trump administration's plans to livestream a military execution, which were later scrapped.
Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are Catholics who have visited the Vatican during Trump's second term.
A Midwestern member of the bishops' conference, Robert Barron of Minnesota, agreed to serve on the president's Religious Liberty Commission last year, as did former New York Archbishop Timothy Dolan.

articles.title: Police arrest teenager after shooting that injured 12, including children, in Florida
articles.summary: The incident happened on Saturday night, close to an American football stadium where a game had just been played.

blocks.text: Police have arrested a teenager in connection with a shooting on Saturday that injured 12 people in Florida.
The incident took place at 20:00 local time (01:00 Sunday GMT), close to an American football stadium in the city of Tallahassee where a university game had recently been played.
Eleven people were injured by gunfire, local police said, while another hurt their ankle while fleeing the scene. Six of the victims were children.
Anthony Rivers III, 15, has been charged with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent.
Police said the shooting followed an altercation between people who knew each other and that additional arrests were possible.
None of the victims appear to have been the intended targets, they said in a statement.
"What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families," Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said.
"We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family impacted by this tragedy."
Police said on Sunday that six people were in hospital, including one person who was in a critical condition. Five people had been released.
Revell told a press conference on Sunday that police had had to carry victims in their arms to get them to emergency responders because of the crowds from the football game.

articles.title: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp chat helped turn Brazil election around
articles.summary: As polls pointed to defeat, millions joined a 'Lula's Army' channel that is credited with helping transform online enthusiasm into real-world mobilisation.
articles.byline: Julia Braun, Rute Pina, Luiz Fernando Toledo

blocks.text: The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.

Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.
Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off".
"Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.
On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.

The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.
In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".
Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult.

While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.
Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback.
Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.

According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights.

"It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."
By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.
Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media.
"It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."
In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement.
"Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.
She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration.

"I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."
Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.
In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed.
"We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

articles.title: What Germany thinks of carmaker Audi's $4 billion deal with Trump
articles.summary: The luxury carmaker is set to open its first factory in the United States — a move Trump credits to his tariffs. DW examines the German reaction amid a massive auto industry cull at home.

image.caption: Audi hopes that its plans to build SUVs in the US can revive the company's fortunesImage: AFP

blocks.text: 1. What is Audi's $4 billion US investment plan?
US President Donald Trump announced the investment on Saturday, during a campaign rally in Georgia, a key battleground state for his Republican Party in the midterm elections next week.
Audi quickly confirmed the plan, saying it would build its first US factory near Macon, Georgia, costing around $4 billion (€3.6 billion) and creating some 4,500 jobs.
The German automaker said construction would begin next year, with a planned annual production of up to 200,000 vehicles due to start in the early 2030s.
The firm plans to build premium SUVs for the US market at the plant, marking a "long-term commitment" to what it said was "one of the world's most important premium markets."
The US investment comes as German automakers face unprecedented pressure from China, rising costs and two conflicts.

Backed by huge government subsidies, Chinese rivals have stolen a march in the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), scaling up production of new models that are fast gaining market share in a crowded global auto market.
BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Audi's parent company, Volkswagen— the world's second-largest automaker — have all issued profit warnings in recent months as margins come under pressure.

They've also announced major cost-cutting. VW is preparing to axe up to 100,000 jobs by 2030, while Audi's factory in Neckarsulm, which has around 15,000 staff, is one of four plants at risk of closure.
2. Why is Audi investing in US car production?
Trump credited his 15% tariffs on European-made vehicles for Audi's investment, saying it "would not have happened without tariffs."
While the commitment does feed into Trump's plan to bring manufacturing back to the United States from abroad, Audi said it was making the huge outlay for growth and resilience.
“We have much greater ambitions for Audi in America," said the carmaker's CEO Gernot Döllner, who appeared alongside Trump at the Republican's campaign rally.

"The United States is one of the world's most important premium markets, and we have not yet realized our full potential. We are determined to change that ... This is about building a stronger Audi business in America — not only about building a factory," he said.
However, Trump's tariffs have undoubtedly added to the automaker's woes.
Audi, which currently exports to the US market from Europe and Mexico, said the additional costs amounted to about €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) last year.
With more than 160,000 vehicles sold, Audi's US sales last year fell 16%, amid intense competition and after Trump scrapped subsidies on electric vehicles in its second-biggest market.
By building a US factory, Audi should be able to avoid or reduce Trump's tariffs, industry analysts say.
EU to weaken combustion engine ban amid industry pressure
3. What is the reaction in Germany amid huge cuts in the domestic auto sector?
There's been fierce criticism of the deal due to the severe pressure facing German automakers and because the new US investment could mean further job losses at home.
Much of the criticism focused on Döllner's rally appearance alongside Trump.
The center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)'s transport policy spokesperson Isabel Cademartori described it as campaign assistance for an autocrat who is waging a trade war against Germany.
"This is a disgrace, especially considering the history of the Volkswagen Group," she stated, referring to the party's links with Adolf Hitler's Nazi party during World War II.
Christiane Benner, president of the powerful IG Metall union, labeled the rally appearance as "extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and not worthy of the company."
VW works council chief Daniela Cavallo went further, saying Döllner had let himself be turned "into a puppet in [Trump's] propaganda show."

blocks.caption: Audi's CEO Döllner (right) has been strongly criticized for appearing alongside Donald Trump at a midterms campaign rallyImage: Edgar Su/REUTERS

blocks.text: Cavallo, however, noted that the US plant could make sense from a business perspective, as VW needs to grow its market share there.
An Audi spokesperson defended the US investment, saying it was "not a decision against Germany, but rather a step toward strengthening our global competitiveness."
Manfred Döss, chairman of Audi's supervisory board, insisted the automaker's future cannot be secured by cost-cutting and efficiency alone.
"We need the courage to invest, to seize new opportunities and to make decisions that will shape our company for decades to come," he added.
4. Will Audi's investment help Trump in the US midterms?
The announcement certainly appears timed to coincide with the US midterm elections on November 3.
Voters will decide whether the Republicans or Democrats hold the balance of power in Congress during Trump's last two years in office.
Holding the announcement in the key battleground state of Georgia is seen as a strategic move to boost the fortunes of local Republican candidates.
Since he returned to the White House last year, Trump has used tariffs and political pressure to force global automakers to relocate their factories to American soil.
Audi's investment follows moves by Stellantis and Japan's Toyota to expand US production, while Honda is in talks to build a new US plant.
US auto giants General Motors and Ford have also promised to increase domestic production.
While one investment announcement may not be enough to sway many voters, it serves one of Trump's main election promises — to revive industrial production in the US.
Germany under pressure

articles.title: Brazil elections: Merz, world leaders congratulate Lula on his win
articles.summary: Brazilian President Lula secured a surprise win over far-right challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede. DW has the latest.
articles.byline: Matt Ford, Akanksha Saxena, Richard Connor, Alex Berry

image.caption: Lula won a fourth term in the runoff despite having trailed Flavio Bolsonaro in the first round of votingImage: Raquel Cunha/REUTERS

blocks.text: October 26, 2026
African leaders congratulate Lula, seek to 'advance shared interests'
Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu was one of several African leaders to congratulate Lula on Monday, saying that his renewed mandate offered an opportunity to strengthen bilateral ties.

"As two leading nations of the Global South, we can promote economic integration and advance our shared interests in a rapidly changing global order," Tinubu said online, saying he looked forward to expanding cooperation in a raft of areas.
Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu also extended her "sincere congratulations" to Lula.

"Tanzania values its longstanding friendship with Brazil, and looks forward to continue building on this foundation to further strengthen bilateral relations and deepen cooperation, for the mutual benefit of our two nations," Suluhu said.

Seychelles President Patrick Herminie called the runoff election result "a powerful affirmation of the trust the Brazilian people have placed in President Lula's leadership," in comments published by his office online.

He said Lula's win was "a testament to his lifelong commitment to the dignity and well-being of ordinary men and women," saying the Seychelles shared Lula's values like "social justice, equality of opportunity, the protection of workers and the most vulnerable, and a model of development that places people at its center."
Herminie expressed a desire to deepen bilateral cooperation, particularly in tackling climate change, protecting the oceans and advancing the interests of the Global South.

articles.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
articles.summary:
Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze

Senior Sudanese…

blocks.text: Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

articles.title: Why Ukraine may be involved in Mali's conflict
articles.summary: Allegations that Ukrainian specialists are supporting Tuareg rebels in Mali highlight Kyiv's effort to challenge Russian influence far beyond the battlefield in Europe.

image.caption: There are growing indications that Ukraine is providing military support to Tuareg rebels and jihadists in MaliImage: Souleymane Ag Anara/AFP

blocks.text: Ukraine is fighting Russia — and the conflict may extend into Africa's Sahel region.

According to an investigation published by US media outlet CNN this month, around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists are reportedly supporting Tuareg rebels in northern Mali. Their common enemy: the military government in Bamako and its Russian allies.
But how reliable is the information? And what price could Kyiv pay for engaging in Africa?

Marta Oliynyk-D'omochko, coordinator of the African Studies Program at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, sees a strategic motive. "Ukraine's main interest is to weaken Russia's influence around the world," she told DW. If Russia's military influence were rolled back, she added, the economic opportunities arising from it would also diminish.

Russian historian Irina Filatova, professor emeritus at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, also considers Ukrainian support for the Tuareg movement plausible. However, she says she has no independent evidence to confirm such involvement.

Kyiv's alleged partners are controversial. The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) cooperates with the Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimeen (JNIM), a jihadist group affiliated with al-Qaeda.
Suspicions dating back to 2024
In July 2024, DW reported on possible involvement by the Ukrainian military intelligence service (HUR) in an ambush on Russian Wagner fighters near Tinzaouaten in northern Mali.
At the time, HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov said the Tuareg rebels had received information they needed to carry out the attack. Ukraine denied direct involvement.
Jihadist groups in Africa and their links
Paramilitaries from Russia's Wagner Group and Malian troops suffered heavy losses in the July 2024 attack.
CNN's investigation has reignited the question of whether the Russia-Ukraine war is also being fought on African soil.
Signals from Kyiv, but no confirmation

The suspicions were renewed by a post on X by Kyrylo Budanov. The former head of Ukraine's military intelligence, now chief of staff to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on September 7 that Ukrainian intelligence protects the country's interests worldwide — "from Russia to Africa … in the burning desert sands and in the snows of icy Antarctica...".

Budanov did not explicitly mention Mali and his post does not confirm any specific operation. CNN reported that the Ukrainians provided drone training, operational planning and remote support for drone missions. DW has not independently verified those claims.

DW reached out to the HUR for comment. Among other things, DW wanted to know whether personnel had been deployed to Mali, whether the political leadership had approved such a mission, and what measures were in place to ensure that the JNIM — which cooperates with the FLA — does not indirectly benefit from Ukrainian support.
DW did not receive a specific response. An HUR spokesperson said the agency might provide information at a later date. The extent of any potential Ukrainian involvement therefore remains unclear.
Why Mali matters to Kyiv

Following military coups in 2020 and 2021, Mali increasingly turned away from Western partners and toward Russia. The Wagner Group was subsequently replaced by the Africa Corps in 2025 as Moscow reorganized its military presence.
Russia has sought to consolidate its influence in the Sahel region and present itself as a reliable security partner.
Ulf Laessing, former head of the Sahel program of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Mali and now head of Konrad's Syria and Iraq program, says Russia is continuing to expand its activities in Africa.

"I have received information that the Africa Corps still uses Syria and Libya as transit points for flights from Russia, including for refueling and loading, to support its operations on the continent," Laessing told DW.
How could Wagner Group revolt impact Africa?
From Ukraine's perspective, it could be attractive to exert pressure on Russian forces in Africa.

Filatova sees a strategic logic to this: "The Ukrainians regard Russian troops anywhere in the world as legitimate targets." Setbacks in Mali could tie up Russian resources and undermine Moscow's reputation as a security partner, she argued.

However, Oliynyk-D'omochko stresses that the relationship with the Tuareg is not a comprehensive alliance. The FLA is not seeking to replace the government in Bamako. Instead, it is focused on northern Mali and is pursuing self-determination or extensive autonomy.
Oliynyk-D'omochko describes the relationship as a tactical arrangement: "It is more of a situational alliance against a common enemy than a comprehensive partnership."
The alliance with jihadists

The FLA is fighting for an independent state in the north of Mali, a region predominantly inhabited by Tuaregs. JNIM, by contrast, aims to impose strict Islamic rule. Both groups oppose the military government and its Russian allies, but their objectives differ.

Any potential Ukrainian support for the FLA would not, in itself, prove that Kyiv is directly supporting JNIM. However, jihadists could benefit indirectly if they conduct joint operations with FLA or gain access to knowledge and equipment.
Cooperation between Tuareg and Islamist groups dates back more than a decade.

After the ousting and killing of Libya's longtime dictator Muammar al-Gaddafi during the Arab Spring in October 2011, heavily armed Tuareg fighters returned to Mali and took up the struggle for an independent state.
In the process, separatist ambitions became intertwined with Islamist movements. Iyad Ag Ghaly, the current leader of JNIM, was himself involved in the Tuareg rebellion before turning to jihadism.

According to Oliynyk-D'omochko, the cooperation is primarily tactical in nature. The two sides have collaborated during past uprisings but later fell out. It remains unclear how long the current alliance will last.

For Kyiv, this also poses a political risk. In many African countries, the Tuaregs are viewed as separatists. Cooperation with them could therefore create the impression that Ukraine is interfering in another country's internal affairs.
Claims of support for armed groups

Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso accuse Ukraine of supporting armed groups and threatening their territorial integrity. The three Sahel nations, all ruled by military governments, have severed diplomatic relations with Kyiv and deepened their cooperation with Russia.

In September, Mali's Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop accused Ukraine at the United Nations of "providing clear and open support to terrorist groups and other mafia-like groups to undermine our country's territorial integrity," reported Agence France-Presse. Diop did not provide evidence for his claim.
The three nations' governments have may have an interest in legitimizing their partnership with Moscow and portraying Kyiv as a destabilizing actor.
Filatova considers Ukrainian activities in the region plausible but says she has no evidence to substantiate the accusations.

Oliynyk-D'omochko has likewise found no definitive proof. At the same time, she warns of the potential consequences for Ukraine's Africa policy: Kyiv advocates equal partnerships with African countries. Any alleged cooperation with separatists could undermine that message and affect how potential partners view Ukraine.
What price could Ukraine pay?

Engagement in Mali could offer Ukraine a relatively low-cost way to weaken Russian interests beyond Europe. A small team of specialists could train local fighters and improve their capabilities in the use of drones.

But a potential partnership with the FLA carries political risks. Because the Tuareg separatists cooperate with the JNIM, Kyiv could face accusations of indirectly supporting Islamist fighters. That could undermine Ukraine's efforts to strengthen its relations with African countries.
How Mali's big bet on Russia is backfiring

articles.title: Part of Antarctica named after former BBC science correspondent
articles.summary: A stretch of water in the west of the continent is now called the Amos Channel after the ex-BBC journalist.

blocks.text: The melting ice sheets of this remote continent are just one of many aspects of polar science that Amos reported on while at the BBC. He also covered colossal icebergs, the fate of penguin colonies and a BBC exclusive about the discovery of Ernest Shackleton's lost ship, the Endurance.
"It's absolutely incredible - what an extraordinary accolade. I'm so touched that there's a little bit of Antarctica named after me," Amos said.
Despite his fascination with the South Pole, he has not yet travelled to the continent.
"I've written about it so often, but always from my desk - this is quite the incentive to go and visit.
"Antarctica is the front line of the biggest news story on planet Earth - climate change," he added.
The naming of geographical features in Antarctica follows strict rules.

The Amos Channel was recommended by the UK Antarctic Place Names Committee, which looks after names for sites within the British Antarctic Territory, as well as South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.
Athena Dinar, from the British Antarctic Survey, said: "Jon's passion for Antarctica and engaging journalism offers something for every reader, viewer or listener.
"The naming of an Antarctic place in his honour is a fitting recognition of his outstanding contribution to the promotion of Antarctic research."

Amos joined the BBC in 1986 as a local radio reporter in Cambridge. He was part of the team that launched the BBC News website in 1997, and ran the online science desk for many years. He later worked as a BBC science correspondent across TV, radio and online, before leaving the organisation in 2024.

"Jon consistently highlighted the importance of Antarctic research, explaining not only what science is being done there, but why it matters for society, climate understanding and the global environment," said Fiona Fox, from the Science Media Centre.
