articles.title: Audi boss under fire in Germany for Trump rally appearance
articles.summary:
Gernot Döllner criticised for in-person announcement of major investment in US days before midterm elections

The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a…

blocks.text: The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a rally with Donald Trump just days before the US midterm elections, to announce billions of dollars of investment in battleground state Georgia.

Gernot Döllner joined Trump on stage after the US president gave a speech criticised by the head of an elected body of employees at Audi’s parent company, Volkswagen, as being full of “racism, sexism, transphobia [and] contempt for democracy”.

Daniela Cavallo, the head of the VW works council, added that anyone who heard Trump’s speech and then saw that Döllner had become an active participant in the event must “sink into the ground with shame”, according to internal company communications released to German media.
She said the investment deal and Döllner’s appearance showed VW’s management had allowed itself to be “turned into a puppet in the propaganda show of a highly dubious political figure”.

Isabel Cademartori, the transport spokesperson for Germany’s Social Democrats – part of the country’s ruling coalition – called Döllner’s actions a “disgrace”. She added this was particularly so “in view of the history of the Volkswagen Group”, in an apparent reference to VW’s founding as a showcase company under the Nazis.

A spokesperson for the German government declined to comment on the matter, calling it “a business decision regarding where the company invests and, in this case, where the company’s chief executive appears”.

blocks.caption: Döllner announced plans to spend $4bn and create 4,500 jobs in the battleground state of Georgia. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP

blocks.text: Döllner and Trump announced to the crowd on Saturday that Audi would spend $4bn to build its first factory in the US and create 4,500 jobs, even as VW aims to slash tens of thousands of positions and close plants in Germany.

“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Döllner said at the rally in Perry near Macon, in a highly unusual move for a European executive during a hard-fought US electoral campaign.
He called the plans, which foresee factory construction starting next year and car production beginning in the 2030s, “a long-term investment because we believe in the American market”.

Audi is the only premium car manufacturer without its own factory in the US, making it particularly vulnerable to Trump’s punishing 15% import tariffs, which cost it an estimated €1.2bn last year. The Macon plant would build 200,000 SUVs annually.

The head of the powerful German trade union IG Metall, Christiane Benner, called Döllner’s US appearance “extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company, but above all of Audi’s employees”.
She accused Döllner of being in “flagrant breach” of the company’s code of conduct, “which expressly requires political neutrality in the run-up to elections”.
She warned that any major investment like the Macon plant would have to go before VW’s supervisory board. Benner is the board’s deputy chair.
after newsletter promotion

Volkswagen is currently locked in a battle between management and labour over a push to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the downsizing on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as US tariffs and the expensive transition to electric vehicles.

Its German ​factories are under particular pressure to drive down costs, with Audi’s facility in Neckarsulm, which employs 15,000 people, among four VW plants threatened with closure from early next decade.
“Each site must do its part in terms of competitiveness and the long-term strength of Audi,” a company spokesperson said.

Trump is deeply unpopular in Germany and has riled its political mainstream by vocally backing the far-right Alternative für Deutschland. The AfD is the country’s most popular party according to polls, and has actively courted Trump’s support.

The 3 November election in Georgia could be decisive in the Democrats’ battle to regain a majority in the Senate. The incumbent senator, Jon Ossoff, is fighting a tough re-election battle against Republican challenger Mike Collins, in a state Trump won in 2024.
Trump has argued ahead of the midterms that his tariffs on car imports are helping the US economy.

articles.title: US Marine indicted for murder and robbery of woman in Japan
articles.summary: Prosecutors have indicted Devin Jacob Ballard for a killing that has caused outrage in Japan, local media reports.

blocks.text: A US Marine has been indicted on suspicion of murdering and robbing a woman in Japan earlier this month in a case that has triggered protests, Japanese media reports.
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who was stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested on suspicion of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa.
Prosecutors have now indicted him for allegedly strangling Yagi with a telephone cord and then stealing her backpack and wallet on 3 October, media reports, citing the indictment document.
It wasreported Ballard had denied the allegations, but Asahi Shimbun and Kyodo News cited investigators saying he has made some statements suggesting involvement.
Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings.
Yagi's death has caused outrage in Japan, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi describing the crime as "brutal and heinous".

Earlier this month, the Marine Corps said it was "actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine" and extended condolences to the victim's family.
It is the latest case involving a US serviceman in Okinawa, which hosts the highest concentration of around 55,000 US soldiers stationed in Japan.

Previous criminal cases have sparked anger and protests, the largest of which took place in 1995, when tens of thousands took to the streets following the abduction, beating and rape of a 12-year-old girl.

In 2024 alone, there were four sexual assault cases involving US troops in Okinawa, including that of air force member Brennon Washington, who was given five years for the rape and kidnapping of an underage girl.
In 2025, US marine Lance Cpl Jamel Clayton was sentenced to seven years in prison for sexually assaulting a woman.
Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said the prefecture has repeatedly demanded that the US take action to prevent such incidents, and said he sees the alleged crime as a sign of a lack of discipline.

The prime minister said her government has registered a "strong" protest with the US and called for "strict disciplinary action against US military personnel and thorough measures to prevent a recurrence of such incidents".

People in Japan have been voicing anger, with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo earlier this month. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice, with one user saying: "Enough is enough."

articles.title: High-level delegation in Iran in push to avert flare-up of conflict with US
articles.summary:
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey travel to Tehran as bellicose rhetoric heightens

High-level diplomatic delegations from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have…

blocks.text: High-level diplomatic delegations from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have travelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent renewed fighting between Iran and the US and Israel as rhetoric sharpens on both sides.

Security officials and diplomats at Monday’s meeting were expected to discuss how Iran could persuade the Houthis in Yemen to end their crippling missile and drone attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. With fighting raging across Yemen, the Houthis claimed to have closed Riyadh airport and inflicted heavy damage on the Saudi economy.
The officials were also understood to be discussing Iran’s possible inclusion in a new security pact involving Islamic countries.

The Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and the head of Turkey’s intelligence service, Ibrahim Kalın, were to meet Iran’s top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington.

The three countries signed a defence agreement in Mecca in August. Some in Iran feared the deal was constructed to challenge Tehran, but the signatory countries have insisted it is simply a mutual defence pact.

The balance between exploring a new long-term security architecture and demanding Iran start to compromise in the conflicts in which it is engaged will be critical. It is possible the two sides came to the meeting with different priorities.

blocks.caption: The Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, meeting Pakistan’s Field Marshal Asim Munir in Riyadh in September.  Photograph: Saudi Press Agency/Reuters

blocks.text: The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role, and the US-Iran conflict has potentially reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran.

No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attack on Iran either last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said the meeting could pave the way for broader regional cooperation on security based on shared interest.

“The events of the last two years, especially the past eight months, have shown that sustainable and reliable security in our region will only be possible by building trust and cooperation among the countries of the region,” he said.

Javad Zarif, a former foreign minister and long-term advocate of a regional security alliance called for “a comprehensive regional network based on non-aggression, mutual trust building, and shared prosperity”.
“Regional security is not imported, it must be created by the people of this very region together,” he said.

He published his message alongside an image of verses 103 and 159 from Surah Ali ‘Imran, the third chapter of the Qur’an. The verses emphasise being saved from a fiery pit by avoiding division, fostering unity, seeking forgiveness and consulting others.

The meeting takes place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators, it was confirmed, spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz.
Israeli media reports claimed the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been trying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iran before the Israeli elections on Tuesday.
Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that modern-day US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity in the region.

The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners also increasingly argue Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb, ending the fatwa on the possession of a weapon of mass destruction.
A pact likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted.

articles.title: HIV infections among young people expected to increase by 2030, says AIDS society
articles.summary: By the year 2030, more young people aged 15 to 24 are projected to be diagnosed with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), the AIDS Society of the Philippines (ASP) reported Monday.

blocks.text: By the year 2030, more young people aged 15 to 24 are projected to be diagnosed with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), the AIDS Society of the Philippines (ASP) reported Monday.

“Let’s look at our young people kasi they are now getting infected… The estimate is that by 2030, which is above four years from now, I just don’t know baka nagbago ‘to, baka tumaas pa ‘yan. Makikita ninyo that we are estimating that the majority of our infections will be among the young people,” ASP President Dr. Rossana Ditangco said.

(Let’s look at our young people because they are now getting infected… The estimate is that by 2030, which is around four years from now—though I don’t know, this might change or go even higher—you will see that we are estimating that the majority of our infections will be among young people.)
“... Talagang magpe-predominate na siya. Paakyat nang paakyat and mostly young people, if wala talaga tayong ginagawa,” she added.
(... It will really become predominant. The numbers are continuously rising, mostly among the youth, if we do not take action.)
In the projected data presented by ASP, around 47,029 HIV cases by 2030 would belong to the 15 to 24 age group, while 17,446 would come from those aged 25 to 30.
Delayed access to services

According to Ditangco, a 2015 study by the Department of Health (DOH) found that risky behaviors among individuals in their sexual activities start early, but access to services remains delayed, putting young people at greater risk of contracting HIV and other sexually transmitted infections.

“How about the female sex workers? The first sex is at age 17. First paid sex and first condom use, age 20. Again, there’s a delay. So in between, nahahawa na sila or nakakapanghawa na sila, di ba?” Ditangco explained.

(How about female sex workers? Their first sexual encounter occurs at age 17, while their first paid sex and initial condom use happen at age 20. Once again, there is a delay, during which they can contract or transmit infections.)

“Ito namang mga MSM [men having sex with men], first sex and first anal sex… 16 at 17 years old pero ang first condom use ay 18 [years old]. So may delay. So in between that, pwede nang mahawa,” she added.

(As for men who have sex with men, their first sexual experience and first anal intercourse occur at ages 16 and 17, but their first condom use is at age 18. Because of this gap, transmission can already occur.)

Ditangco urged the public, especially government agencies and stakeholders, to provide young individuals with proper sex education and encourage responsible participation in sexual activities before they become sexually active.
The ASP said data show that among the general population of young males and females, only 17% have comprehensive knowledge about HIV.

“Studies have shown that people who use condoms consistently are the ones who used it during their sexual debut kasi they don’t know na the difference. Kasi ‘pag nag-umpisa ka ng sex nang walang condom at pinag-condom ka, parang hindi mo na gusto,” Ditangco said.

(Studies show that consistent condom users are those who used them during their first sexual experience, as it sets the baseline. If one begins having sex without a condom, introducing it later becomes much harder.)

“... So dapat talaga ‘yung pagse-sexual debut may condom na para talagang masanay silang gumamit ng condom subsequently. Ang condom pa naman napakaimportanteng intervention niyan for safety,” she added.
(... Condom use should ideally begin at sexual debut to build a consistent habit. Condoms remain an indispensable safety intervention.)
Further showing the disparity in access to services, the ASP noted that young MSM aged 15 to 17 face similar risks as older MSM, yet they have less access to condoms.
Destigmatizing, holistic approach
While a lack of condom access contributes to the growing number of HIV cases among young people, the ASP stressed that it is not the root cause of the country's HIV epidemic.

According to Ryan Pinili, a DOH-certified trainer in HIV Counseling and Testing, stigma and misconceptions heavily hinder efforts to raise awareness about HIV and assist people living with the virus in seeking treatment and support.

“We have to destigmatize kasi meron pa rin po tayong pananaw na pag nag-avail ng condom, nag-avail ng PrEP—kakanood lang po namin kanina, meron pong isang sikat na personalidad… mayroon po siyang masamang pagtingin sa PrEP and PEP, ang kailangan daw ituro ay abstinence.But the choice is nasa tao po,” Pinili said.

(We have to destigmatize because we still have that perspective that when you avail of condoms or avail of PrEP—we were just watching earlier, there is a famous personality… they have a bad view of PrEP and PEP, saying what should be taught is abstinence. But the choice is with the person.)
“... We have to destigmatize at kailangan sabihin natin kung saan po makakakuha ng readily-available na commodities. Libre naman po itong pinamimigay ng ating gobyerno,” he added.
(.. We have to destigmatize and make sure to inform people where they can get readily available commodities. These are distributed by our government for free.)
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a pill or injection that can reduce the chances of getting HIV, or stop the spread of HIV in the body once a person is exposed.
Meanwhile, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is taken within 72 hours by an HIV-negative person who has been or may have been exposed to HIV to reduce the risk of HIV transmission.
Pinili reminded the public that when a person living with HIV undergoes treatment and is declared to have an undetectable viral load, they are unable to transmit the virus to their sexual partners.
In an appeal to agencies and institutions, Ditangco emphasized the importance of adopting a holistic approach to HIV prevention and treatment in the country.

“Kaya nga ang ating prevention strategy must be a combination. Hindi pwedeng biomedical lang, na condom lang, PrEP and ARV. Dapat holistic— you address the emotional, the psychological, the social issues at different ages. Kasi pine-prepare mo na 'yung tao to behave responsibly,” Ditangco said.

(That’s why our prevention strategy must be a combination. It cannot be purely biomedical, relying solely on condoms, PrEP, and ARVs. It must be holistic—you need to address emotional, psychological, and social issues across different ages. That is how you prepare a person to behave responsibly.)
HIV epidemic
At present, the ASP noted that HIV in the Philippines can be considered an epidemic due to the increasing case counts and the rapid increase in data in recent years.
From January to March 2026, the Philippines logged 4,367 diagnosed HIV cases.

Data show that sexual contact remains the primary mode of transmission during the first quarter of 2026, with male-to-male contact accounting for the highest number of cases at 3,095, followed by contact with both male and female partners at 567.
Meanwhile, male-to-female sexual contact recorded 331 cases among males and 221 among females.
The ASP added that the occurrence of mother-to-child transmission is particularly concerning, with nine male and four female cases reported.
Ditangco emphasized that the DOH maintains zero tolerance for mother-to-child transmission, reiterating its call for universal testing among pregnant women.
Cases involving the sharing of infected needles were also recorded, with one case each reported for males and females. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Endangered turtles and ‘exceptional’ coral at risk from Woodside’s gas drilling in WA, watchdog says
articles.summary: Exclusive: EPA flags oil spill risk from proposed gasfield and threat to pygmy blue whales

blocks.text: Woodside Energy’s plan to drill for gas off Western Australia’s north-west coast could significantly damage “exceptional” coral reefs and it may be impossible to reduce the risk of an oil spill to an acceptable level, according to advice from the state’s independent environmental watchdog.

A draft letter from WA’s Environmental Protection Authority written in 2023, seen by the Guardian, sharply criticised Woodside’s proposal to develop the Browse gasfield, saying its plans to protect endangered turtles and blue whales near Scott Reef would be ineffective.

Woodside, Australia’s largest fossil fuel company, is hoping to win approval next year to develop the Browse basin, about 300km off the Kimberley coast. Scientists have warned it could damage the Scott Reef ecosystem, which is home to more than 1,500 species, many unique to the area.

EPA staff presented the draft letter to the authority’s board for approval in December 2023. In February 2024, two months after it was discussed, the EPA sent a letter to Woodside saying its preliminary view was to reject development of the vast gas reserve.

It was a significant setback to Woodside’s plan to drill more than 50 wells and pipe the gas 1,000km to its ageing North West Shelf gas export plant adjacent to the world heritage-listed Murujuga rock art.

The company won approval last year to run the North West Shelf until 2070. But it needs the gas from the Browse basin – Australia’s largest undeveloped source of gas – to feed it. If the processing plant was to operate until 2070 it could lead to about 88m tonnes of carbon dioxide being released into the atmosphere each year after the gas was burned.

blocks.caption: Scott Reef off the coast of Western Australia is home to more than 1,500 species. It sits over the underwater Browse gas basin. Photograph: Greenpeace

blocks.text: The concerns presented in the letter to the EPA board show the pressure on authorities to recommend against the gasfield development being approved. The development is being assessed by both the state and commonwealth EPAs. Ultimate decision-making power lies with environment ministers.

The letter shows the EPA board was advised by its staff that there was a threat of serious or irreversible harm to turtles and whales and more generally due to oil spills. The threats were considered serious enough that the staff said the precautionary principle should be invoked. It meant the EPA should assume the worst possible outcomes could occur.

In response to this near rejection of its proposal, Woodside added explosive-driven shear rams to its drilling plans, a step that could allow it to seal a leaking well in seconds. The company said this would reduce the “longest credible duration” of a “highly unlikely” well blowout, and potential oil spill, to about 12 hours.

Not all companies have faith in shear ram technology. In 2024, fellow WA gas exporter Chevron rejected “pyrotechnic shearing” technology for its own wells, describing it as unproven and impossible to test in the field.
A Woodside spokesperson said if the shear rams failed it would deploy a capping stack to stop the oil flow within 16 days.
But the EPA was advised in 2023 that if a well leaked for 13 days it was possible there could be “irreversible consequences” to Scott Reef.

The draft letter said Sandy Islet, a part of Scott Reef considered critical to the survival of endangered green turtles, would be threatened if the seabed subsided after Woodside extracted gas from beneath it. It said a proposal to top up the sand on the islet, where about 1,000 turtles breed each year, was a “high-risk” measure and its success was “likely to be limited”.

Woodside said it would address this by changing its plans so that no wells would be drilled within 20km of Sandy Islet. It also said the flaring of gas, which produces bright light that can confuse turtle’s navigation, would be restricted.
after newsletter promotion

The EPA board was also told noise, traffic and vessel strikes would have a significant impact on pygmy blue whales migrating between Timor and southern Australia. Scott Reef is the only known whale feeding ground on the migration route, according to the draft letter.

Woodside’s spokesperson said the company understood whales did feed at Scott Reef, but that this was opportunistic and the area was not as important as the ocean off Perth and other areas further south. Woodside agreed that Scott Reef and Sandy Islet had exceptional environmental value and it was important to protect them for future generations.

Glenn Walker, Greenpeace head of nature, said Woodside’s plans to address the concerns raised by the EPA did not go far enough and relied on “fanciful and unproven technology” to prevent a catastrophic oil spill.

“It would be a major backflip for both the WA EPA and the national EPA to now recommend approving this project,” he said. “It is now critical that these regulators maintain their independence from corporate and political influence and reject this destructive project.”
Greenpeace last week nominated Scott Reef for national heritage listing based on its ecological and scientific values.
Just two of the current nine-strong WA EPA board were in place when the watchdog told Woodside it was set to reject Browse.

One of those – the current chair, Darren Walsh – said in a statement the assessment had been lengthy because it was a complex project in a sensitive area. He said a final state report and recommendations on the proposal would be provided to the WA environment minister, Matthew Swinbourn, when it was complete. There would then be a three-week public appeal period before a decision was made.

A spokesperson for the national EPA said the development was being assessed under the national Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, and the “decision clock” had been paused while the agency waited on “further technical advice”.

Issues that have to be considered under national law include the potential impact on pygmy blue whales, green turtles, the marine environment in commonwealth waters and Murujuga rock art near the gas processing facility.

articles.title: The chaos in France is a ‘warning signal’ for Australia’s public spending and rising costs
articles.summary:
Australia’s public debt may be well below that of France but there are lessons to be taken from its economic woes

  • Get our

blocks.text: The explosion of discontent that led to major protests and violence in France and across Europe is a “warning signal” that Australia could follow the same path without an “honest conversation” about the budget, economists say.

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday to protest underfunded schools, as complaints of insufficient teacher numbers and dilapidated infrastructure mingled with broader discontent about cost-of-living pressures.
Here, and across the developed world, people are struggling to cope with the affordability crisis, as households grapple with high and rising prices.
The scale of the challenges in individual countries may be of a different order of magnitude, but the grievances are common.

Luke Hartigan, a senior economics lecturer at the University of Sydney, said it was clear there was no single factor behind the discontent in France, but soaring energy costs were having a major impact.
Fuel prices are up 36% this year in France, or three times the increase in Australia. The US-Israel war on Iran has sent European gas prices soaring as the northern hemisphere approaches winter.
More fundamental, however, is that France’s finances are buckling under its generous welfare state.

France’s high public debt, stagnant economy, and universal social security benefits have created a “binary” situation, Hartigan said, where citizens’ demands for better services and cost-of-living help are clashing with the country’s increasingly dire fiscal position.
France has not balanced its budget since 1974. Meanwhile, total public debt as a share of the economy has swelled to nearly 120%, according to the International Monetary Fund.
Australia’s total government debt pile looks benign in comparison at 53%. But a decade ago our debt was 40% of GDP, and a decade before that it was just under 10%.
Hartigan said France’s lacklustre economy had compounded its fiscal problems, underlining how Australia needed to work hard to boost productivity.
“If you think about trajectories, they [France’s challenges] give us an idea of where we could potentially be if we continue down this path,” Hartigan said.
“It’s a warning signal.”

Bob Breunig, the director of the ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, said there was a growing gap between what voters believed the government should be able to do, and what politicians were able to deliver.

“One thing that is happening everywhere is this narrative that the government should be able to solve all your problems, and that narrative has probably been pushed further in Europe than it has here. It’s failing in both places, but it’s pointier there than here,” Breunig said.
The evidence of this growing demand for government intervention is that French public spending now accounts for 58% of the economy, the IMF data shows.

In contrast, Australia’s total public spending is equivalent to 40% of our national output – the highest in data stretching back to 1990, outside the pandemic, and at similar levels to the United States and the United Kingdom.
after newsletter promotion
“All these protesters are asking the government to help them out, but the government has maxxed out the credit card,” Breunig said, who said France’s debt was “reaching levels that are unmanageable”.
“The federal government here can still borrow and has a lot of flexibility, and the French just have no money.”
President Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power has been marked with failed attempts to rein in spending.
“There’s a real sense that people don’t know what to do,” Breunig said.
The bond market reflects growing alarm with France’s fiscal trajectory.

France typically has to pay a higher interest rate on its 10-year debt than fiscally prudent Germany, and the gap between the two rates is a measure of financial markets’ confidence in France’s fiscal position.
That gap is now at its widest since the European debt crisis in 2011.

Amid structural pressures on the budget from an ageing population, the NDIS, higher interest rates, and the push for greater spending on national defence, Breunig agreed there were lessons for Australia in not allowing the country to drift too far and for too long.

“We need an honest public conversation about what the government can be expected to do and what it can’t, and then a conversation about how much that would cost and whether we are willing to pay for that.”

While the opposition has attacked what it sees as the deadening effect of high government spending on economic dynamism, Breunig said he was broadly “agnostic” whether repairing the budget involved lower spending or higher taxes.
“At the end of the day, making these decisions is exactly what democracy is for.”

articles.title: AI giant Anthropic unveils plans for blockbuster share listing
articles.summary: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
articles.byline: Kali Hays, Rachel Clun, Liv McMahon

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic has revealed details of its business ahead of its plans to sell shares to the public in what will likely be the largest stock market debut in history.
The company behind AI chatbot Claude revealed losses of more than $80.7bn (£60.5bn) in the first half of the year. It said it generated revenue of $16.3bn over the same period.
The number of shares to be released and their price range is yet to be determined.
Anthropic's valuation when it goes public has been expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which this summer was the biggest-ever stock listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion.
Anthropic said it will often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".
"In order to fully capture the opportunity in front of us, we need to invest more aggressively than would a business that operates in a more slowly changing technological regime," the firm said.
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets."
Anthropic said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT. It will be the first true AI company to go public, marking a test for the future of the technology.

Tech companies have been heavily investing in costly AI infrastructure and tools, like data centres and the informational models that underly all AI technology, pouring more than $1tn into the efforts over the last year alone.
Anthropic, which was founded just five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, announced its intention to go public in June.

Its most significant rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit, saying it, too, intended to go public. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

After the companies had decided on such plans, a wave of cyber-security and other types of technological breaches occurred involving their AI agents, or AI bots that are designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also gained public attention with new warnings that AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect the whole of humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

articles.title: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback
articles.summary: The left-wing incumbent president had lost the first round to right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.

blocks.text: Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.
Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since the return to civilian rule in 1985 to win an election after losing the first round of voting.
Lula told celebratory crowds this election is a "loss for negativity, lies", later adding "long live democracy".
Flávio Bolsonaro, who is the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled, which experts say is unlikely.
In an unprecedented move, polls were also extended for two hours on Sunday evening after both candidates made requests for different reasons.

Lula's team had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Senator Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as the reason for their request.
The decision - issued by the Supreme Court just as polling stations were due to close - meant that some had already shut and were not able to re-open.

Supreme Court President Kassio Nunes Marques - appointed by the older Bolsonaro - confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voting extension did not cause issues for the count or the electoral process.
Lula secured 51.79% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.21% - a difference of 4.4 million votes between the two candidates.
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.
His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030.
But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump.

Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" - which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard".

Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support.
Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.
While Trump has yet to react, other world leaders have been congratulating Lula on his win.
Ecuador President Daniel Noboa Azin said the region had "common enemies, shared challenges, and much to gain when we work together."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "democracy and multilateralism" had won. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez - also a left-wing leader - called it a "great victory", saying "the comeback of global progressivism has just begun". French President Emmanuel Macron said the two nations should work "in service of a more just world".
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called Lula's victory one for the "global south and progressive forces throughout the world".
Additional reporting by Vinícius de S. Mendes, BBC Brasil

articles.title: Macron vows 'strong measures' to combat protests that rocked France
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron said his government will announce "strong measures" in response to violent protests in France in recent weeks. But he also acknowledged that students have…

image.caption: President Macron visited Marseille city hall which was vandalized during recent protestsImage: Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The French government is set to announce a series of "strong measures" to assuage protests which have rocked France in recent weeks, President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday.

Speaking in the southern city of Marseille, Macron warned that fresh demonstrations planned for this coming Saturday were "risky" and said that protest routes would remain outside city centers in order to protect public order.
France braces for 'lively' Halloween
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told broadcaster BFM that he was expecting further disturbances on October 31.
"Halloween evening is traditionally always a bit lively," he said. "We expect it to be complicated again."

Prior to Macron's arrival in Marseille, the Elysee Palace said the president intended to "pay tribute to and thank the internal security forces that helped restore republican order" in France's second-largest city where protesters briefly stormed the city hall on October 17.

He acknowledged that French authorities had "not anticipated at all" the scale of demonstrations which descended into widespread violence in looting in several major cities, leading to suggestions the state had lost control of the streets.
Macron: 'Social media is damaging our democracies'

The French president also highlighted the role of social media in the protests, saying the online networks were "damaging our democracies" by "bringing young and not-so-young people to places where criminal acts, attacks and looting were taking place."
He described social media as "tools for mobilizing the worst impulses."
France protests continue despite police crackdown

While Macron admitted that French security forces underestimated the extent to which "extreme left forces" would meet up "so early in the day" on October 17, Interior Minister Nunez highlighted the phenomenon of organized far-right mobs confronting left-wing activists in several cities.
"We ​knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out to defend businesses," he told BFM.
"In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organized formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement."
A presidential aide said Macron wanted to demonstrate that "the state is present, standing firm and fulfilling its mission to protect."

The president said that curfews enabled relative order to be maintained during last Saturday's protests (October 24), when authorities also deployed 70,000 police officers across the country, making 1,435 arrests.
"The state prevailed this weekend. The state was strong," government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon told RTL radio.
France: Macron acknowledges 'legitimate' student demands

Nevertheless, President Macron also said he had instructed his government, led by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, to "respond to the legitimate demands that lie at the root of this social movement."

He said the government will soon announce several "concrete and huge" measures aimed at addressing student concerns over education and university admissions, following a nationwide consultation with high school and university student representatives.
France: Why students are taking to the streets
"There are demands that must be heard and answered," confirmed government spokeswoman Bregeon.
"But to answer them, ​there is a prerequisite: a return to calm. We cannot have a functioning social dialogue in a climate of violence such as the one we experienced a week ago."

articles.title: Germany's Merz heads to Asia as security issues loom large
articles.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz will be meeting the leaders of Singapore, Japan and South Korea as Germany seeks to adjust its foreign policy to rising uncertainty and threats to global supply chains.

image.caption: Merz's visit to Asia will be his longest foreign trip since he took office in May 2025Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz kicked off five-day tour of Asia on Monday, traveling to Singapore before his scheduled visits to Japan and South Korea. Merz is accompanied by an entourage of 30 senior businesspeople, including representatives of Germany's industry, tech and defense companies, and energy suppliers.
At the same time, Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is visiting China.
While the trips are not officially related, they both seem aimed at boosting Berlin's economic and security relationships at a time of geopolitical instability which threatens global supply chains.
Japan needs close allies

In Singapore, Merz is set to deliver a major foreign policy speech and meet Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. He will then travel to Japan on Wednesday to meet with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and take part in the German-Japanese Business Summit.
Merz's visit "will be very much welcomed in Tokyo," said Ben Ascione, an assistant professor of politics and international relations at Tokyo's Waseda University.
"For more than a decade, Japan has been looking to generate new security allies and closer trade partnerships," he told DW.
Will Japan become the Indo-Pacific's most trusted power?

"This greater outreach was started under Prime Minister [Shinzo] Abe, but Takaichi is very much following that blueprint because of the growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific region and the greater uncertainty around the second administration of [US President] Donald Trump," he added.
Germany and Japan face different, but connected threats

The challenges posed by an increasingly expansionist China in the region are of deep concern to Tokyo, particularly as Beijing is forging closer ties with both Moscow and the unpredictable regime in Pyongyang. China and Russia have conducted joint military exercises off Japan, and Beijing is resolute in its insistence that Taiwan be brought under the control of the mainland.

Ascione points out that any conflict over Taiwan, the disputed islands of the South China Sea or territorial claims elsewhere in the region would have a major impact on global trade. Such disruptions would also impact Germany.
How Japan, South Korea and Taiwan hedge vs. US shifts

"Japan and Germany have different primary security threats at the moment, with Germany focused on the Russian invasion of Ukraine and Japan keeping a close watch on China, North Korea and Russia, but I do believe that Germany has come more into line with Takaichi's perception of the security threat that is posed by China," Ascione said.

"Takaichi is going to underline the importance of a rules-based order and the policy of a free and open Indo-Pacific at a time of such geopolitical uncertainty," he added. "Japan has in recent years moved towards greater resilience building, supply chain resilience and more and deeper security partnerships."
German military assets welcome in Japan

According to Ascione, Japan would also "welcome" Germany deploying its military assets to the region, following its Bayern frigate docking in Tokyo in 2021 and its fighter jets conducting air drills with Japanese fighters in 2024.

The frigate Bayern became the first German Navy warship to dock in Tokyo in 20 years in May 2021 and went on to conduct air and maritime exercises with Japanese units. In July 2024, German Eurofighter Typhoon aircraft similarly carried out air drills with Japanese fighters over northern Japan.
Merz and Takaichi are expected to exchange views on responding to geopolitical threats.
Pacifist Japan is rearming — this is why

This would include ensuring supply chain resilience, protecting strategically important industries and ensuring access to technologies and components, such as the rare earths that are critical to a range of advanced technologies but remain largely controlled by China.
European nations 'irritated' by Seoul's outreach to North Korea

Merz is then scheduled to visit South Korea, where he will meet with President Lee Jae-myung and open the 19th Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul. He is also due to visit the Demilitarized Zone that marks the border between North and South Korea.
Security issues will again dominate discussions in Seoul, believes Saeme Kim, a research fellow at The Asan Institute for Policy Studies.
However, the German leader could voice concerns about South Korea's perceived "outreach" efforts by towards North Korea and, by extension, Russia.
"There has been discussion recently about exports of petroleum to Russia, although Seoul says it has not breached sanctions," she said.
Why Seoul wants an apology from Zelenskyy
South Korea is trying to set up a way to communicate with Pyongyang, according to the expert, despite the regime of Kim Jong Un sending troops to the conflict in Ukraine.
"It's not just Germany, I think a lot of European countries will be irritated by the Lee administration trying to improve relations with North Korea and Russia," Kim said.
The South also continues to provide humanitarian assistance to North Korea, even as the regime forges ever closer economic ties with China and Russia.
"The government needs to keep in mind that some of these policies are going to be damaging to South Korea's own interests over the long-run," she said.
Can South Korea learn from Germany's history?
At the same time, Merz could also offer insight into two Koreas trying to work with one another, drawing on the German experience of reuniting in 1990.

"There are lessons that South Korea can learn, of course, but there are a lot of differences," Kim said. "The two Koreas are still technically at war and Seoul has to deal with an aspiring nuclear power on its border."

Merz will have the opportunity to see the North at a distance when he visits the DMZ. His visit to the border, however, could also be canceled due to lingering tensions over the North Korean mine injuring three South Korean soldiers last month. Pyongyang has accused the South of staging the incident.

articles.title: Chris Brown given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack
articles.summary: The R&B star previously pleaded guilty to affray, after attacking a music producer with a glass bottle.

blocks.text: US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub.
The R&B star was given an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, over the attack at private members' club Tape in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023.

Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Both men, who had pleaded guilty to affray, were also ordered to pay £1,500 costs.
Judge Tony Baumgartner said Brown's use of the glass bottle to hit the victim twice over the head "was plainly dangerous", adding that the violence of the attack was "intense".
The sentence means Brown will not be imprisoned unless he commits another offence during the 12-month period of suspension.
The court heard Brown's attack on music producer Abraham 'Abe' Diaw left the victim in need of hospital treatment for his injuries.

In sentencing, Judge Baumgartner said: "The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained."
CCTV footage was shown where Brown struck Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head, and then hitting his shoulder.
Sentencing Brown, Judge Baumgartner said: "This was not planned violence. It was nevertheless serious violence by two people in a crowded nightclub."
The judge told Brown: "Violence of this kind in a crowded nightclub is serious, it creates an obvious risk, not only to the person against whom it is directed, but also to others nearby."
He added that Brown's conduct was "particularly dangerous" and that he had to be "physically pulled away" from the attack.
The judge said Brown's fame, commercial success and professional standing "do not entitle you to special treatment - the law applies equally to everyone".

But judge Baumgartner also said he had noted Brown's guilty plea, compliance with bail conditions, and the impact a custodial sentence would have on Brown's children, and said the singer's "risk of further offending is low".
Brown and Akinlolu pleaded guilty to a charge of affray at Southwark Crown Court in July.
The singer had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied, and which were subsequently dropped.
These were assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon.

Following Brown and Akinlolu's guilty pleas, the CPS released a statement outlining that Brown had approached Diaw on the dance floor, hitting him over the head with a glass bottle twice, before Akinlolu then punched Diaw in the head.
"They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club," the CPS said. "The victim was kicked while he was seated defenceless on the floor."
On Monday, the court was shown three pieces of CCTV footage from inside Tape nightclub on the night of the attack.
The attack lasted no more than 20 seconds, but Brown could be seen hitting the victim four times with a tequila bottle, twice to the head.
Prosecutor, Heidi Stonecliffe KC, described the weapon as a "heavy square-shaped tequila bottle" and said Diaw was approached by Brown at around 03:00.
The footage showed that the nightclub was very small and packed at the time.
The defence described Chris Brown as a "dedicated and a loving father of four children," someone who is "positive and present".
The singer is described as having lived "a good and law-abiding life" since his last conviction in 2013.
The events in Tape nightclub were described by the defence as a "short and deeply regretted incident".
Brown's defence lawyer told the court that he apologises to all those present at the club at the time of the attack.
"This is an ugly and unattractive incident," Sallie Bennett-Jenkins KC said.
"It is, however, an incident which was very short-lived, lasting something more than 17 seconds but no more than 20.
"It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr Brown... offers a profound apology to all those present."
The court heard Akinlolu "genuinely believed" that Brown was "under attack" when he joined the attack, punching Diaw.
Brown was described as being like a "brother" to Akinlolu, his lawyer Laurie-Anne Power KC told the court.
She added: "He genuinely believed him to be under attack and became involved, and thereafter accepts his initial involvement very quickly evolved into the events he has pleaded guilty to."
Diaw was taken to St Mary's Hospital in London after the attack. Ms Stonecliffe KC said he was discharged with "pain relief and a diagnosis of head injury and superficial injury of the knee".
An MRI scan taken in early March showed a "high grade injury to a ligament on the inner side of the left knee", the court heard.
Defending Brown, Ms Bennett-Jenkins KC said there was a "relatively low level of force" and disputed how significant the injuries were.
The defence argued that the attack left no fractures or broken skin and there was an absence of serious injuries.
Diaw, the victim, was "not supportive of the prosecution" and "withdrew" his support some time after the incident, the court heard.
Brown and Akinlolu stood up and faced one another and clasped hands after the judge concluded his sentencing remarks before walking out of the glass dock.
There were loud cheers outside the court as Chris Brown left the building as he appeared to stop to sign an autograph.
After the sentencing, Brown shared a video from inside his car on his Instagram story, showing him looking out the window before turning to the camera and giving a thumbs-up.

Affray is an offence under the Public Order Act and a person is deemed guilty in law if they use or threaten "unlawful violence towards another" with their behaviour, leading someone to fear for their personal safety.
Brown, 37, is considered one of the biggest stars in R&B, with a string of hit songs including Turn Up The Music, Ayo, Freaky Friday, Run It, Forever, Yeah 3x and Don't Wake Me Up.

articles.title: Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973
articles.summary: The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border.

blocks.text: Algeria is to send troops to Niger in its first foreign deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war in 1973.
The deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister, as the country seeks support against armed groups, some of which are linked to al-Qaeda or Islamic State.

Algeria has economic interests in Niger, including a planned gas pipeline that would carry Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria. The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border.
The deployment comes as the two neighbours rebuild ties after a diplomatic rift in 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers.

Algeria's upper house of parliament held an emergency session on Sunday to vote on the proposed deployment. According to AFP news agency, 148 of the 174 senators voted in favour. It was later backed by the lower house of parliament.
However, the timing and number of soldiers to be deployed have not been announced.
The move would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision allowing overseas military deployments and a significant shift in Algeria's long-standing policy against sending forces abroad.
"We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure," Algerian senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after the vote.

Algeria's state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has also signed an agreement with Niger's petroleum ministry to explore for oil in the Kafra region. Two exploration wells are estimated to contain 168 million and 100 million barrels, respectively, Reuters reported.
Relations between Algeria and Niger have not always been smooth in recent years.
Algeria condemned the 2023 coup that ousted Niger's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum, and brought Gen Abdourahamane Tchiani to power.
Tensions rose again in 2025 after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border. Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers in solidarity with Mali, a close ally which is also under military rule.

Relations have since improved. Tchiani visited Algeria in February 2026, and in late August, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune sent fighter jets to Niger to help suppress a coup attempt and also donated four military helicopters.

articles.title: Steinmeier in China: A major state visit in uncertain times
articles.summary: President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is traveling to China on a state visit in a period of political and economic uncertainty. Germany is seeking alternative partners in the region, but also wants good…

image.caption: Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to China on MondayImage: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Eight years have passed since Frank-Walter Steinmeier's last trip to China. Since then, the relationship between China and Europe has changed significantly. The German president plans to spend several days touring China before concluding his visit in Beijing, where he will meet with China's leaders.
His visit comes just as the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee is convening for its plenary session, a major annual event that foreign dignitaries usually avoid when timing their visits.

The focus of the president's five-day trip will be "Germany's diverse and complex relations with China, as well as the challenges involved," his office said in a statement. In addition to sites of cultural exchange, the itinerary will also include a visit to a Volkswagen plant in Hefei.
A diplomatic balancing act

The automotive industry, in particular, illustrates the dilemma facing Germany's China policy. China is one of the most important markets for German automotive and machinery manufacturers, as well as for the chemical industry. At the same time, state-supported overcapacity in China is putting pressure on European manufacturers.
Not only that, Germany and Europe are dependent on China for raw materials and technologies, which means they are increasingly seeking out alternative partnerships.

Steinmeier was once an advocate of the policy of "change through trade" — the idea that other countires could be persuaded to become more democratic with the leverage of global trade, now considered something of a failure.

Now he must now pursue a tougher European line in Beijing. Caught between partnership and competition, Europe leaders recently managed to reach an agreement: Imports of plug-in hybrid vehicles from China are to be scaled back.
"That was a concrete step, but it can only be the beginning," said Michael Laha, an expert on China at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) in Berlin.
Why big automakers are losing China
Chancellor and president both in Asia

Coinciding with Steinmeier's state visit to China, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is traveling to the Indo-Pacific with business representatives. His visit to Japan, Singapore, and South Korea will focus on competitiveness, technological upheavals, defense cooperation, and critical raw materials. Merz is visiting companies and attending important regional economic conferences in Tokyo and Seoul.

The dual trips are Berlin's attempt to send a twofold message: While the chancellor is "deliberately strengthening Germany's partnerships in the Indo-Pacific at a time of global upheaval," says Laha, the president is seeking dialogue with Beijing at a time when Germany and Europe are recalibrating their relationship with China.

"This joint trip sends a very well-coordinated message to the Chinese that we remain committed to the partnership but at the same time are taking steps to reduce risk," said Laha, before adding that this is a difficult balancing act that also allows China to save face.

blocks.caption: Steinmeier and Merz are traveling to Asia at the same timeImage: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Little room for human rights

While Merz will be accompanied by a large economic delegation, Steinmeier will be traveling to China with representatives from German culture, politics, and academia. Mikko Huotari, director of the China Institute MERICS, is also expected to be part of the delegation — even though Beijing has imposed sanctions on the institute. "The fact that he is coming along sends a clear message to the Chinese side that we do not approve of the sanctions," said Laha.

In 2021, the EU imposed sanctions against several Chinese party and regional officials, as well as an organization accused of serious human rights violations and oppressing the Uyghur minority. It was the first time such sanctions had been imposed on China since the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989, and Beijing did not take kindly to them: In response, the Chinese government imposed entry bans and other sanctions against European politicians, scholars, and institutions, including MERICS.

Laha does not expect human rights to play a major role in the German president's trip. Steinmeier is considered a pragmatist when it comes to China policy. As foreign minister, he distanced himself from his predecessor Joschka Fischer, a critic of China, and even criticized Chancellor Angela Merkel when she hosted the Dalai Lama.

blocks.caption: China's Xi Jinping is seeking greater influence in international affairsImage: Florence Lo/Reuters/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: China should assume international responsibility

On the subject of Ukraine, Steinmeier is likely to be more direct and raise the issue of China's role in the conflict. "Beijing is clearly on Moscow's side," said Laha. In Berlin, however, officials are convinced that China can do more to persuade Russia to engage in serious negotiations and find a solution to the conflict.

Steinmeier may make this clear in his speech at Peking University on Thursday. Germany has "long viewed China's emergence with respect and goodwill," reads a statement from the president's office. Today, however, the focus is less on China's continued rise and more on how it uses its growing power.

"If the president points out that Russia used its power to attack a sovereign state, he could be alluding to another regional connection: Taiwan," says Laha. That could be seen as an appeal to Beijing to assume more responsibility for the regional and international order.

To conclude his visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership in Beijing. Talks are planned with President Xi Jinping, whom he has known for nearly two decades, as well as with Premier Li Qiang and the chairman of the National People's Congress, Zhao Leji.

The trip marks the culmination of Steinmeier's focus on Asia during his second term in office. Since then, he has deliberately sought to forge close ties with partners in the region and has advocated for greater diversification. Now China – the most important and most challenging partner – will come to its own conclusion.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: LemFi launches ‘Ambition has no passport,’ its biggest product expansion yet
articles.summary: An expanded platform for people living and moving across borders? Meet LemFi's newest milestone

blocks.text: An expanded platform for people living and moving across borders? Meet LemFi's newest milestone

items: LemFi launches the biggest product expansion in its history, adding UK savings, credit, and data eSIM in 100+ destinations.
This rebuilt app brings transfers, savings, credit and connectivity together in one platform for people building financial lives across borders.
New global brand "Ambition has no passport" reflects LemFi’s evolution from remittances into a broader financial platform serving more than two million customers.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by LemFi and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

LemFi, the financial platform for people building lives across borders, announced the launch of its new global brand platform, “Ambition has no passport”, alongside a completely rebuilt app, launching the largest product expansion in its history.

More than two million customers use LemFi to move money to more than 30 countries, with over $2 billion in monthly transaction volume, and the company plans to add more countries next year. The expanded platform now includes savings and credit in the UK, eSIMs in more than 100 destinations, alongside LemFi’s existing international payments service.

People who move countries arrive with a career, a qualification and a savings record, only to find that almost none of it counts. A credit history rarely survives a border crossing. Around 304 million people now live outside the country where they were born, sending some $905 billion home each year. However, many financial services remain designed around individual products or customers living their financial lives in a single country. LemFi is building its platform around that gap, extending from the international transfers on which the company was founded into a wider range of financial services designed for people whose lives span borders.

“We started LemFi because sending money home was broken. What we learned is that the harder problem starts after the transfer,” said Ridwan Olalere, co-founder and CEO of LemFi. “Our customers are building careers and businesses in one country while supporting people in another, and the financial system treats them as if they can only exist in one place at a time. That is the wrong answer for people this ambitious, so we have rebuilt LemFi to work the way their lives do. Ambition travels. The infrastructure behind it should travel too.”

blocks.caption: LemFi co-founder and CEO Ridwan Olalere and co-founder and CFO Rian Cochran

blocks.text: Transfers, still at the heart of it. Send money to more than 30 countries across Africa, Asia, Europe and beyond, from the same account that now saves, borrows and connects.

Savings that stay within reach in the UK. The LemFi Instant Access Savings Account currently pays a boosted 5% AER for the first six months from account opening; it then reverts to 3.04% AER (tracker), tracking the Bank of England base rate. Accounts open from £1, with no penalty for withdrawals. Deposits are held by ClearBank and protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) up to £120,000 per eligible depositor.

A credit history that travels in the UK. A revolving credit line, available subject to availability, is issued by Lemfi Credit through Pillar, the FCA-regulated credit provider LemFi acquired in 2025. It is available as a virtual card through Apple Pay and Google Pay and can be used for both spending and sending. Eligible customers can also see their Equifax credit score in the app for free.
eSIM in more than 100 destinations, in every market. Buy mobile data before arriving, with no SIM swap and no roaming bill.

The app has been re-architected from the ground up to hold several products across several countries in a single account, rather than bolting them onto a transfer app. The redesign also brings LemFi’s products to the forefront of the experience, making them easier to discover and creating an architecture that lets the company add new services as it expands.

The company has also introduced its new global brand platform, “Ambition has no passport”, reflecting its focus on customers building careers, businesses, families and financial lives across borders. The new identity spans LemFi’s product interface, website, marketing and social channels and will roll out across its global markets.

“LemFi started as a way to send money home. Our customers turned it into a way to build a life across borders,” said Isabel Ron-Pedrique, vice president of design and brand at LemFi. “They are not defined by the country they left. They are defined by what they are building. Ambition has no passport is not a line we placed on top of the product. It is the idea the whole system is built from, from the app you open in the morning to the poster you walk past on the way to work. We have built this brand to keep up with them.”
Savings and credit are available in the UK at launch, with other markets to follow. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Molbog leader raises fears, concerns over Balabac EDCA site
articles.summary: Molbog people, still awaiting certifications of their claim to ancestral lands, protest the developments on Balabac Island

blocks.text: REPRESENT. Molbog indigenous people Emmanuel San Esteban and Anjilon Flores during a presser in Quezon City on Monday, October 26.
Molbog people, still awaiting certifications of their claim to ancestral lands, protest the developments on Balabac Island

items: A Molbog indigenous leader expressed concerns over the construction of military facilities on Balabac Island, which disrupts their ancestral land and daily lives.
The construction includes a three-kilometer runway, and the indigenous community is protesting the developments, citing loss of sacred sites and intimidation from unknown individuals.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – A Molbog indigenous leader raised fears and concerns over disruptions to their ancestral land and daily lives caused by the construction of military facilities on Balabac Island in southern Palawan.

Balabac Island faces the West Philippine Sea and sits between the Sulu Sea and the South China Sea (connected by the Balabac Strait). It is designated as one of the four additional sites under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA).

As Balabac is becoming what defense experts say is one of the most consequential military hotspots, indigenous people are protesting the developments on the land they claim as ancestral domain. Among the constructions on the island is a three-kilometer runway.

“‘Yung libingan ng aming ninuno, tinambakan (The graveyard where we bury our ancestors, they filled with soil),” Emmanuel San Esteban, president of indigenous-led group Bangsa Molbog, said during a briefing in Quezon City on Monday, October 26.

“At ‘yung bundok na pinagri-ritwalan noon ay wala na po. Tinibag na rin.” (And the mountain where we hold our rituals before is gone. It was cleared.) The Molbog leader also said he experienced physical harm and intimidation from unknown men.
Last May, US, Australian, and Philippine Army soldiers conducted a live-fire assault on the island as part of the Balikatan exercises.
San Esteban said their people were taken aback by the military drills conducted earlier this year.

“Hindi namin po alam na magpapaputok pala sila doon sa sinasabing EDCA,” said San Esteban. “[‘Yung] mga tao, nagtakbuhan, lalo na po [ang] mga kabataan.” (We didn’t know they would open fire in the EDCA site. The people fled, especially the young ones.)

He was accompanied by Anjilon Flores, also of the Molbog people, who expressed concerns about livelihood and the government’s National Greening Program (NGP). Flores, who spoke in the Molbog language translated by San Esteban, said the state’s program restricted them from farming and their access to food. Some lands where they used to farm are now covered by the reforestation program.

The Molbog people have been applying for their certificate of ancestral domain — an area spanning 26,000 hectares in Catagupan village on Balabac Island. Balabac, composed predominantly of Molbog people, has a population of 42,662. Catagupan, San Esteban’s village and the site of the runway, has a population of a little over 2,000 people.
Earlier in October, human rights group Karapatan denounced alleged military and police harassment of journalists and researchers in Balabac.

Karapatan said “the incident has brought even more fear to the local Molbog community, which has been suffering intimidation and the destruction of the environment in their ancestral lands due to the construction of the EDCA site.”
Rappler has reached out to the Armed Forces of the Philippines Western Command for comment, but it has yet to respond as of posting. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Prenup won't dispute VP Sara and husband's undeclared assets, says Ridon
articles.summary: A prenup between Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio won"t change the fact that the couple had over P800 million worth of undeclared assets, Rep. Terry Ridon said.

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 8:54pm

A pre-nuptial agreement between Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio won’t change the fact that the couple had over P800 million worth of undeclared assets, House prosecutor Terry Ridon of Bicol party-list said Monday.

Ridon made the response when asked of the take put forward by private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan in a separate television interview that the defense might bring up a prenup between Duterte and Carpio to disassociate the Vice President from her husband's assets.
Ridon said that the spouses filed a joint Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth and jointly filed income taxes.

“It is an observation of one of our private prosecutors and that fact should still be put in place during the defense’s presentation of evidence. But irrespective of whether it is absolute community property, conjugal property or separation of property, the SALN law does not make distinctions. Kailangan pa rin po ilagay iyong pag-aari ng mag asawa,” Ridon said in a press conference.
(The SALN law requires spouses to declare all their assets.)
“And in fact, in each and every document… the tax document or the SALN document, joint ho iyong filing nila. So, antayin natin kung papaano nila ilalapag ito pong defense na ito,” he added.
(They have joint filing of SALN and tax records, so we'll see how they defend this.)
Ridon said that in 2023 alone, the Duterte couple had P100 million in their bank deposits, compared to their declared joint net worth of P80 million.

“More than P100 million in bank deposits, investments and insurance had not been stated in the SALN of the Vice President. Just for that matter, they would have to explain why is such discrepancy,” he said.
Ridon speculated that Duterte will declare her ignorance when the defense starts its presentation of evidence on November 9.

“I think ‘yung magiging defense po doon ay hindi niya po alam ‘yun pong lahat po ng mga financial transactions, una ng kanyang ama at ng kanya pong asawa. But again, I don’t think that is a defense,” Ridon said.
(I would think her defense is that she would not know the financial transactions of her husband and father.)

The House prosecution panel dropped three of the four impeachment charges against Duterte—Article 1, alleging misuse of confidential funds; Article 3, bribery; and Article 4, grave threats against President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos, Jr.—after lawyer and certified public accountant Alex Cabrera testified on Duterte's alleged unexplained wealth.

Cabrera concluded that Duterte and Carpio had unexplained wealth amounting to P817 million to P1.5 billion, after reviewing the couple's financial records including SALNs, bank transaction and bank deposit records, insurance payment records, income tax returns and corporate records of their business interests.

As a result, the impeachment case against the Vice President rests only on Article 2, which alleges unexplained wealth due to non-declaration of assets in the SALN and non-divestment of businesses despite a Constitutional prohibition.

Lawyer Ronel Buenaventura of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) also identified P4.4 billion in aggregate covered and suspicious transactions involving Duterte and Carpio from 2007 to 2025. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman
articles.summary:
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, denies charges that he fatally strangled Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel on the island of Okinawa

Prosecutors in

blocks.text: Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media.

Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported.

Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges.

NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.

Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station when he was arrested, Japanese media reported.

Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.
Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies.
A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman.
US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61.
The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972.
There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high.

After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting
