articles.title: Sara Duterte's husband Mans Carpio is complainant in cyberlibel case, says Lustre lawyer
articles.summary: The lawyer of journalist Philip Lustre Jr., who was arrested over the weekend for a cyberlibel complaint, said that Vice President Sara Duterte's husband, Manases Carpio, was the complainant in the…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 8:36pm

The lawyer of journalist Philip Lustre Jr., who was arrested over the weekend for a cyberlibel complaint, said that Vice President Sara Duterte's husband, Manases Carpio, was the complainant in the case, as shown by a document filed with the Davao City Regional Trial Court.

“Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio, is behind the online libel complaint that led to the arrest of 72-year-old journalist Philip Lustre Jr,” said Atty. Dino De Leon in a statement on Monday.

De Leon said that according to a copy of the information his law firm obtained from the Davao court, Lustre was accused of posting statements on Facebook imputing a crime to Carpio on or about March 6, 2026.

“That on or about March 6, 2026, in the City of Davao, and within the jurisdiction of this Honorable Court, the above-named accused, with deliberate intent, willfully, unlawfully, and feloniously, through his Facebook account, under the name ‘Philip Jr Lustre,' published and posted written statements, thereby making an imputation of a crime against Atty. Masanes R. Carpio, a private individual and on the said date, was actually residing in Davao City, through the internet using the social networking platform called Facebook.com,” a portion of the Information read.

blocks.caption: (From the FB post of Atty. Dino De Leon)

blocks.text: (From the FB post of Atty. Dino De Leon)

Lustre was arrested by police officers in Quezon City on Saturday morning based on an arrest warrant for cyberlibel issued by a Davao court. He said he was unaware of any complaint lodged against him.
The 72-year-old journalist is the author of the book Kill, Kill, Kill, which is about the Duterte administration's war on drugs, and is a longtime critic of the Dutertes.

Sought for their side, Carpio's camp said, "The lawyers of Atty. Maneses Carpio are carefully reviewing the latest developments. We will provide an update as soon as an official reaction statement is available."
‘Unlawful, illegal arrest’
Lustre’s camp likewise described his arrest as “unlawful and irregular,” saying it “came like a thief in the night.”
De Leon said Lustre had no prior knowledge of the case before his arrest, adding that the address indicated on the warrant was not the journalist’s actual residence.
He questioned whether notices during the preliminary investigation had also been sent to that wrong address, thereby depriving Lustre of the opportunity to respond to the complaint.
“If it was easy for the authorities to find Philip Lustre in a media forum, why is it that they were not able to use a proper address during the preliminary investigation stage?” De Leon said.

According to De Leon, arresting officers were also unable to identify the complainant or explain the factual allegations during the arrest because the electronic warrant system displayed only the warrant itself.
He underscored the timing of the service of the warrant, noting that it was executed at a time when obtaining court documents and posting bail are more difficult.
Lustre’s arrest took place following a Saturday forum, a move De Leon argued could intimidate other members of the media.
“Make no mistake, I think this is an attack on the freedom of media and free press,” De Leon said. —LDF, GMA News

blocks.text: Toronto·New
Eric Bauza of Scarborough, Ont., the Emmy-award winning voice actor best known for the iconic Bugs Bunny, has died.
Emmy-award winning voice actor's family said he passed away 'suddenly' in an Instagram post
Eric Bauza of Scarborough, Ont., the Emmy-award winning voice actor best known for the iconic Bugs Bunny, has died. He was 46.
Bauza's family announced he had passed away "suddenly" in a post to his Instagram profile Sunday night. The family did not say the cause of death, but indicated they would share more at a later time.

Bauza grew up watching Bugs Bunny's exploits on the Looney Tunes cartoons at his home in the city. In 2020, he was charged with bringing the character to life in all his carrot-munching, prank-pulling glory.
"It is a dream come true," Bauza told host Ismaila Alfa on CBC Radio's Metro Morning at the time.

In addition to Bugs Bunny, Bauza voiced multiple other characters including Daffy Duck, Tweety Bird and Marvin the Martian. It took two auditions and plenty of practice to land the parts, he told Alfa.
In 2020, he gave his advice to young voice actors, telling them to remember that, at its base, it's "about the acting, first."
"You have to instill a performance that's grounded in reality," he said.
With files from CBC's Kate McGillivray

articles.title: 3 Negros groups unite vs ‘World Bank-DOTr scheme’ on transport modernization
articles.summary: Gerry Llena, LTFRB regional director for Negros Island, tells Rappler the allegation that three traditional jeepneys will be junked in exchange for one modernized unit is 'just a myth’

items: Three transport groups in Negros Occidental and Bacolod City, representing over 3,000 jeepney operators, are protesting against the World Bank and DOTr's Public Transport Modernization Program (PTMP), fearing it will eliminate traditional jeepneys.

The PTMP aims to replace traditional jeepneys with modernized units, but operators are concerned about the financial burden and lack of feasibility studies, as well as the potential scrapping of their vehicles.
Transport leaders are calling for legal challenges against the program and seeking intervention from local officials, emphasizing their commitment to fight for their rights and livelihoods.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

BACOLOD CITY, Philippines – Three transport groups in Negros Occidental and Bacolod City, representing over 3,000 traditional jeepney operators and drivers, have united against a joint scheme by the World Bank and the Department of Transportation (DOTr) that they say is poised to completely wipe them off the streets.

As they spoke up against the project, they intensified their protests at the start of a five-day Electric Vehicle Summit that kicked off at Ayala Malls Capitol Central in Bacolod on Monday, October 26.
On Thursday, October 22, they also staged a walkout at a World Bank–DOTr dialogue at Seda Hotel-Bacolod and held a surprise protest outside the hotel.
They condemned what they labeled as choreographed but nonsensical dialogue, designed just to please them into supporting the World Bank-DOTr transport modernization scheme.
These groups are:

items: Bacolod Alliance of Communters Operators and Drivers in Negros Island – Samahang Manibela, Mananakay at Nagkakaisang Termina ng Transportasyon (BACODNO-MANIBELA)
Kabakod Negros Transport Coalition (KNETCO)
United Drivers and Operators Center-Pinakaisang Samahan ng mga Tsuper at Operator Nationwide (UNDOC-PISTON)

blocks.text: Previously, they were known as fragmented transport groups in the province and its capital, Bacolod.
But faced with the proposed World Bank-DOTr Public Transport Modernization Program (PTMP), they were left with no alternative but to unite, or else they would be completely wiped off the streets.
PTMP is the rebranded version of the 9-year-old Public Utility Vehicle Modernization Program (PUVMP), which was originally implemented through DOTr Department Order No. 2017-011.

The PUVMP appears to be failing, having incurred a massive debt of approximately P5 billion with the Landbank of the Philippines (LBP) and Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP) as the primary government lending institutions for the program.
Under the PUVMP, traditional jeepneys will be gradually phased out across the country and replaced by modernized units equipped with Euro 4-compliant engines.
Since each unit of a modernized jeepney costs more than P2 million, operators were required to form a cooperative before they could apply for a loan from the LBP or DBP.
In Negros Occidental, however, eight of the 11 transport cooperatives under the Bacolod Modernized Jeepney Transport Association (BMJTA) are facing significant issues.
A total of 329 units of modernized jeepneys belonging to the BMJTA are in danger of being repossessed by either the LBP or the DBP.

But under the PTMP, the World Bank is ready to extend loans—not to cooperatives, but to well-established transport companies and corporations with sterling performance records—to become the next operators of modernized jeepneys in the Philippines.
With PTMP, all modernized jeepneys will be upgraded from standard Euro 4 engines to Euro 4L-equipped units.
Under this scheme, three traditional jeepneys will be replaced with one unit of a Euro 4L-compliant modernized jeepney.

Once all hindrances are cleared, the DOTr will pilot the PTMP in five highly urbanized cities in the country, including Bacolod, Iloilo, Cebu, Baguio and General Santos, and in the National Capital Region (NCR).
In a press conference on Monday, October 26, Rudy Catedral, president of BACODNO-MANIBELA, however, said they are opposed to the program at all costs.
“It is the same intention, but this time, the DOTr is just masquerading as the World Bank to cover up its failed PUVMP,” Catedral emphasized. “PTMP will wipe us all out—it will ‘kill’ us all.”

blocks.caption: POWER. Women lead KNETCO protesters against the World Bank-DOTr’s new scheme on transport modernization program, on October 22, 2026. Photo by Ambo Delilan

blocks.text: For KNETCO president Lilian Sembrano, it is premature to fully roll out these modernized public utility vehicles—whether Euro 4L-compliant or fully electric (EV)—given the lack of guarantees regarding their capacity, reliability, and sustainability.

“But if the DOTr is really sincere about the PTMP, then they have to pilot it in areas without transport service entities (TSEs) for a year so we will know how effective the EVs to be funded by the World Bank are,” the KNETCO president said.
However, mixing those EVs with existing routes covered by TSEs will only complicate the situation, she added.
But Sembrano said their greatest fear is that under the PTMP, the DOTr will designate a scrapping center where traditional jeepneys will be hauled and demolished.
“Then, our traditional jeeps will be brought to a scrapping center? Gosh! What will happen to our treasured assets? Will they be junked, will they be shredded? Sakit naman (it hurts),” she added.
Sembrano stated that because the PUV Modernization Program is mandated only through a DOTr department order rather than a law, they intend to challenge it legally.
“We will fight for our rights. We will fight for our families,” she said.
Sembrano asked Bacolod Mayor Greg Gasataya to help them by intervening in the negotiation between the World Bank and the DOTr.

“Why force us to succumb to modernization when we cannot afford the P3 million to P4 million unit price of the modernized jeep to be financed by the World Bank?” Sembrano asked. “Can’t we focus on rehabilitation first?”
“Besides,” she added, “there’s no feasibility study presented to them about PTMP. So, are we ready for another mistake like the failed PUVMP?”
Rodolfo Gardoce, Jr., president of UNDOC-PISTON, said they will not hesitate to hold a massive “untat byahe” (stop the trip) at any time once the planned scheme of World Bank and DOTr pushes through.
Gerry Llena, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) regional director for Negros Island, told Rappler on Monday that he has yet to hear both sides of the issue.
“But the allegation that three traditional jeepneys will be junked in exchange for one modernized unit under the PTMP is just a myth,” he said.
“We are guided by the so-called Local Public Transport Route Plan (LPTRP), so we cannot just scrap jeepney units, or else we will face an even greater shortage,” he added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [Ask the Tax Whiz] BIR backs down on QR badges. Will it dare audit the powerful?
articles.summary: Listening to taxpayers is good governance. But reversing a requirement five days before its deadline raises a bigger question.

blocks.text: An open letter to Commissioner Charlito Mendoza: Suspending the QR badge mandate is a welcome development. But the real test of tax reform is whether the BIR can investigate unexplained wealth without fear or favor.
Dear Commissioner Mendoza,
Your decision to suspend the mandatory display of BIR Registration Seal Badges under Revenue Memorandum Circular (RMC) No. 113-2026 deserves recognition.
The October 31 deadline has been suspended. Display is now voluntary, with no penalties solely for non-display during the suspension.

Listening to taxpayers is good governance. But reversing a requirement five days before its deadline raises a bigger question: Why weren’t privacy concerns, technical readiness, and stakeholder consultations addressed before compliance was required?

The Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) reported that more than 52,700 registration documents with badges had been secured by October 14. This warrants an assessment of taxpayers’ time and compliance costs.
The suspension should not mark the end of reform. It should establish a new standard for taxpayer-centered regulation.
Consider electronic invoicing or e-invoicing.

The TRAIN Law established a system-dependent framework beginning in 2018. Eight years later, RMC No. 98-2026 requires specified taxpayers to comply by December 31, with micro e-commerce taxpayers exempted. RMC No. 110-2026 introduces accreditation requirements for third-party service providers. (READ: [Ask the Tax Whiz] Guidelines on VAT for Nonresident Digital Service Providers)
I support digitalization. But if government needed eight years to implement reform, why should taxpayers shoulder disproportionate software costs, technical difficulties, and potential penalties?
Accreditation must safeguard data and promote competition—not create unnecessary barriers for Filipino technology providers.
GOVERNMENT DELAYS MUST NOT BECOME TAXPAYER PENALTIES.
Businesses struggling to comply are not automatically tax evaders. Modernization must make compliance easier for taxpayers—not merely administration easier for the BIR.
According to 2024 government statistics, MSMEs account for 99.63% of Philippine establishments and 66.58% of employment.
These enterprises deserve proportionate regulations, not unnecessary bureaucracy.
Meanwhile, the Philippines scored just 32 out of 100, ranking 120th among 182 countries, in Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index.
The index does not establish wrongdoing by any individual. But it underscores a serious public-trust challenge.
One disturbing sentiment circulating online captures the frustration: “PAYING TAXES AT THIS POINT FEELS LIKE SPONSORING CRIMINALS.”
This is no justification for tax evasion. It is a warning about eroding confidence in government accountability.

Commissioner, I challenge the BIR to launch a NATIONWIDE, RISK-BASED TAX AUDIT INITIATIVE targeting credible evidence of undeclared taxable income and unexplained wealth involving politicians, political dynasties, and public officials—from barangay halls to Malacañang.
NO SACRED COWS.
NO POLITICAL EXEMPTIONS.
NO SELECTIVE ENFORCEMENT.
Wealth or political connections alone do not establish wrongdoing. But credible discrepancies between lawful income and accumulated assets deserve investigation.

Use legally authorized cross-checks of tax returns, Statements of Assets Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), property records, and beneficial ownership information. Coordinate with the Ombudsman and the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) when warranted.
Build on RMO No. 22-2026 through three measurable reforms:

First, protect low-risk taxpayers. Generally exclude startups during their first three years and MSMEs with annual sales not exceeding ₱100 million from routine audit, except where credible tax risks exist.
Second, reduce compliance costs. Provide affordable electronic invoicing, just transition, and competitive provider accreditation.
Third, demonstrate accountability. Publish anonymized results on high-risk investigations, final assessments, actual collections, and taxpayer compliance costs.
Commissioner, suspending the badge requirement shows that the BIR can respond when taxpayers raise legitimate concerns.
But the bigger test is whether it can investigate the politically powerful with the same determination it regulates ordinary Filipinos.
CAN THE BIR AUDIT THE POWERFUL WITH THE SAME ZEAL IT AUDITS ORDINARY TAXPAYERS?
Because honest taxpayers are not the enemy. Corruption and tax evasion are.
AUDIT THE POWERFUL.
PROTECT THE SMALL.
RESTORE PUBLIC TRUST.

Mon Abrea, CPA, MBA, MPA (Harvard) is a global tax policy expert and Chief Tax Advisor of Asian Consulting Group (ACGlobal). He advises governments, multinational enterprises, and international organizations on tax policy, investment competitiveness, and fiscal reform. He is the author of Reimagining the World Without Corruption and Why Invest in the Philippines? CREATE MORE Edition, and has represented the Philippines in policy dialogues at the OECD, World Bank, and other international forums.

articles.title: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again
articles.summary: The firebrand left-winger, who has at times been at odds with Trump, has won his fourth term as Brazil's president.

blocks.text: Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.
The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old.
He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s.
Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism.

Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement.

In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history.
The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform.
Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system.
He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation.
In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities.

By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor.
However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education.

He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades.

Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012.

Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash.

Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years.

Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used.
He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated.
In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted.
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro.
When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday.
Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office.

And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.

His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.
Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump.
The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public.
The Brazilian leader told the BBC in September 2025 that he had no relationship with Trump.

Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, Flávio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off.

Lula accused Trump of foreign interference and said "he's not emperor of the world". But their relationship improved after a White House in May this year, after which the two leaders exchanged public compliments - Trump called Lula "dynamic", while the Brazilian president said he left the meeting "very satisfied".
In July of this year, the US imposed 25% tariffs on most goods, external from Brazil.
The two governments still disagree on key issues such as crime, and Lula acknowledged they are especially far apart on trade.

Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".

articles.title: Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US
articles.summary: This is how his signature policy has played out after returning to power promising a closed border and mass deportations.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByBernd Debusmann Jr and Mike Hills
Immigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.

When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico for of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since.
Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts.
But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress.
Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency.
He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both.
But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far.
His signature policy has played out in five key ways.
1. A border that is largely closed

Crossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border.
His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing.
When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted.
By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone.

On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings.

blocks.caption: Bar chart showing the numbers detained at the southern US border since 2017. The red bars denote Trump's first term and his second term so far. The blue bars show Biden's term. The chart shows numbers peaked midway in Trump's first term at about 140,000 a month but came down again before starting…

blocks.text: To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach.

That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north.
"President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October.
"The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works."
2. Building of wall speeding up
A vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign.
Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill.

According to government figures, external, about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US.

Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction.
Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated.
Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate.

blocks.caption: Map showing where Trump has built a border wall between US and Mexico

blocks.text: "Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.
There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging.
Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it.

"I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."
3. Detentions and deportations rocketing

Most of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country.

During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first.

Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, external, a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA.

But the same data, external shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%.

Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office.

blocks.caption: Monthly bar chart of people detained by ICE for the first time between 2019 and 2026. Arrests were generally around 10,000 to 12,000 a month during Trump's first term before falling in 2020. Under Biden, arrests gradually rose from around 2,000 a month in early 2021 to about 8,000 by late 2024. A…

blocks.text: But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 2026 that left two US citizens dead.

A New York Times and Siena poll, external released on 21 October found that 50% of voters trust Democrats to handle the issue, compared with 46% for Republicans - despite the issue being a traditional Republican strength.

A separate poll, from Politico and Public First, external in late September, found deep splits between Republicans on the issue, with 31% of non-MAGA Republicans, meaning those not aligned with Trump's movement, believing that campaign has become too aggressive.
Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midterms
4. Refugee intake down sharply
After returning to the White House last year, Trump almost immediately suspended refugee admissions, saying at the time these could only restart if they were shown to be in US interests.

In February, however, an executive order signed by Trump narrowly re-opened that process for Afrikaners from South Africa, who the White House has repeatedly said are being killed and "persecuted" - a claim that the government in Pretoria has denied.

The cap for refugee admissions for the 2026 fiscal year was initially set at 7,500, which was raised to 17,500 in May this year because of what the administration described as an "unforeseen emergency refugee situation".
Overall refugee admissions have slowed to a relative trickle. State Department data shows that 16,292 refugees were admitted into the US in the 2026 fiscal year - of whom 16,287 were South African.

blocks.caption: Bar chart showing annual refugee admissions to the US from 2017 to 2026. Admissions fell sharply during Donald Trump’s first term, dropping from about 53,000 in 2017 to around 12,000 in 2020. Under Joe Biden, admissions increased each year, reaching about 100,000 in 2024. After Trump returned to…

blocks.text: By comparison, in the final two fiscal years of the Biden administration - 2023 and 2024 - 60,000 and 100,000 entered the country, respectively. In the 2024 fiscal year, the highest numbers came from Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela.

Hundreds of thousands of people protected from deportation lost that protection when a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was also ended in Trump's second term. It gave vetted individuals the right to live and work in the US if their home countries were deemed to be unsafe to return to.
One of those countries was Haiti. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.
5. A squeeze on visas - and a $1m golden ticket
Other legal pathways to come to live and work in the US have also been tightened up, through various policy changes.
Dozens of countries the Trump administration has deemed a security risk have been subject to a full or partial freeze on visas and travel.
Enhanced vetting and new rules that send people residing in the US back to their home countries to apply for green cards has slowed that process down.

And in September 2025, a $100,000 fee on new H1-B visas for skilled workers, mostly held by Indians, stunned the US tech industry. In May this year, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X, external that registrations for 2027 were down 40%.

"The data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the program is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers and protecting the wages, working conditions and job opportunities of American workers," the statement added.

While a court has blocked the $100,000 fee - for now - the threat of it appears to have deterred employers. But some experts have cautioned the administration's aim of protecting American jobs, raising wages and stopping firms from outsourcing may prove elusive.

One study, from the Wharton School of Business, external, found that the H1-B changes would have "no significant impact" on the wages of US-born workers, with any reduction in competition offset by reduced productivity growth.

blocks.caption: Bar chart showing annual H-1B visa registrations from fiscal years 2021 to 2026. During the Biden administration, registrations rose from about 275,000 in 2021 to nearly 800,000 in 2024. Registrations then declined, with fiscal year 2025 at about 480,000 and fiscal year 2026 at around 360,000 aft…

blocks.text: Other pathways to the US have been opened, however - if you have a spare million.
The "Trump Gold Card" launched in 2025 sought to entice wealthy foreigners to come live in the US in exchange for a $1m "gift" to the US government, plus a non-refundable $15,000 application fee.
At the time, Trump said that the programme would boost the US economy. Its uptake, however, appears to be minimal so far. By April, only one applicant had been accepted.

articles.title: Trump intensifies anti-Muslim rhetoric against Abdul El-Sayed at Michigan rally – US politics live
articles.summary: The US president was condemned for remarks that questioned the senate candidate’s loyalty to the country

blocks.text: Trump escalates anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed in Michigan
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security.

The president also questioned his loyalty to the United States in remarks that drew a sharp rebuke from a former top Arab American ally. Trump called El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists” and would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”

He also repeatedly invoked 9/11, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93, AP reported.
El-Sayed, who would become the nation’s first Muslim senator if elected, has called attacks on his loyalty to the country “shameful” and repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups.

The Republican president’s remarks were condemned by Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump, the group that helped lead the president’s outreach to Arab American voters in 2024. “The president’s statements are out of line,” he said in a phone interview. “They are crossing a red line. They are racist.”

Trump also reiterated his apparent love for buxom bums and encouraged the crowd to compliment rapper Nicki Minaj’s behind. The comments about Minaj’s derriere came as he explained his recent observation on the Republican Ohio senator Jon Husted’s rear end.

Earlier in October, Trump said of the former college football player: “I don’t do this with men very often. I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass and I looked at the whole – and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He’s got these, like, claws.”
“You are a great athlete,” Trump also said to Husted. “Congratulations.” Trump was speaking at the rally to support Mike Rogers, the Michigan Republican Senate candidate.
Read our full report here:
In other developments:

items: Mary Peltola, a Democrat who is running for Alaska’s lone US Senate seat, and her family suffered minor injuries in a car crash while driving to a campaign stop on Saturday, her campaign said. The family was on its way to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet when another vehicle crashed into the one transporting Peltola and her family, her campaign said in a statement on Sunday. Peltola required medical attention after the collision.

Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s attorney general, lashed out during an interview on Sunday while defending the justice department’s pre-emptive lawsuit to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate results if the GOP incumbent loses, calling a TV host’s question “crazy”. The testy repartee unfolded on CNN’s State of the Union over the DoJ’s unprecedented legal action, which alleges that there could be “voter confusion” due to two candidates named Dan Sullivan on Alaska’s ballot. Trump told reporters, “I’m the one that said do it” when asked about the suit.

The US military has given Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to restricted space tracking data, raising a new round of questions about whether the Trump administration is attempting to hand over traffic control in Earth’s orbit to a controversial donor. The access also raises new national security questions, industry observers say.

Enrollment in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) has decreased significantly over the past year in the US following restrictions imposed by the Trump administration, which has forced more people to seek help from food banks or go hungry, stakeholders say. The number of people who receive food stamps has dropped from 41.6 million in July 2025, before the One Big Beautiful Act took effect, to 36.5 million in June 2026, a 13% decrease, according to the latest data from the US Department of Agriculture, which administers the program.

articles.title: Filipino-Canadian voice actor Eric Bauza dies at 46
articles.summary: Bauza was best known for voicing iconic 'Looney Tunes' characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Filipino-Canadian voice actor Eric Bauza, best known for voicing iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, died on Sunday, October 25. He was 46.
His family announced his death in a statement posted on Instagram on Sunday. They had referred to his passing as “sudden.”
View this post on Instagram A post shared by 𝙀𝙍𝙄𝘾 𝘽𝘼𝙐𝙕𝘼 (@bauzilla)

Born in Scarborough, Ontario, Canada, on December 7, 1979, Bauza grew up watching Looney Tunes and imitating its characters.He later became one of the franchise’s defining modern voices following in the footsteps of legendary voice actor Mel Blanc.Bauza voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tweety, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, and Road Runner, among other characters. He lent his voice to films like Space Jam: A New Legacy, Super Mario Bros., and King Tweeny.
His latest work before his passing was Coyote vs. Acme, which premiered in August 2026. He had voiced Wile E. Coyote in the Dave Green-directed comedy film.

In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza said the appeal of Looney Tunes crossed cultural and language barriers.“Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures,” he said. “It doesn’t matter what part of the planet you’re from. You get the comedy.”Beyond Looney Tunes, Bauza lent his voice to hundreds of projects across film, television, and video games, including The Adventures of Puss in Boots, Teen Titans Go!, Ben 10, and The Super Mario Bros. Movie. His career spanned more than 25 years, with over 400 acting credits.He won three Children’s and Family Emmy Awards between 2022 and 2025 for his voice performance.
@CoyoteACMEMovie pic.twitter.com/H992Ff6tSO— Eric Bauza (@bauzilla) August 24, 2026

In a statement reported by the Hollywood Reporter, Warner Bros. Television Group chair Channing Dungey paid tribute to Bauza, saying he brought “joy and laughter to millions around the world.”“He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc,” Dungey added, honoring Bauza’s 15 years with Warner Bros. animation. – Neo Croox/Rappler.com
Neo Croox is a Rappler intern taking up journalism at the University of Santo Tomas.

articles.title: Lustre denied due process in cyberlibel case -- Fadullon
articles.summary: Prosecutor General Richard Fadullon on Monday said veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was denied due process because he was not given the opportunity to respond to the complaint before an arrest…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 7:02pm

Prosecutor General Richard Fadullon on Monday said veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was denied due process because he was not given the opportunity to respond to the complaint before an arrest warrant was issued against him.

“Apparently, in this particular case, reliance was made on the information provided in the investigation data form saying that he was connected with Philippine Daily Inquirer. That’s why he never received his copy of the complaint,” Fadullon said in an ambush interview.

“That’s why I believe the respondent and the lawyer are claiming that they were not given due process. I would have to agree with them that they were not given due process, as they were not given the opportunity to answer,” he added.
GMA News Online reached out to the Office of the City Prosecutor in Davao City and will update this story once a response is received.
Police officers arrested Lustre in Quezon City on Saturday on the strength of a cyberlibel arrest warrant issued by a court in Davao City.

Lustre’s camp said it was looking into what appeared to be a violation of his right to due process during the preliminary investigation, as he had neither been served nor received a subpoena or notice.
Fadullon said Lustre could file a motion to reopen the preliminary investigation.

Earlier, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said the Department of Justice (DOJ) should investigate claims that Lustre was not served a subpoena. Remulla also alleged that there was a “modus” in which complainants provide incorrect addresses for respondents.

Under existing DOJ circulars, Fadullon said, the prosecutor should have exercised due diligence in verifying the information in the investigation data form, including the respondent’s address and employment details.
He said a proper evaluation would have established that Lustre was no longer connected with the Philippine Daily Inquirer (PDI).
“As I said, if there had been a proper evaluation and the evaluating prosecutor had exercised due diligence, they would have ascertained that this person was no longer connected with PDI,” he said.
Fadullon, however, said he did not believe the error was intentional.

He added that his office could not initiate an investigation into the matter, but Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida could order a motu proprio investigation, or one initiated on the department’s own initiative.
Meanwhile, Fadullon said the complainant could face a perjury charge if an investigation established that the wrong employment information was deliberately provided.

“If it turns out later in the investigation and evaluation that the complainant knew that he was never really connected with PDI but still made it appear that he was, that could become an issue,” he said.
“Remember that the investigation data form is under oath so ( complainant) can be held liable there for perjury,” he added.
Lustre has been temporarily released from detention after posting bail of P48,000.— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
articles.summary: Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to…

blocks.text: The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.
“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”

blocks.caption: Cayni Ali with her child Mandeq at a health centre in Kismayo, Somalia.  Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.
“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”

Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.
The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.

The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.

Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.

blocks.caption: An aerial view of the Juba River, close to the town of Kismayo.  Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: “The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.
Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.
“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.

When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.

Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”

blocks.caption: The aftermath of the 2023 El Niño in Luuq district, Jubaland, which caused the worst floods ever seen in the country.  Photograph: Feisal Omar/Reuters

blocks.text: US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”
Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.

Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”
Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.
“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.

US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.

blocks.caption: Arbey Abdi Famu, a resident of the Dalhiska displacement camp in Kismayo. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.

Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.

His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.

blocks.caption: People on the streets of Kismayo, where long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.   Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.
The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.

Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.
“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.

Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.

Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.
Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.
Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”

Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.
“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”
Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.

blocks.caption: A mother takes her baby to a Somalia Red Crescent Society health centre in Kismayo to check for symptoms of malnutrition.  Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.
Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.
Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.
David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”

blocks.caption: A malnourished three-month-old baby in Kismayo hospital’s intensive-care ward in September. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”
Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.

Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.
Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.
Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”
In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.

Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.
El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.

Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.
Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.

blocks.caption: Fadumo Abdi with her 14-month-old baby, Maryan, in the infant intensive-care unit in Kismayo hospital.  Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.
“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.

Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

articles.title: Bill filed establishing ecozone for Pax Silica ops, other critical industries
articles.summary: The House of Representatives has proposed establishing an Advanced Industries Zone in New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac, saying it will create jobs and attract investments, including those from the…

blocks.text: The House of Representatives has proposed establishing an Advanced Industries Zone in New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac, saying it will create jobs and attract investments, including those from the US-led Pax Silica initiative, which involves developing artificial intelligence (AID) systems, critical minerals, and more.

The National Union Party (NUP), led by House Deputy Speaker Ronnie Puno of Antipolo and Bataan Rep. Albert Garcia, made the proposal under House Bill 11758, or the Advanced Industries Development Act (AIDA).

The bill provides that the Advanced Industries Zone will serve as “the country's national platform for strategic technology, advanced manufacturing, and innovation, under a dedicated authority empowered to attract investment and deliver government services efficiently.”

In return for competitive incentives, the bill states that enterprises or locators in the Advanced Industries Zone must create jobs for Filipinos, train Filipino workers, and transfer skills and know-how, so that Filipinos will not only assemble these technologies but ultimately design, build, and manage them later on.

The lawmakers noted that although the Philippines joined the US-led Pax Silica coalition in April 2026 alongside more than 20 other countries to build secure and resilient supply chains for AI technologies, membership alone would not guarantee investments without a clear, institutionalized legal framework that ensures policy continuity beyond the terms of incumbent public officials.

“The 1987 Constitution commands the State to give priority to science and technology and to pursue the industrialization and full employment of the nation. Today, the global technology supply chain is being redrawn, and the decisions being made now will shape where factories, research centers, and high-paying jobs will be located for a generation. Membership in Pax Silica opens the door, but it does not guarantee that the investments will come to us,” the bill read.

“Investors of this magnitude do not commit on promises alone. They look for clear rules, efficient government, and the assurance that the terms they rely on will not change with every administration. Our communities, in turn, deserve the assurance that growth will respect their rights and benefit their families. Only a law passed by Congress can provide both,” the bill added.
The bill sets a minimum investment of P15 billion per locator or qualified enterprise, exclusive of the value of the land.
The AIDA will have the authority to adjust the foregoing amount to reflect the cumulative change in the Consumer Price Index as published by the Philippine Statistics Authority every five years.
Further, it states that no adjustment will reduce the amount below that first prescribed, and no adjustment will affect a project already registered.

An expansion of the registered project of a qualified enterprise involving an additional investment capital of at least P5 billion exclusive of the value of the land may also be registered as a separate registered project but will only be entitled to limited incentives.
A qualified enterprise shall be entitled to the following incentives:

items: income tax holiday for seven years from the start of commercial operations of the registered project, but not later than three years from the date of its Certificate of Registration

a qualified enterprise can avail of either the Special Corporate Income Tax (SCIT) or the Enhanced Deductions Regime for a period not exceeding 20 years upon expiration of the income tax holiday, provided that the aggregate period of availment under subsections will in no case exceed 20 years from the date of the Certificate of Registration of the registered project

special corporate income tax equivalent to 5 percent of a locator’s gross income earned from the registered project, instead of all national and local taxes, fees, and charges, except real property tax on land, provided, that customs duties and the value-added tax on importation, among others.

blocks.text: Goods brought into the Advance Industries Zone from a foreign country will be subject to customs duties, value-added tax, excise tax, or other national internal revenue taxes upon entry, and will not be deemed imported into the Philippines for so long as they remain within the Zone.

The bill allows such goods to be stored, warehoused, broken up, repacked, assembled, sorted, graded, cleaned, mixed with foreign or domestic goods, processed, manufactured, tested, refurbished, or otherwise manipulated within the Advance Industries Zone without the payment of duties and taxes, and may be exported directly from the Advance Industries Zone free of duties and taxes.
This treatment, however, will only cover goods admitted for storage, processing, manufacturing, testing, research, or use in the operations of a locator or qualified enterprise.

“This is the most meaningful piece of legislation that I think impacts the future of our country that resolves many of the doubts and problems that we face today. If we push this [for passage into law] with all the vigor that we have, we can look forward to a better generation of Filipinos who will live better and be happier,” Puno said.
Garcia said the Philippines has long had the potential of being a manufacturing hub since the first economic zone was established in Mariveles, Bataan in the 70s.
This resurgence, Garcia said, was not sustained due to a lack of permanent policy on such initiatives.

“A lot of big companies, global companies [were] located in Mariveles. There’s Ford, Mattel, which makes Barbie dolls, United Apparel, among others. It created thousands of jobs. In fact, it resulted in migration to Mariveles; that is why we have Ilocano, Bisaya community, even up to now, in Mariveles,” Garcia said.
Likewise, Puno and Camarines Sur Rep. Migz Villafuerte addressed the concerns raised by the indigenous people that the Pax Silica initiative will displace them from their ancestral domain.

“On the matter of the displaced original residents of those areas, we recognize that it's something we have to deal with properly. We recognize that it is a reality that cannot be avoided. And I'm pretty sure that it will get the attention that it deserves. We will stay away from those areas as best we can,” Puno said.
“Hindi tayo mangwawalanghiya ng tao rito,” Puno added. (We will not disrespect the people there.)
Villafuerte said the area of the Advanced Industries Zone will only cover the government’s patrimonial land.
“Only the areas of patrimonial land will be for lease. The ancestral land, those other areas in question, will be under negotiation,” he added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Jordan says its military struck 'militant hideouts' in Syria after deadly church attack
articles.summary: Jordanian armed forces carried out strikes on "militant hideouts" in Syria that it said were linked to a deadly church attack on the kingdom last week. Syria gave a different account.

image.caption: Jordanian security forces arrested three suspects after a dawn shootout earlier on MondayImage: Alaa Al-Sukhni/REUTERS

blocks.text: Jordan said late Monday that its air force has struck military hideouts in southern Syria after determining that suspects linked to last week's deadly church attack were hiding there.
Jordanian forces said the deadly attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church was linked to "terrorist groups" hiding in Syria.
The assault left nine dead and 40 others were injured.
Jordan's armed forces said the strikes on southeastern Syria was carried out in coordination with Damascus.
But Syria gave a different account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks.
A health official told Syria's state news agency that at least five civilians, including women and children, were killed as a result of strikes carried out by Jordan, Reuters reported.
Jordan also arrested three men during a pre-dawn raid on their hideout in the Karak governorate early Monday morning.
Jordanian security forces arrest 3 men in Karak province
Jordanian security forces earlier on Monday morning arrested three men in connection with last week's deadly attack at the church that killed nine people and injured 40 others.

Officials said the arrests took place following a dawn shootout with the armed men who were discovered hiding in an abandoned house in the Karak governorate, located some 120 kilometers (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.
All three suspects were wounded in the operation, but Jordanian security forces reported no casualties.

"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," said Jordanian Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya in a phone interview with state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka on Monday.
"[The suspects] put up fierce resistance but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."

He added that there were "three individuals involved" who were "identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident" and that the security services had "employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."
Jordan's King Abdullah called for 'iron first' response
King Abdullah II of Jordan had ordered authorities to respond with an "iron fist" against anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he added in a statement on Monday, following the arrests, which relatives of the victims had said brought some relief.

"Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief — and the grief of the Jordanian people — not just for us, the families of the martyrs," one relative, himself a survivor of the attack, told Al-Mamlaka.

blocks.caption: King Abdullah II (center) visited victims in hospital and called for Jordanian security forces to respond with an "iron fist."Image: Royal Court of Jordan/Handout/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Who carried out the attack in Jordan?

There has been no claim of responsibility for Friday's deadly attack and Jordan's Public Security Directorate has not named the suspects or publicly ​identified possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.

Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, a relatively stable middle-eastern state which is a close ally of the United States and which maintains diplomatic and military relations with neighboring Israel.

articles.title: [Rappler’s Best] Yes, Marcos still shuffling his Cabinet
articles.summary: Ghosts from the past continue to haunt

blocks.text: Vince Dizon, pulled out from the transportation department a little more than a year ago to head the scandal-ridden Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), is back in his old gig as transportation czar, Malacañang announced on Monday, October 26. He swaps posts with the man who replaced him as transport secretary, Giovanni Lopez, now the new DPWH secretary.

Until his latest transfer, Dizon’s appointment as DPWH secretary had yet to be confirmed by the Commission on Appointments, and this showed in an awkward exchange between him and estranged presidential sister Senator Imee Marcos last month.

Dizon’s transfer also came on the heels of a spat with Senator Panfilo Lacson over the latter’s allegations that he seemed to be covering up for Senator Alan Peter Cayetano, who is being accused by Lacson of having anomalous flood control projects in Taguig. Dizon and Cayetano are longtime allies, having both served under the previous Duterte administration after playing key roles in the strongman’s successful 2016 presidential run.
Indeed, ghosts from the past continue to haunt.

On Saturday, October 24, we were disrupted by the news that a team of Quezon City cops, showing uncanny efficiency, arrested a 72-year-old veteran journalist while he was attending a media forum, over a warrant issued by a judge from Davao City, and in relation to an unknown case filed by an unknown complainant.

Philip Lustre Jr. is known to journalists of my generation as a savvy and prolific political reporter who did the rounds and made waves in his heyday, poking fun at power and unmasking its unholy alliances. For all his acerbic posts on social media especially against the Dutertes, he did not see this coming — a warrant bare in substance and brazen in form.

items: It broke the norm that journalists and newsrooms are used to: when they are charged with libel or cyber libel, they get notified of the complaint and have the right of reply.

Lustre said he was clueless about who filed a cyber libel complaint against him, and what about. That it reached the court meant it already passed the desk of a prosecutor who should have informed him about it.
The arrest warrant, dated October 2, came from Davao City Judge Retrina Fuentes, and this gives room for a reasonable assumption that this had something to do with the Dutertes.

Fuentes is the same judge who issued a warrant in 2022 against public intellectual and former vice presidential candidate Walden Bello, who was also arrested in Quezon City over two counts of cyber libel filed by a longtime aide of Vice President Sara Duterte, Jefry Tupas. Unlike Lustre, Bello knew that a prosecutor had indicted him and that an arrest would follow. He spent the night at a police headquarters and was released the following day after posting bail.

blocks.text: Lustre’s arrest came in the same week that Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte, a brother of the Vice President, filed a cyber libel complaint against executives and staff of media giant, GMA Network, over stories linking him and his sister to bribery. Included in the complaint were National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag and whistleblower Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. Read about Gracioso’s claims here.

Philippine journalists and media organizations have been pushing for the decriminalization of libel and, shortly after the cybercrime law was enacted in 2012, they have moved to declare it unconstitutional.

items: The High Court eventually declared the cybercrime law constitutional, but struck down some controversial provisions.
Still pending for justices to decide on, however, is a petition filed by Bello in 2023, that essentially asked the Tribunal to decriminalize libel.

blocks.text: The criminal aspect means that one who is charged with libel faces arrest and will be freed only after posting bail. To decriminalize libel does not absolve journalists of accountability; it simply turns it into a civil case that will still be litigated on top of the constant hurdles that powerful people in the Philippines throw at them — threats and harassment, reputational attacks, killings, bribery, closed access to information that the public needs to know.

The Philippines remains to be one of the most dangerous places for journalists globally, ranking 114th out of 180 countries and territories. “Despite its extremely dynamic media landscape, the Philippines is one of the most dangerous countries in the world for journalists,” according to the 2026 World Press Freedom Index.
Because in plain truth, beyond the reach of libel are those in power, who are already gifted with all means fair and foul for their so-called grievances.

items: Former president Rodrigo Duterte’s words, for instance, killed. And he’s proven it, as we wrote in this piece.

From 2012, when the cybercrime law was enacted, up to 2022, nearly 4,000 cases were filed in various agencies, with the national police saying that cyber libel makes up 20% of the crimes they investigate. Just imagine the other crimes that need more police attention.

Simply for practical reasons, decriminalizing libel “will free our public prosecutors to allocate their time… to prosecuting criminal cases that affect the national interest and our territorial integrity,” said lawyer Gilbert Andres in this story.

blocks.text: Speaking of territorial integrity: China’s agent-provocateur in Manila, Ambassador Jing Quan, also knows how to weaponize language, as we’ve seen in the past days as he fired volleys of criticism against Philippine officials.
How do we make sense of this gutter talk from the Chinese envoy? Bea Cupin weighs in in this piece.
But still a happy Monday to you! In a dramatic victory, Brazil President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva fended off a rally by far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, winning a historic fourth term.

image.caption: Döllner faces criticism from Germany's IG Metall union over his appearance at the rally, where Trump announced plans for a new Audi factoryImage: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 26, 2026
Audi CEO's Trump rally appearance was with company's 'best interests in mind'

Audi on Monday issued a statement responding to "the current situation," as it coyly referred to the controversy following CEO Gernot Döllner's appearance with Donald Trump at an election rally in Georgia on Saturday.

Audi said that while a delegation was in Georgia for talks on its plans to open a production site in the US, "we were asked to present our plans publicly together with the President of the United States."

"We accepted this invitation solely with Audi's best interests in mind," the company wrote. "At the same time, we acknowledge that the circumstances surrounding the announcement may have been perceived as a political signal. We take this very seriously."

Audi said that it remained "firmly committed" to its values and principles but also said it had a "responsibility" to safeguard the company's economic future and believed these responsibilities went "hand in hand."

The company noted that it was currently not making a profit in the US, the second-largest premium car market on the planet, saying that producing in the country could help it rectify this and help secure Audi's "long-term success."

Despite expressing an intention to "provide context" on the decision and the approach taken, the statement neither named CEO Döllner or US President Trump, mentioned the upcoming US midterm elections, or spoke to the perceived poor judgment in Döllner appearing at a Republican Party campaign rally weeks before the vote.

articles.title: Sudan paramilitary drone strikes cause mass power cuts in eastern states
articles.summary:
Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese army

Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five…

blocks.text: Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.

The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref, and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.
All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has been at war with the RSF, its former ally, since April 2023.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people who are already facing the world’s largest hunger crisis.
Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao, in Gedaref, said the power had been out there since early morning.
“My son is diabetic, his insulin has to be stored in the fridge,” he said over the phone, adding that he was scared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoiled.
“We have no idea when the power will come back,” he said.
Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams.
Sudan’s war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October, drone strikes killed more than 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.
Africa’s third-largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.
The majority of Sudan’s hospitals have been forced to close, at least 8 million children are out of school and swathes of the country cannot access basic services.

Abdelhafez Daafallah, a 54-year-old farmer, said over the phone from Al-Jazira’s Al-Junaid town: “The electricity had just started to improve three months ago, the power station the militia had destroyed was just repaired and we had hope our irrigation pumps would finally start running again.
“We hoped we would be able to finally get back to farming, but now the station has been hit,” he said, frustrated after nearly four years unable to work his land.
Farmers in Al-Jazira have struggled to rehabilitate and replant their land since the army recaptured the state from the RSF last year.
Further east, in Gedaref, Ibrahim Mohammed, 37, a grocer, said he was “already facing power cuts for hours before the strike”.
“Now I have chicken in the fridge, we either lose our entire stock, or will be forced to sell it off at any price, which is still a loss.”
Sudan is also grappling with unprecedented inflation and a currency that lost more than 25% of its value in recent weeks.
